- CONTENTMENT. A labourer toiled at his work one day ; When the sun shone bright and the earth was gay, . And, resting awhile, he ',hewed the land That stretched around him on every hand; He saw the king's palace, its outline dim, Be viewed the king's land till he envied him, And, as round him he gazed, to himself _said he, 1 "If I only had these how happy I'd be:" The monarch proud from his castle tower Viewed his vast domains at the mid-day hour; • Orchard.s and fields in splendour lay, Mountains and valleys in grand array; • He saw his labourers, he watched them all ' From the ancient tower of hik castle tall, And he murmured, as from his seat he rose, ." My kingdom I'd give to be one of those." •. Oft we think as this earth we journey through That God gives us the hardest task to do, But He, who in Providence ruleth all, Bath given a work to great and small, And if we do with our might that work And not from its trials and troubles shirk, • If we patiently wait till the Master come We shall hear his welcome and glad "Well done." ..—Preston, March 10th. ExCElsiOn. A GOLDEN WEDDING. A rainbow span of fifty years, , Painted upon a cloud of tears, In blue for lives and red for fears, Finds end in a golden hour to-day. . Ah ! you to our childhood the legend told, "At the end of the rainbow lies the gold," ' And now in our thrilling hearts we hold The gold that neVer will pass away. : Gold crushed from the quartz of a crystal life, Gold hammered with blows of human strife, Gold burnt in the love of man and wife, Till it is pure as the very flame. Gold that the miser will not have, Gold that is good beyond the grave, Gold that the patient and the brave Amass, neglecting praise and blame. Oh, golden hour that caps the time Since, heart to heart like rhyme to rhyme, You stood and listened to the chime Of inner bells by spirits rung, That tinkled many a secret sweet, Concerning how two souls should meet, I And whispered of time's flying feet With a most piquant silver tongue. ' Oh, golden day, a golden crown ; For the kingly heads that bowed not down To Win a smile or 'scape a frown • Except the smile and frown of Heaven. Dear heads still dark with raven hair, . Dear heads still whitoin spite of care, Dear eyes still black and bright and fair • As any eyes to mortals given. ' • Old parents of a restless race, r You miss full many a bonny face That would have smiled a filial grace, • Around your Golden Wedding wine. 1 But God is good and God is great, , His will be done, if soon or late, Your dead stand happy in you gate And call you blessed while they shine. So drop the tear and dry the eyes, YOur rainbow glitters in the skies. Here's golden wine; young, old, arise With cups as full as our souls, we say: "Two hearts, that wrought with smiles through tears This rainbow span of fifty years, , Behold how true, true love appears True gold for your Golden Wedding day !" POEMS OF SIDNEY LANIER.

TARING THOUGHT von THE FUTURE.—Pretty Cousin: And what do you think of doing after leaving Harrow? —Tommy: Oh, I shall go into the Indian civil Service. —Pretty Cousin: Do you think you'll like India, then?— Tommy: Oh,it's not that. But, you know,in the Indian Civil a fellow's widow gets such* good pension !—Punch. Two young married French ladies were talking about their husbands. Said oneof them, "Do you really think your Jules went shooting yesterday ?" " Well, I don't think he tried to deceive me yesterday; Tam inclined to think he went." "But he didn't bring backany game ?" "That's what makes me feel sure he did go," was the wife's reply. " When he only prebends to go, he always buys a lot of game to bring home with him." "Well, that beats me," exclaimed a sour-looking pas- senger to a subdued sort of a man who sat in the seat in front of him. "Just listen to that woman -across the aisle. If I had a wife like that I %could get a<livorce in two weeks." ." Do you think it would be possible?" "Possible! You bet; Pm a lawyer, and F'd'find a way to do it so quick it would make her head swim." "Do you mean it?" inquired the subdned-looking an earn- estly. " Of.course. But What's that to you ?" '"To me, stranger? Ah, were it nothing! She is my wise?" Sr. DAVID'S Dar.—St. David is the patron saint of Wales, and the first day of March is St. David's Day. Many of the Welsh folk wear the leek on this day. How this custom arose is not exactly known. Some say the leek is worn in memory of a victory over the Saxons, when the Welsh placed it in their hats to mark them out from their enemies. Others say the custom dates from the battle of Agincourt, when the Welsh soldiers of Henry the Fifth wore leeks in their caps. For a long time the Kings of England and their courtiers used to adopt the custom out of compliment to their Welsh subjects. There arc some who hold theopinion that the -practice bad no historical origin, but was due simply to the fact that the leek being the favourite vegetable of Wales, the people wore it -ea their Saint's day.—Little

Folks :Magazine.- NATrneS BaloomErses. animals are very ex- cellent barometers. Among the best are snails, which do not drink, but imbibe moisture during rain, and exude itafterwards. They are never seen abroad except before a rain, and may then be observed climbing the bark of trees and getting on the leaves. Ants, before a storm, will hnrry and scurry, 4rushing here and there. Dogs grow sleepy and dull, and like to lie Ipsore a fire as rain approaches; fowls roll in the dust; .flies sting and bite more viciously; frogs croak louder; gnes assemble under trees, and horses display testlessne,ss- When a 4 swan is seen ffying against the wind, spiders crowding oil a wall, toads coming out of their holes in unusual numbers of an evening, or pigeons gtoing to the dovecot carrier than usual, all these may be put down as rain signs. ,Nearly all animals have some way of telling the weather in advance, due, probably, to some electrical change in the atmosphere which makes them feel un- comfortable or otherwise. "IS IT GOING TO BAIN ?77—The:man who is out of doors at sunrise can form a pretty accurate opinion of . -what the day will be. If just before sunrise the sky— especially in the west—is suffused with red, rain gene- rally follows in the course of the day. In winter, often - snow. If, borverer, it be frosty weather, the downfall is sometimes delayed. On the 4other hand, if the sky be a dull gray, and the sun rises clear, gradually dispersing the vapours, it will be fine. If he retires behind the clouds, and there are reddish streaks about, it will rain. Should the sun, later in the day, Shine through a gray watery haze, it will probably be .a rainy night. The sunset is very, unreliable. Often a beautiful sunset will be followed by a bad day. After a rainy day, suddenly at sunset, in the far west, will appear a magnificent streak of crimson (not copper- colour)—this generally foretells a fine day. A tinted halo round the sun at setting occurs in long-oontinued rainy weather. A "halo round the moon, especially if some distanee fromit, is a sure indication of downfall at hand. Rainbows are unreliable, except they occur in - the morning, when rain may be expected. Sundogs, and fragments of prismatic colours during the day, show i continued unsettled weather. 'A dazzling metallic lustre 1 on foliage, durizwa cloudless day in summer, precedes a change.--CasseMs Family Magazine. A LIBEL ON -"AUNT CHLOE:7—A contemporary has 1 the following is about the way“ itorthwbome a smallantells another how to make a pudding pudding, why, of course, I don't use much flour, and the bigger it's to be, why, the snore flour I take. Sometimes I have to use a great deal of flour, and then'again I can very often get up quite a pudding without having to use very much. You see it depends a good deal on the baking powder. If that's reel good it don't make so -very much difference about the flour, you know." "I suppose you use raisins ?" "Well, now, sometimes I do. and then, sometimes I don't. It depends altogether on whether I want it very rich or not, and what kind of sauce I am going to use. Of course, the richer I want it the more raisins I put in; but if the sauce is to be very rich, you must be very =dui about the pudding, or you will be sure to get it too much so. The best way is to make your pudding first and then fix your sauce to naitch it." "How much sugar do you take?' "Well, now, some folks take a, good deal and some folks don't. As for me, I never did like to have anything too sweet, and for that reason I'm always, careful not to get in too much sugar. After you've made it once or twice you won't have a particle of trouble in getting it just to suit you." " How many eggs do you use?" "Web], now, that's the beauty of it. With this kind of a pudding it does not make so very much difference how many you take. If you've got plenty of eggs, and you're going to make a big pudding, why you can put in several; . won't hurt; but if eggs are scarce, you can get along with one or two just as well, and nobody will ever notice the ' difference." "Do you mix your dough with milk?" Well, now, sometimes I do, but it's not Si) very parti- cular about that. If you've got plenty of milk, and don't need it for anything else, it won't hurt to use it, - but if you haven't, why, don't do it. If you get every- thing else right, it won't matter about the milk at all." • "How about spices?" "Use 'ern if you want to. Some folks likes 'em, and I think myself they rather help a pudding sometimes, especially if you use plain sauce. But you must follow your own taste about that, and if you don't get it right the first time dezet blame me, for I've done my very best to tell you just exactly how to do it and all about it." • KArs ComPOHND, a deUlUleer,t anodyne expectorant. for Coughs and Colds. bold by all Chemists, 94c1, Is, Is lid, 2a 9d.-4drt.

A SMART LITTLE BOT.—A city toiler and his son met a sturdy farmer in the country, whereupon the toiler remarked, "That's a fine field of oats you. have there." "Don't you know the difference between oats and wheat ?" asked the sturdy farmer contemptuously. "No, I don't." "I thought every donkey knew that," exclaimed the rustic. "You see father," said the toiler's little boy, who had not taken any part in the debate, "if every donkey knows the difference, it's lucky you said you didn't." Those who, having recovered from the Byronic fever of youth, now run to-the other extreme of Byronic dis- like, will enjoy this—" When Lord Byron published his sentimental Farewell,' after his separation from his wife, the matter was the subject of, much after-dinner com- ment. Currati's opinion was once appealed to. I pro- test,' said he, do not understand this kind of whim- pering. Here is a man who first weeps over his wife and then wipes his eye., with the public.' How TO Plea A HUSBAND.—Chooge a busy man for a • husband, one who has plenty to occupy his mind and to talk about. It is the man with many interests, with engrossing occupations, with plenty of people to fight, with a struggle to maintain against the world, who is the really domestic man, in the wife's sense; who enjoys home, who is tempted to make a friend of his wife, who relishes prattle, who feels in the home circle, where no- body is above him, as if he was in a haven of ease and relaxation. The drawback of home life, its containing ,possibilities of insipidity, sameness, and consequent weariness, is never present to such a man.THe no more tires of his wife and children than of his own happier moods. He is no more bored with home than with sleep. All the monotony and weariness of life he encounters out- side. his the pleasure-loving man,,the merry companion, who requires constant excitement, that finds home life unendurable. He soon grows weary of it, and considers everything so tame that it is impossible for him to be happy or not to feel that he is less unhappy there than elsewhere. FROM SERGEANT TO KlNG.—Among the captured in this sortie was a handsome young sergeant of the French marines, whose appearance and manner attracted the notice of Colonel Wagenheim, of our 15th Hanoverian Regiment, who took him to his tent, had his wounds dressed, and treated him with much kindness, for though but a sergeant, he- seemed much above his station, having been bred to the law, yet his parents were humble people of Pau. Long years after, when the army of France in its great career of conquest entered Hanover under Marshal Bernadotte, his levee- was attended by Wagen- heim, then an aged general officer, "You have served, I understand, in India ?" said Bernadotte. "Yes." "At Cuddalore?", "Yes" "Do you remember taking a wounded French sergeant there 'under your protection?" After a time the veteran called the episode to memory, adding, "He was a fine young man ,and I should be glad to hear of his welfare:" "I was that young French ser- geant," replied the Marshal, "and now will omit no means of testifying my gratitude." And old Wagon- beim lived to see the marine he had protected Prince and Marshal of the Empire. Prince of Ponta Corvo, Crown Prince of Sweden, and finally Charles John XIV., King of Sweden and Norway.7—Cassell's Illustrated History of India.

A SUNDAY SCHOOL TEACHER'S BEST METHOD.—The putting of Gospel truths into dry words (though without any severity of carriage) is a sore injury to the person- ages of scripture. They find no entrance when made to approach a child in dreary procession. There is no, witnessing to Christ in many a string of the most con- vincing statements. The invisible armour in which a Sunday scholar can clothe himself against them when they present themselves in decorous file is simply im- penetrable, and the best intentioned teacher retires baffled from the attempt to make his testimony tell. The magic of the parable is wanted to open the closed doors. And then another mode of our Lord's doctrine may well be used to bring the child closer within the atmosphere which breathes a knowledge of the Christian life. I refer to the frequency with Which Jesus " questioned " His disciples. If the 'teacher stands at a distance, as it were, and discharges the most salutary truths upon his scholar, the invisible armour of which I have spoken is quickly put on; but when an appeal comes to the scholar's own experience and consciousness he is disarmed. The weak- est is best won, not by taking advantage of his weakness, but by that addition to his power which comes of an appeal to his intelligence and feelings.—" The Quiver" for March. "As OTHERS SEE Us."—There is something interest- ing in the stories of kings in the olden times, disguising themselves and mingling in easy intercourse with their people, from the desire to see things as they really were, and not in the light in which they were apt to be pre- sented to them. The Scotch jameses were said to be fond of -this, and the disguise of Fitz-James, in the "Lady of the Lake" s a case in point. These were not the days of daily newspapers, nor had Royal Commissions, to inquire' into everything begun to be thought of: Humbler men than kings, and in days more recent, have been known to follow the example. It is recorded of Thomas Campbell, the poet, that once, being in a remote part of Scotland, he made an effort to find out whether the fame of his poetry had travelled so far. It happend that a plain woman, with whom he came into contact, had been greatly interested in another member of the clan, John Campbell, of Sings- land Chapel, who had recently astonished the world by his exten.sivetravels in South Africa, having visited Lat- takoo, and other remote missionary settlements. When the poet .asked her if she had ever heard of Mr. Campbell •and his bookasshe replied with an emphatic yes. "Then," said the poet, greatly pleased, "I am Mr. Campbell."— " What,' asked the woman, in delight," and are you really the great Mr. Campbell?" The poet was framing a modest answer,when she burstonhim with some ques- tion about Lattakoo. The spell was broken' and the vision of delight vanished. Whether the poet had ever 'heard of Lattakoo may be doubted, but he knew at least that he was not "the great Mr. Campell.--The Rev Dr. Iltaikie in "The Quiver." ON FAT Grims.—Now of fat girls there are several varieties. There is your ft baby-girl, a delightful little dumpling of a child, every one of whose dimples is a mine of delight, and every one of the creases in whose rosy limbs inspires you with an irresistible propensity to tickle it. These are the little baby-children that Rubens painted so gloriously. He made their little puffed-out cheeks celestially roseate; he curled their flaxen locks like unto the young tendrils of the vine; he tipped their little heels and elbows with rich carnations; he took away their sex, and made them epicene; and when he had added little wings of green and golden plumage to their shoulders, they were no longer baby- children, but angels, ministering in the apotheoSes of kings and emperors, who, I siticerelY trust, have reached the destination which the courtly pencil of Peter Paul ascribed to their dead majesties. Then there is your fat school-girl, long fair ringlets, profuse as a Louis-Quatorze perruque with fixed blue eyes that remind you unplea- santly of the Pantheon Bazaar and Madame Montanari's wax-work shop, and with a dull, listless fixity of de- meanour that makes one always wish to find out where- abouts the string is, in order to pull it, and cause the eyes to move and the great doll to squeak " pa-pa " and "ma-ma." Yet another variety of the fat school-girl is there in the romp, or "tom-boy," who has cheeks as ruddy and as hard as a Ribstone pippin; who is con- tinually grazing the skin off her arms, and tearing the trimming off the ends of her trousers ; who, if she lives in the country, is in the habit of catching young colts, and riding them without saddle or bridle round pad- docks; who is always getting into domestic trouble through her transactions with a big black dog fond of the water and of chivying cats; who is always laughing, has a tremendous appetite, and once fought with a boy and came off victorious. The uecline of the: old- fashioned system of education, and the rise of seminaries and collegiate institutions, where young ladies attend lectures on the Od force and the Therapeutic Cosmogony of Ancient Art, has made the tom-boy fat girl an ex- ceedingly rare specimen of femininity; but she is still occasionally to be met with—notably in Westmoreland boarding-schools, and in farm-houses of the west. I la- ment the progressive extinction of the merry fat girL She usually grew up ta be a jolly, comfortable matron, with a tribe of sunny children, all as great roinps,as she had been. Her pickled walnuts were perfection. She was one of those admirable women who always give you something to eat when you call upon them, and if you are neither hungered nor athirst, insist upon you carrying away a pot of preserves or a slice of bride-cake with you. It was in the golden age, and England was merry England indeed, when those fat matrons who had been fat girls flourished. They used to entertain you at "meat teas "—bounteous repasts, where there were sausages and pressed beef, soused mackerel, and potato- cakes.—G.S.A.

Mr. Alston, Crosslee, Selkirkshire, has just sold two Clydesdale stallions for exportation to America. The one is the four-year-old "Jumbo," which trivgllea-two season in Peeblesshire; and the other "Poete winner:of

the first prize at West Kilbride, West Linton, and Gala- • shiels. , We hear Mr. W. Tait, on behalf other Vajesty the' Queen, has hired from Mr. T. H. Hutchinson, Manor House, Catterick, his two-year-old Shorthorn bull Royal Leopold, for use in the herd at the Prince Consort's Shaw Farm, Windsor. Mr. Tait has also purchased for her Majesty from the Catterick herd a very handsome bull-calf, by Riby Star, dam Lady Grey, calved January 3rd, 1886. This youngster is own brother to Lady Golightly and Lord Gordon. Do BEES. BREHM IN WINTER P—An American bee- keeper states that, late in November, he superseded a black queen in a good stock, giving it an Italian queen of his own rearing in exchange. At the time of her in- troduction there was no brood in the hive. He placed the swarm in the cellar with others. His cellar was kept .at an average temperature of 35 deg. The following spring, on setting out the bees upon the summer stands, this hive, with the Italian queen introduced to black bees in November, *was found to have fully one-third of its be pure Italians. _

SWINE. FEVER.—Mr. Heath, M-R.C.V.S., Exeter, has drawn attention to the probability of swine fever being spread by rats. Ho narrates a case in which the carcase of a diseased pig was left for a short time, and, while yet warm, was attacked and partly eaten by rats. Re- course was had to the poisoning of them with strych- nine and sugar mixed with some barley meal, on which the pigs were fed. On the following day eleven large- sized rats were picked up dead, and he adds that doubt- less many were killed in their runs. He adds rats are well known to travel long distances in search of food, and might doubtless in this way carry the infection to other pigs in the neighbourhood. COWS EATING EtEA.THER.—QUERY.—" W. T." writes: —Please say if the encolsed heath is injurious to cows, especially those in milk and calf, as mine get into the forest and eat it greedily. lam told the cow will not breed; is this the case ?—We have never known cows to directly injure themselves by eating heather; but, at the same time, it is not very nutritious food, and would need to be supplemented by cake or meal at home. It is conceivable that a cow might gorge herself with the highly-indigestible fibre of even the young shoots; but the number of milk cows of all breeds in and about Epp- ing Forest proves that owners find no great harm result- ing. If a bull and heifer are dropped at one birth, the latter is almost certain to be a "free-martin," and be barren if reared to maturity. You had better rear it for beef alone, or sell as a fat calf. THE STATE OF FARMING IN SCOTLAND.—An appeal to the Pritte Minister is being signed extensively by farmers throughout Scotland. The appeal sets forth the great depreciation that has taken place in the value of farm produce, including live stock, and complains that, while some landlords have honourably taken into considera- tion their tenant's losses and reduced, their rents, others have refused to allow any reduction. Resolutions passed by several agricultural bodies in different parts of Scot- land, asking that tenants under leases existing before November, 1881, should have the option of a revaluation of rent or liberty to leave their farms after a year's notice, with compensation for their improvements and all the privileges of way-going tenants, are also referred to, and imthediate legislation is requested. SIR JOHN LAWES AND PROFESSOR GILBERT ON EN- siLA.GE.—The result of their first year's experiments on ensilage has certainly not been such as to make Sir John Lawes and Professor Gilbert ardent enthusiasts on the subject. Sometimes they speak guardedly, as when they say that so far as the yield of milk is concerned, the evidence is not adverse to the silage, when used in mode- rate quantity, according to the amount of solid and digestible matter it contains. They conclude as follows: —"There can be no doubt that good food may be pre- served in a favourable state for future use by being properly. ensilaged. But the results obtained at Rotham- sted do not favour the idea that produce which is itself j not good food can be made good food by being ensilaged. Good ensilage, given in such amount as to supply the same quantity of dry substance as would be given in chaff and roots, is no doubt a very good food for fatten- ing oxen. Good ensilage, giien in less proportion and in conjunctipn with roots, with the ordinary dry foods in addition, is no doubt a very good food for milking cows."

Hoosg.—" Perplexed" says :—" Can you inform me whether or not the worms which cause “ hoose " in lambs and calves breed in the windpipe and lungs, or are the worms found in these situations only in exact proportion to the number of eggs or germs picked up by the ani- mals? I am anxious to know, as I have been a great sufferer by this complaint among my young stock' I believe authorities are undecided; but from my own ex- perience I am inclined to think that the worms do breed within the hangs of their hosts; so that in two, three, or more months we may find a considerable quantity of worms in excess of the number of germs actually intro- duced into the system from without. I have arrived at this conclusion from the fact that it sometimes happens an outbreak of "lioose " of a slight character will linger among a flock or herd, and then, after the lapse of weeks, or even months, assume a severe form, although the animals have had no opportunity of procuring fresh germs during that time; and I take it that the increased severity of the complaint is caused by the worms which were first introduced reproducing their kind while exist- ing within the windpipe, lungs, or bronchial tub's. I think the question asked by " Perplexed " is one lequir- ing investigation and worthy our attentian. THE WRATIIIIR AND FARMING OPERATIONS.—The editor of the Mark Lane Express writes :—" The tremendous snowstorm which set in with the beginning of last week will long' be remembered as one of the most disas- trous which has ever vitited the United Kingdom. More trains were snowed up, probably, than on any occasion within the memory of any living man; and, what is worse, cattle and sheep in considerable numbers, in Scotland and the north of England, are reported to have been killed. The continuance of .winter at a time when the comparatively genial 'weather of spring should be with us is a great misfortune. The time has come not only when beans had peas should be sown, but when preparations for sewing barley and oats should be well advanced. In the south and east of Faagland the pulse crops had been partly put in before 'the snow came; but .scarcely a beginning has been made with the sowing of the sprmg cereals. The land, after so much frost, would work splendidly if we could only get fine weather, and sowing would be carried on with a minimum: of labour: but where the depth of snow was greatest its melting , will have made the land so wet that some days of drying sunshine or wind will be necessary to bring the surface of thsoil into working order. It is not only on account of the delay in sewing, however, that the prolongation of winter is to be regretted. The wheats need a milder temperature to enable them to make a start in growth after the long trial to which their vitality has been sub- jected. In some eases,, where they were sown in De- -1 cember, it is reported that they are not up a full plant yet, and it is doubtful if they ever will be. Certainly, if they are kept much pnger from emerging from the soil their chance of covering the ground-will be a very poor one. Winter beans have stood the winter remark- ably well, but such frosty winds as prevailed in the early part of last week are bad for them, and thdy will be stunted in growth if they do not boon get a chance of making progress. Most important of all is the need of genial weather for the pastures and cultivated fodder crops. The scanty stock of roots, economised as it has been by the use of cheap feeding stuffs, is nearly ex- hausted on most farms, and stockkeepers will be short of succulent food for their cattle and sheep if grass and other green crops do not soon begin to grow. It is to be hoped that when spring does come it will, as our American cousins put it, 'come to stay,' and that, having had a continuously severe winter, we shall be re- warded by what is sometimes termed an 'old-fashioned spring.'" MILKLNG AND GENERAL MANAGEMENT.—Continuing his lectures on milking and general *Management, Mr. Primrose M'Connell says :—" Cows ought to receive the greatest amount of quiet and gentle treatment possible. Every movement of the limbs, in addition to the ordi- nary processes of life, is equivalent to a loss in the wear and tear of tissue, and it follows, therefore, that the less exercise or motion the cow is compelled to undergo— making due allowance for the preservation of health— the better able will she be to utilise her food for milking purposes. The pastures ought to be as near to the cow- sheds as possible, so that she may have the minimum amount of walking, and thus be less likely to be hurried or harassed by careless attendants. A cow with a full milk vessel is quite unable to move quickly, so that it is an unpardonable offence to hound a dog at her. For this reason the irritation and worry induced by hot weather and flies is also a very greit source of loss in milk production, and therefore the animals ought to be put indoors during the 'hottest part of the dayiin sum- mer time, and get some forage, such as tares. We have known a herd of sixty cows to have a sudden drop of twenty gallons of milk on a hot day from the tormenting of flies alone. The parasitical warble fly is another great source of loss, the irritation caused by the grub under the skin being excessively injurious to the yield of the animals. One writer estimates the loss at about two and a half millions of money per annum, but this is most likely overdrawn. Miss Ormerod has done good work in calling attended to the ways and means of dealing with this pest, and there is every reason to believe that joint action on the part of farmers would exterminate it. Exposure is a matter the bad effects of which many farmers do not seem to be sufficiently aware of. Cows are not only kept outside during the daytime in winter, but even through- out the night by some masters, and yet they expect them to milk on this sort of treatment. There has-been a very great change made this yeat in the arrangements Of the show annually held in the Palais de L'lndustris,,Paris. Hitherto the show has been held all together, but in consequence of- the growth in the number cf exhibits in all sections, and the introduction of new features in the cattle section; a division was
.made and virtually two shows, though the poultry have been split up to suit the requirements of the larger stock. Thus the division has not :beat so satisfactory to the

poultry and,pigeon exhibitors, for they have been com- pelled to remain a much longer period at the show than before, without any corresponding advantage. The first portion of the exhibition was, opened -to the public on Feb. 20th and closedron , Feb, 23rd, comprising turkeys, geese,•citicksfpigedne, and rabbits: The second portion opened on Feb. 27th and closed on March 3rd. This 'em- braced all the other sections of poultry and the dead'l fowls-which are so remarkable a feature of this exhibi- tion, and which we can say are without a single rival. We have in previous 'years fully described the arrange; ments of this show, and it is unnecessary to repeat them again, as they arelust the same as before with the. ex ception of the change already noted. There has been a large advance in numbers and the show is growing very rapidly, as the following fignres will show : . 1884. . 1885: 1886. Poultry Pigeons Rabbits Totals 1,420 2,052 2,526 . It is impossible in a short article to give anything like a complete account of the show, and we must therefore content ourselves with noting just a few of the general features. _There is always one great prize given every year called the Prix d'Honnewx. This is awarded to What the judges regard as the best lot of fowls in the exhibition. Two of these pave been offered this year, one for each part of the show. The one was won by a very grand lot of black turkeys,, owned by M. Courtin, the great French breeder of turkeys. These Were large and well formed:. The other was won by M. Lemoine with Houdans. These were also good. For the reception :of these winning birds, a grand pavilion was erected in the centre of the Palace. This was elaboratein its velvet hangings, and quite fit for the accommodation of a prince. The turkeys as a whole were very' good indeed, and there were some specimens which would have taken high honours at Birmingham. We were much pleased with' the specimens of bnff, or Chamois, and the red turkeys' eihibited. The geese were not np:lai the mark, and -there have been better exhibitions at Paris. before. Still these classes were interesting in that these are varieties which are seldom seen except on the Continent. The variety called Du Danube look very peculiar. They, are white in plumage, and are entirely frizzled. The size is small, but the specimens here exhibited Were very good in colour and shape. We never saw any of these before last year, when there' were a lot at this show. Another lot were called D'Alencon. These, but for their colour, which is red, appear very much of the Toulouse type, but there is more white in the plumage. Ducks were not so good as last year,-when, it will be remem- bered, Rouens won the Prix d'Honneur. The failing in this breed was in colour, which might be considerably amproved. Aylesburys were fair. in quality, and there were some very decent Pekins. The collection of fancy ducks was a miserable one, at which we were much sur- prised for ,within a couple of miles, at theJardin D'Ac- climation, there is one of the best collections'of fancy ducks that we Wive ever seen. The way in which the show is managed induces a large number of entries, and also causes a very. great,diversity in ..he quality of the stock. No charge is made for the entrance of specimens or for the provision of the, eages, and as the exhibitors are permitted to vend thbir fowls in, the show, it is sim- ply a market which is fully made use of. The pens are decorated by the cards of the owners' and visitors are being constantly importuned to buy. Thus, whilstthere maybe many good 'birds in a- class, evidently serious competitors for the prizes, there are large numbers of others which are sent for sale. This does not, certainly, conduce to a high average quality in the classes. • The section for 'French breeds contained many first- class, specimens: Both the lots of Crevecoeurs were very good indeed and most numerous; about 200 birds in all. It is a pity that this valuable race of fowls doss not rind more favour out of France. It is generally regarded as delicate, but there are those who have found it able to withstand even a cold, clay soil. For quality and quantity of flesh it cannot be surpassed. MM. Lemoine and Farcy were the principal winners. We are glad to see that the size is maintained—an important point in a table fowl. Houdans were on the whole better than last year, when there was a decided falling off in size. As already stated, the Prix d'Honneur was won by this variety. There were nearly 400 Houdans in the two classes. As a rule, the French Houdans are much lighter than the English, for there is little doubt that the latter have a lot of Creve blood in them. One French writer Makes the two into different varieties. But at the show this year there were quite a number of birds shown in the Houdan classes which were more like the English than the French type, namely, darker in plumage and larger in crest. This we think a mistake, and our pre- ference is strongly in favour of the French type. Up- wards of 200 La Fleche made a very grand show, and the quality- was very good, indeed. Size and shape are very carefully sought for by the breeders, and the constant teat imposed by the marketing of the fowls compels attention, to the economic qualities. The weight attained by these birds is very remarkable, and the way in which they fatten mark them as one of the most suitable breeds for the table. The Dumans were hardly 'so good as we have seen them at the Paris Show, but the La Bresse came out very well indeed. Both these breeds are more useful than ornamental. There was a capital lot of La Barbezieux, which have been oalledthe Minorca of France, and is undoubtedly very nearly allied to that valuable breed. All the other varieties of native f0w1.4 were put into the omnivorous last classes, wherein Courtes-Pattes took all the prizes. The specimens of this 'useful but somewhat peculiar-looking breed were 'very good, and well deserved the position assigned to them. There were several kinds of fowls in this class which can only be seen in France, and some of them are evidently, sports from the standard varieties, especially the Hou- dans. The Du Mantes have Houdan plumage with a heavy tail, clean white legs, and only four toes. The De Gournay are strongly built, single combed, non-crested birds, with Houdan plumage, and only four toes. There is also a variety called De La Savoie, which seem very similar to the De Gournay, except that they are smaller. The Glissades are very like the Courtes-Pattas, but are longer in the leg and somewhat lighter in build. They are also entirely black in the plumage. A variety evi- dently allied to the latter are the De La Tozere, the only difference being that they have white legs. The De Banassac are large birds of the Wyandotte plumage and shape, but have dark tails, slightly feathered white legs, and no combs. Cosaquei aro smallish black-whiskered fowls, something like the Cussades. Amongst what are foreign breeds in France, the Cochins are the most popular, and of these there were nearly 500 specimens at the show. All ,varieties were represented, and there were some very good birds, but not a4y that would stand a chance with the best at our English exhibitions. The buffs were decidedly the best. The Brahmas were not nearly so numerous, but on the whole the quality was higher. The lights were the more inunseroui, but the darks rather better in merit. Dork- ings were a gokl lot, and _this_ valnable breed is rapidly making its way in France.. The table qualities for which it is noted are sure to win it favour. Strange to say, only the silver-grays are to be seen'. • Spanish were poor, but Polish very good indeed, numbering quite 500 birds. Here were all varieties, the Chamois being the best. Lang- shans came out well, and the specimens were very pure in type, In France this breed has from its first intro- duction wort its way very well indeed. The variety class for the larger breeds contained almost every kind that have not already been named. There were a few decent Leghorns, some moderate Plymouth Rocks, a lot of Ham- burgs, one moderate pen of Dominiques, and several 'pens of fair Yokohamas. The Bantam class was a very large one, and there were some good and novel birds in it. The Japanese shown by M. Lemoine were especially fine, and a few pens of silky Japanese entirely new. This dead poultry, &e., will be dealt with next week.

General Boulanger has signed a decree authorising French officers and soldiers of all,arros and in al i regiments to wear their beards. This wilt enable the persons to whom it ap- plies to economise about £130,000 sterling annually which is spent in the barber's shop. THE MURDER BY A MADMAN NEAR DERBY.—Mr. W. H. Whin held an inquest on Saturday at Quarndon, near Derby, upon the body of Mary Ann Morrell, aged 44, Who was murdered on Thursday morning by her cousin, a farm labourer, named William Wagstaff, whose son. ill of brain fever, she bad gone to nurse. At the lock-up he had another violent attack, and it took seven men to hold him. In the course of the attack he again admitted his guilt, and burst out singing Salvation Army songs. The coroner told the jury that it was not for them to inquire into the state of • Wagstaff's mind, and they thereupon nAurned a verdict of wilful murder against him, and the coroner issued his war- rant committing him for trial at the next assizes. COTTAGE 4.11,D . . ~ 4 , , Contrary to exnectation, the .sm still remitins, and yo the operations ot wing and planti' are nekmore likely ,-) -be perform now than theYvere a month ago. .;‘,iough disapp nted, we are not disheartened, endive' ,eel sure the wintry elements have been doing great and needed work in the economy of Nature by pulverising and sweetening the soil, and so preparing a wholesome suitable seed bed. Though our operations are delayed, we are still hopeful. The sun's rays assert their influence more and more daily, giving assurance that eeed time and bar- vest shall not fail. Few can reabirect vegetation in such a backward state, - The fruit birds are ai quiescent' as they were at Christmas, which augurs well for a bounti- ful fruit year. Cauliflowers; Those sown in August and only partially protected, have; we fear, perished, but those under frames will be safe. Those who. have lost their all should sow a few Early London ins box and place them in the greenhouse or frame, and with careful attention they will, be reedy to prick out by the time the ground is in a fit state to receive any seed. Lettuce have also a distressing appearance, and early plants will , be very scarce. We would therefore advise that a box of Giant Cos (Alexandra) be sown, and treated similarly to the cauliflowers. If the boxes are Placed in frames it will be as well to stand them on bricks to' save the bot- tom from. decay, as well a.sproviding some security from slugs. THE FRONT GARDEN..—As soon as the frost goes, it will be necessary to look over all small plants, as well as all planted in auttimn, and, if they have been disturbed' by the frost, they should be pressed down with both hands, and not by the foot. Cuttings of violas and pansies, even when covered by a frame, are invariably disturbed by less frost, then 20 degrees, which wait registered on the morning of the 7th in different places round Preston. If the euttings have net formed' roots, it, would be more expeditious to take them up, place each sort in a flower pot, and then beat the soil gently with the back id the spade, and proceed with the planting at once. Rase cut- tings cannot be made too firm. We press them with the feet by walking with a kind of shuffle between the rows, snd close up to the cuttings. Tim WlNDOW.—Fuchsias that may have been stored, in cupboards or cellars should be brought into the light and prunecl,to their proper shape, if that has not been, already done. As a rule, two or three joints are sufficient to leave of,last year's wood. When these have pushed out shoots halt an inch long, turn the- plant out of the pot and shake most of the soil away from the roots, and the strongest of these should be moved with a sharp kßife. From these shortened roots numerous fibres will issue, which are of far more service than the thick woodyenes. 'Prepare some clean, pots of the sama size as those the plants previously occupied by placing 'an. oyster shelf over the hole, and over this .some crocks the size of a niodorate-sized bean to the depth of an inch in a 3in. pot, and 2in. for a 6in. Over these place some half-decayed leaves or the largegt pieces of turf out of the potting compost, and so prevent the small particles of soil washing down amongst 'the crocks and obstruct, ing the free egress of water. The soil suitable for grow- ing fuchsias should be, rich and light, i.e. if • a handful is taken up it should not feel half the weight of the same bulk of ordinary soil.. The weight of the soil will, in h. measure, depend on the moisure it contains, and here we must apply another simple test. Take a handful of the soil and press it. If its particles adhere, it evidently retains too much wet, and rather than use it we would prefer waiting a few days for it to dry,. or else hold it on a shovel over the fire. Some of our readers may smile: at this, and will be ready to ask what good will the soil be after baking? Now, a compost that has loam for its chief ingredient contains more or less clay, which is so adhesive that air cannot get into it nor water out of it, and the roots cannot penetrate into it in its natural I state. Burning gives the soil a new character. Its tex- ture is changed,- and the particles of clay lose their ad- - hesiveness, and the viscid mass crumbles readily when taken up in the hand. : Such is the value we attach to it in its altered state that we would undertake to grow:first class fuchsias, and many other good things, in a mixture :composed chiefly of burnt clay. This, however, is not always available, and we have to fall back on three-parts loam, one leaf mould and about one-eighth of coarse sand, and to every gallon of this add a handful of bone meal or Clay's fertiliser. In potting, care should be taken to'work the soil well in amongst the roots. Do not huddle them together, and make sure that they are not •in contact with the side of the pot, where a portion of their surface would be deprived of soil. Give sufficient water to settle the soil round the roots, .and allow, the soil to get moderately dry before any more is given.' The plants will be benefited by an occasional sprinkling over- head in the afternoon of fine days.

div.p: WEDDING PRESENTS.

A young gentleman friend of ours who had " been invited to a wedding party, thought it his duty, as •it , was his pleasure, to make the bride a present. What to buy and what would be suitable for the occasion were difficulties which presented themselves as soon as he had made up his mind to the necessity of doing something to mark his respect for the young couple at whose execu—we beg pardon—at whose marriage llamas going to assist. "Look here, Chicev, old boy," said he, as be entered Foster and Co's Pleasant-street store, "I want to 'buy a wedding present, and I Want you to tell me what you tbirik would be the proper caper. I've had no experience in tbese things and am as much at sea as you would be in bossing A missionary meting." "Well,'! replied " Chacey," taking in the situation at a glance and scenting a customer. "Well, old fellow, the correct thing the lady is a lady whom you respect and to whom. you would like to show that you are comme ii faid, and were not brought up by contraCt in a wood- shed—a pair of diamond drops, a gold watch,' or a silvertea and coffee service. Something neat and good, and indi- cating, your own good taste, and at the same time flattering to her vanity. Now, for 225 dollars, I've a very handsome pair of diamond drops of the purest water and—" •

"Sacred socks" broke in the young fe?low. "What in Hades are you gassing about? Think I've been robbing a bank or coming into a fortune? Have you been having a sunstroke this morning? Do you know who I am? Have you forgotten that I'm only a clerk, on a low salary, and that I have my own board bill to pay, and my tailor to keep quiet, oat of my wages? And you talk to me about diamond drops and gold watches, just as if I could ever pay the interest on such things if I happened to have them hi pawn. Give us a rest, Chacey,' and tell me what I can cover with a V.'"

Ultimately he eeleete4 a plated cruet stand and had it folded up. " You are sure there'll be nothing like this in the col- lection of presents ? I don't want to take a gift that there is anything like in the lot she has already got, and I am told she has had a whole bazaar of nice things sent in. I want mine to be unique and different from the other things. I should hate to do the same as when Sammy Billpet was married and his friends presented him with twenty-seven tidies, sixteen mirrors, and sixty-four table lamps. There was too much confounded monotony in the presents to be pleasant and the bride cried for a week after she had seen the collection, and Sammy went off on a howling drunk." " Chacey " assured him that cruet stands were rarely if ever found among wedding presents, and that, even if they were he would take a solemn three story affidavit that there worth not be one anything like the one just folded up, be- cause it was the first one out of a fresh importation which had only just come over from Paris, and which were being almost given away, in order to introduce a new style into the market.

This satisfied the young man, and he started off to de- liver his present. The same evening he came back again bringing the cruet stand with him. "Look here, Chaney," said he, " didn't you tell me that this was the only cruet sund of the pat- tern you had sold?" "I did," replied the smiling Chaney. "Of course I did."

"Then how in thunder does it happen that when I took this infernal thing to the bride's house I found that she had already got three of the very same pattern of stands, and all bought here, and that so far from cruet stands being unusual gifts, the young lady n thedei-had heightalrad oygf he seas to" as would equip a sea-side hotel A smile of placid and soulful satiefaction rippled over the face of the innocent " Checer " as he explained that the clerks must have sold the stands while he was out in the morning whea he went to pay his pew rent. He would, however, change it for something else. " How would a very elegant set of pic'sle i harse diinad not ink thatrtehesilyers he Youngttandclo? The young man said lady was suffering from too much silver filigree, and he would try it. He did so. "It won't do, Chacey,' said he, the following morning as he again turned up in the store with the pickle set in 'his hand. "She has already one for each day in the week with a spare one or two for Sundays, and I guess we shall have to try something else. How would a Saratoga trunk, or a box of dominoes, or a bicycle do ?" But " Chasey " frowned dowe all these suggestions as being inappropriate, and at last hit upon a handsome mantel clock as just the thing to fill the bill. But the clock came back as the other things had done. "Would you believe it, Chacey, the has already thirteen mantel clocks ticking away in the place, and she said that, if anybody brought any more, she'd need to hire a boy to keep 'em woutici up. We've got to hit upon something else even if I've to make the 'flyer' into a termer'. I cannot afford to be frozen out now." 16 chatey " at last found him the very thing he was hungering for. It was a pretty and elegant butter dish, in silver mountings, and had a nice and cunningly-devised space for holding a chunk of ice, so as to keep the oleomar- garine solid and substantial in melting moments. We had this article sent in as a sample from the maker," slid Chaeea% "It was the only one he had, and we did not offer it for sale, because I thought it was too costly to snit our trade. However, as you have been so much disappointed, I'll let you have it at manufacturer's figures,-and stand you a cigar for luck to the bargain." The young man carried his prize down to the young lady's home, and made his preeentation in due form. "j am very much obliged to you indeed, Mr.—" said the young lady, as she looked at her elegant present, with eyes sparkling with pleasure. "It will just match the other one which Mr. and Mrs. Blank sent in a short time ago. And don't you see how nice it will be when John and I are married. We shall both have our own batter cooler—

two souls with bnt a single thought, two hearts with each its awn pat of butter." And so it was. Toe exact fae simile of his present was shown to him. "I'm very sorry, Miss - that I should be so unfor- tunate in my choice, bat if you only knew hew anxious I have been to get you something different from your other presents, I know you'd forgive me." "Oh, pray don't mentioa it. I'm sure I am delighted with your taste and goodness. Why, Mrs. Blank told me when she brought the other one down that she had searched the whole city through for something sweet and pretty, and it was not until Mr. Chace showed her that cooler—the first one out of a dozen which had just been 'received—that she felt satisfied. And to think that your taste is like hers ! Why, it's wonderful, and I must compliment and thank you both." "And so, Mrs. Blank purchased her butter cooler at the same place where I got mine? It is a remarkable coinci- dence, indeed, Miss —, but I'm glad you like them. And with this he smilingly took his departure. But, in his eyes there was a far-away look, and his hands twitched as if he was yanking somebody around. He called in at a friend's, and borrowed a club and a shot- gun. He said he was going to a dog-fight, and he always liked to be well heeled. And then he hied him to the street called Pleasant. But Chacey saw him coming from afar. And he liked not the look of affairs, and skipped. And whither he went the chronicles say not; only that the young man cried out for him in vain, and awaited for him like a raging lion ' until the setting of the sun, when he had to go hence to have his hair curled for the wedding feast. Selah.—Fall , River Advance.

div.head: DISTRESS IN WARRINGTON-
div.p: THE DISTRESS IN WARRINGTON-

The weekly meeting of the Distress Committee was held on Tuesday afternoon in the Mayor's Parlour, Town Hall. Warrington. The Mayor (Alderman Harrison) presided, and there were also present the Revs. John Yonge, S. Wilkinson, and E. C. E. Carle- ton ; Major Litton, and Messrs. J. Greening, S. Davies, J. White, J. Smethurst, T. Jolley, and F. Monks.—The Mayon said he had got a letter from Miss Allton, daughter of the Rev. Mr. Anton, of St. Barnabas' Church, in which she proposed to give a grand concert in the Public Hall, in aid of the distress fund, if the committee would hire the hall, &c. • He had also received a letter from the Rector. (the Rev. W, Quekett) in which he stated that he had thought they (the committee) could not do better than spend Lso of their large balance in the purchase of blankets, aud lend them out to the destitute. He believed half the applicants for food slept at night in their clothes, and he knew they did it for warmth's sake. He used to lend blankets out to the poor and marked upon them " lent "in large printed letters. He required the security of a respectable person to see that they were renirued washed and cleaned at snid-surnmer, or when the cold weather ceased. It answered very well in London, and likewise at Warrington when he had working curates who felt an interest in these things. The letter, went on to say that during the cold winters he (the Rector) used to make paper coverines to go between the rugs and blankets, and they were highly valued.—The letters were laid on the table.—The MAYOE stated that since the previous meeting he had not received very many sub- scriptions. He had received a cheque from Messrs. Artingstall and Company fcr £ro, and from the Ladies' Committee 4s, which they had collected amongst themselves and other ladiea. The Ladies' Committee; he mentioned, paid their way.— Mr. MONKS mentioned that 165 tickets for relief had been renewed, end 212 cases visited, tan of which were refused. The number of people relieved during the seven days was 10,600.—Mr. JOLLEY was sorry to say that there had been more applicants that morn- ing than there had been for several days before put together' and they had had to dispense over smeolbs. of bread that day. They had started at Soo lbe., and now they had got to 1,200 lbs., and the quantity was not likely to decrease until they had a change of weather. Mr. Jolley ales) mentioned that Mrs. Bea- mont had promised an additional subscription in the shape of So tickets for coal. ()dear, hear.)—Mr. Moenre suggested that they should be careful in the administration of relief; he had heard that ,people were coming from Manehester.—The MAYOR said that he had heard a story that day which he could scarcely credit about some man who went to a certain gentle. man outside the borough and told him that as thy were so liberal in Warrington, and in so wretched a state at Manchester he had come from Manchester to take advantage of the liberality of Warrington. He (the Mayor) did not believe it; he believed it was a trumped-up story, but the gentleman to whom it was I told upon the strength of the statement had with- drawn his subscription.—Mr. Joraxy : It is a weekly subseription.—The MAYOR said it was a pity, as every precaution was taken. As soon as a person came for relief they were handed over to the inquiry officer, and he made every inquiry. (aear, hear.)--In the course of some further conversation, Mr. Mosires said, with regard to the trade of the town, that things were getting worse, and he was of opinion would get worse still.—Referring to the matter of the distribution of coal, the Rev. J. YONGIR said he did not think the public knew that coal could be had. He had been asked several times during the last two or three days by members of his own congregation if the fund was supplying coal. In the course of a subsequent dis- cussion, Mr. Yonge and one or two other members advocated a more liberal donation of coal.—After- wards accounts amounting to nearly £5O were passed, and the proceedings terminated.

div.p: F _)REIGN NEWS.

-.• . THE SOUDAN.—SEVERE SKIRMISH. SUAKIM, SUNDAY.—Major-General Sir Charles Warren yeeterdey sent out a foraging party of 273 men belonging to friendly Arabs. They advanced as far as the Hasheen Valley, where they took the enemy's camp completely by surprise, and captured 15 camels. They then proceeded to Handoub ; but in the meantime the rebels, recovering from their first panic, reformed themselves, their force outnum- bering that of the friendlies, who were driven back towards Suakim. Some mounted infantry were thereupon sent for- ward to support the foraging party, but upon their appear- ance the enemy commenced retreating to Hasbeen, pursued by the friendlies. The rebels fought desperately. but after an obstinate resistance were forced to retreat in disorder to Hasheen, leaving their dead upon the ground. The friendly Arabs pursued them nearly as far as the camp, the mounted infantry taking up position to protect the flank of the British allies. The enemy's loss amounted to 30 killed; that of the friendlies was slight Suexim, MONDAY.—Sir C. Warren sailed to-day for Suez in the Egyptian gunboat Gaffarieh, on his way to England, in order to take up his appointment as Chief Commissioner of the Metropolitan Police. CAIRO, MONDAY.—It is now officially announced that the British troops will retire to ASSOU3D, leaving the Egyptians to occupy Wady Haifa. PETROLEUM AND EGYPTIAN FINANCES. CAIRO, MONDAY. The Egyptian Government has re- ceived intelligence of the discovery at Get el Zeyd, on the shores of the Red Sea, of a petroleum spring, throwing a powerful jet of oil. It is anticipated that the Egyp- tian Treasury will derive a considerable revenue from this source; CAIRO, TIEURSDAY.—Tbe British Government has now officially entered into communication with the Egyptian Government on the question of the conversion of the Daira and Domain Loans into Five per Cent. Preference Stock. The question of the officering of the two new battalions for Suakim is now settled, Ahmed Mukhtar Pasha having as- sented to the appointment of British officers. THE EASTERN CRISIS. CONSTANTIN'OPLE, SATURDAY. The Ambassadors will hold a private sitting on Monday next, but the date for the re-assembling of the Conference is not vet fixed. There still exists some disagreement with regard to the wording of the protocol which is to be submitted to the body. The Sultan to-day ratified the Treaty of Peace between Servia and Bulgaria. VIENNA, SUNDAY.—The representatives of the Powers at Athens have again made serious representations to.tbe Greek Government on the subject of disarmament, and it is confidently expected that this time the Hellenic Cabinet will yield now that the Servo-Bulgarian treaty of peace is ratified and the Turco-Bulgarian agreement in a fair way of settlement. CONSTANTINOPLE, MONDAY. Another obstaele has pre- sented itself to delay the meeting of the Conference in the form of the re-asserted claim on the part of Prince Alexan- der to be appointed governor-general of itoumelia for life, instead of for a period of five years. The ambassadors, however, hope that this difficulty may be met by a com- promise.

FRANCE. Pants, MONDAY.—At the opening of to•day's sitting of he Chamber of Deputies, M. de Freycinet stated that he cc eptdl the order of the day agreed upon this morning by he Moderate and the Extreme Left. This resolution de- three that the Chamber, feeling confidence in the deter- mination of the Government to make necessary amendments in the mining laws, and being persuaded the Government will take account both of the rights of the State and the interest of the workers, passes to the orders of the day. M. Duval expressed himself sati fled with the Premier's explanations, and the resolution was then passed by 379 against 100 votes. EARTHQUAKE SHOCKS. MADRID, MONDAY.—A strong shock of earthquake was felt late last night in the province of Granada, causing great alarm among the inhabitants. No damage was done in the capital, but it is reported that several villages have suffered to some extent. No particulars have yet been received. WIESBADEN, MONDAY.—A violent shock of earthquake was felt here at 28 minutes past midnight. CANADA. OTTAWA, MONDAY.—Quiet among the Indians being com- pletely assured, the Government has decided to abandon the idea of sending a flying column of troops through the North- West Territory in the THE CATIVLIC CHURCH IN PRUSSIA. ROME, WEDNESDAY.—MOBsignor Kopp, the new Bishop of Fulda, having applied to the Vatican for instructions concerning the line of conduct to be followed by him in regard to the new Prussian Ecclesiastical Bill, Cardinal Jacobini replied yesterday requesting the Bishop to obtain the largest possible amount of concession, but to do nothing calculated to endanger the passing of the bill, see- ing that the measure as it stood was a distinct gain to the Vatican. THE AFGHAN BOUNDARY COMMISSION. Mmtv, WEDNESDAY. Intelligence from the Afghan Boundary Commission, dated Marachak, 12th inst., reports that the British members of the Commission recently ar- rived at that place and encamped near Fort ;',larachak, on the right bank of the Murghab. Besides Sir Joseph Ridge- way there have arrived Major Durand, Mr. William Merk, political agent, from India ; and Captain Lassy. RAID ON AN AMERICAN COURTHOUSE.— THIRTEEN PERSONS KILLED. NEW YORK, THIIRSDAY.—During the trial at Carollton, Mississipi, of some negroes, charged with the attempted as- sassination of a white man, a raid was made on the Court- house by fifty whites, who killed thirteen persons and wounded several others.

div.head: --SAVAGE ATTACK ON A WIFE.
div.p: --SAVAGE ATTACK ON A WIFE.

At Warrington Borough Court, on Monday, the magistrates granted a remand in a case in which John Broderick, tanner, of 7, Silver-square, War- rington, was charged with attempting to murder his wife Helen, on Saturday evening. From a state- ment made by Chief Constable Hunt, it appeared that prisoner, after leaving work on that day at one o'clock, went home and gave his wife 18s. Haviii had his dinner, he went out. At about 10-30 in the evening prisoner's wife and her son, a youth of fif- teen, were in Winwick-street, when the prisoner met them and asked where they were goincr. On Mrs. Broderick replying that she was goingto the market to purchase some meat and groceries he said that he would accompany her. On their return home Mrs. Broderick asked her husband where he had been all the afternoon. He at once flew into a passion and, asking her what had that to do with her, lacked her severely. Mrs. Broderick had at the time a child in her arms, and to protect it stooped down in a crouching position. She received kicks on the chin, left hip, right side, and right arm, each one causing a braise. The son, unable to prevent his father's violence, went to call the aid of the police and as he was leaving the house heard his mother say "Johnnie, you're not going to murder me!" Prisoner, it appears, then went to where the coal was kept, picked up a spade, and threatened to kill her. With the spade he then struck her across the left temple, and in striking a second blow caught the child across the back with the weapon. . In- spector Spinks and Police Constable Bruen, who had been informed by the son of what was going en, at once went to the house, and found Mrs. Broderick and her child saturated with blood. - Prisoner was taken into custody, and on being charged said "It's all wrong, I have not done so much." The injured woman was attended to by Dr. Starkey Smith. Michael Broderick, the son, having given evidence bearing out Mr. Hunt's statement, Inspector Spinks was called. He said that on going to the house in Silver-square he found it in darkness. Prisoner was sitting alone in the kitchen, the furniture was dis- arranged, and near the fire place was a large pool of blood. Broderick said his wife was in bed with the children, and the officers subsequently saw the woman and child. Mrs. Broderick was covered with blood, and blood was oozing from a wound on the body of the child, which is about twelve months old. Mrs. Broderick, who was taken to the Infir- mary, had an incised wound on the left temple. She declined to stay in the Institution, on account of her children, and was afterwards treated by Dr. Smith. The child had a wound across the shoulder, which corresponded with the edge of the spade. When charged at the police station with unlawfully wounding his wife with a spade, prisoner replied "I never had a spade in my hands.' His son was present and said" Yes, father, you had," and pri- soner replied" If you say so it must be right." On being charged that (Monday) morninc, with at- tempting to murder his wife, he said " I'am not up to that.' Prisoner will he kept in custody until !Monday next, when he will again be brought before I the magistrates:

A PATIIII,BCIIAL FRIEND.—One of the patriarchs of the Society of Fri.znds has just passed away in the person of Mr. Daniel Pryor Hack, who expired at Brighton on the 7th inst, in his 92nd year. Throughout his long life de- ceasni was a staunch Quaker, and when, in the course of his apprenticeship at Chelmford, he was drawn for the mili- tia, he suffered a term of imprisonment, being unable con- scientiously to serve or to find a substitute.
