HOUSE OF LORDS.--MONDAY. Their lordships met at 4 0. The Royal Assent was given by Commission to the Fresh Water Fisheries (Eels) Bill. THE SOCIALIST DISTIIRBANCES.—Lord STRATHEDEN and CAMPBELL called attention to the report of Mr. Childers on the late riots, and moved a resolution fixing the blame solely on the Executive collectively.—After some observations from Lord Cranbook, Lord Granville, and others, the mo- tion was withdrawn. CRIME IN IRELAND.—The Duke of St. ALBANS called at- tention to the murder of the bailiff Finlay, in county Gal- way, and pressed for some declarations from the Govern- ment as to whether they thought the powers they possessed at present were sufficient for the proteetion of life.—Lml GREVILLE insisted that Government in rreland existed only ,in name, and that the influence of the National League was paramount.—Lord SPENCER, who admitted the existence of crime, believed that it was in many cases committed by fanatics who thought they were doing good to their coun- try, and feared that no repressive legislation would affect that feeling. He contended that some districts were better than others, and gave figures to show that crime had mate- rially decreased during the month of February throughout the whole of Ireland, although the amount of boycotting now practised was, he said, about equal to what it was when the late Government .were in Oka—After some con- versation the subject dropped. The Glebe Loans (Ireland) Acts Continnance Bill was road a second time, and the House adjourned at 7-35.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. There were present the Rev. G. F. Roberts (chairman), Messrs. Harrigon, Brown, Ratcliffe, Foster, Broadbent, Dar- byshire, Blackhurst, Jolley, J. Houghton, Grange, W. Houghton, Bonnell, Humphries, Greening, Gib- son, and S. Sutton (assistant clerk).

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.-MONDAY.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.-MONDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at 4-0. SUAKIII.—Mr. BRYCE, in reply to Mr. Dillon, said so long as the tribes at Suakim maintained an attitude of open hos- tility the Government reserved to themselves entira freedom as to the military amil naval measures which would be taken for the safety of the port and its garrison. It was not in- tended to take any offensive measures. THE VOTE FOR THE LONDON PARES.—Mr. W. H. SMITH asked what the Government intended to do with regard to the vote for the London parks P—The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER said the Governmeet could not assent to any alteration of the present arrangements tar the maintenance of ;the Royal parka. With reference to the other parks, they would be prepared to propose legislation for the pur- pose of transferring them to the charge of the Metropo- litan Board of Works. He hoped the 1101180 would grant the necessary funds to maintana these places of public en- joyment. Mr. GLADSTONE entered the House and took his seat on the Treasury Bench. The right hon. gentleman was warmly cheered by the Ministerial members. BOARD SCHOOLS FOR RELIGIOUS TEACHING.—CaptaiE FIELD asked whether, seeing that according to recent re- turns no religious instruction was given in certain Board schools, the Vice-President of the Council would draw the attention of the School Boards in question to this defect in the system of teaching ?—Sir L. PLAYFAIR answered that it would be against the whole spirit of the Education Acts to make any representation to School Boards or voluntary schools on the subject of religious teaching. (Hear, hear.) BeME RULE.—MR. GLADSTONE'S CORRESPONDENCE. Mr. GLADSTONE, in answer to Mr. Cobain's question as to representations sent to him by the grand juries in Ireland en the subject of Home Rule, said it would be his duty to se what selection eauld be made of the communications sent to him. He had received a great number of letters entering at great length into the details of the question, which although important in themselves, could not be set out and printed for the consideration of the House. Un- doubtedly it wes right that in any selection that might be made the House should be informed of the representations of the grand juries. DISCHARGES AT THE DOCKYARDS.—Mr. R. W. DUFF, in reply to Captain Price, said Hotice of discharge bad been given to 343 men at the dockyards at Devonport, but they were men taken on for a special purpose, and told that they would be discharged at the end of March. It was hoped, however, arrangements would be made to prevent their dis- charge. ILLNESS OF LORD HARTINGTON.—TIIO CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER, in answer to Sir W. Barttelot, said the Marquis of Hartington was not very well, and the Com- mittee on Procedure would not meet to-morrow.
THE NAVY.-£5,500,000 SPECIAL EXPENDITURE
PROPOSED.

On the motion to go into Committee of Supply on the Navy Estimates, Lord C. BERESFORD called attention to the large number of unemployed skilled artisans in the shipbuilding ports, and moved a resolution declaring that a suitable opportunity was now afforded for increasing the efficiency of the Navy at the least possible expense to the country. He asked for five cruisers of 5,000 tons, fifteen of 2,000 tons, three torpedo depot - ships, 121 vessels of the Grasshopper type, and a large number of seagoing torpedo boats. The cotal cost of these he estimated at L 5,577,000, which he recommended should be provided by suspending the sinking fund or creating terminaole annuities: Mr. GOURLEY seconded the motion; and Mr. BETHELL, dwelling on the advantages of torpedoes over guns, recom- mended that improved scientific education in torpedo war- fare should be provided. Sir T. BRASSEY differed from Lord C. Beresford as to the absolute necessity of the immediate expenditure he recom- mended, and pointed out that twice as much money was now being spent in this country as in France. At the same time he hoped that the expenditure during the current year would be in the direction suggested by Lord C. Beresford, and maintained that the completion of the ships now in hand would enable the Admiralty next year to propose an extensive programme of new construction. Captain FIELD, who admitted the importance of increas- ing the strength of the Navy,objected to the method of pro- viding the money proposed by Lord C. Beresford. Sir E. REED denied that the appointment of the Com- mittee was required, because an important change had recently been effected in the method of constructing armour-belted vessels. We were constructing no fewer than seven armed belted cruisers of 5,000 tons each, and to make 18 knots an hour. These were vessels unlikely to be sur- passed. Lord G. HAMILTON expressed satisfaction that the present Admiralty hatl accepted the programme of their predecessors as regards large vessels, but pointed out the necessity for providing smaller ships, torpedo boats, and supplies of am- munition in order to utilise the expenditure which had already been incurred. Mr. DUFF, who spoke for the Admiralty, while giving credit to the late Beard for the manner in which they had carried out Lord Northbrook's programme, expressed his surprise that the late First Lord should ask for £2,000,000 more to be expended, when their own estimates only provided for half a million more than these estimates. Mr. RITCHIE remarked that at least a million of the Vote of Credit spent on the navy daring the late scare had been absolutely wasted. Sir W. HARCOURT reminded the Opposition of a great speech of Lord Beaconsfield against bloated armaments and in favour of a country being in a position of sound finance. Fifteen years ago the Navy Estimates were £9,000,000, now they were £13,000,000. The Army Estimates then were £13,000,000; this year they were £18,000,000, yet we were told we had got no army and no fleet. The addition of millions to the expenditure did not satisfy the naval or military men. The more millions that were granted the more these men wanted. These were not the times when anybody responsible for the government of- the country could afford to add five or even two millions to the highest Naval Estimates ever known, and he strongly deprecated borrowing money in time of peace fir warlike purposes. Lord C. BERESFORD expressed his willingness to amend his motion by leaving out the reference to the Sinking Fund and terminable annuities.—The House, however, refused to allow the motion to be amended, and on a division it was negatived by 206 to 98. EUEPLY.—TDe House went into Committee of Supply. A vote of 61,400 men and boys for the navy, including J 2,500 Royal Marines, was agreed to, and progress was reported. Tern Cole, MINES REGULATION BILL—The House hay-

lug resumed Committee on the Coal Mines Regulation Bill, Six J. PEASE moved to report progress.—Sir R. Cuoss said there was no necessity to wait for the report of the Corn- ' mission before legislating in the sense proposed by this measure.—Mr. F. S. POWELL urged the Committee to go on with the BROADHURST stated on the second reading it was undeisto,i that the bill should not be pro- ceeded with before Mr. A. O'Connor's bill. The report of the Commission would be in the hands of membcrs in a few days. It was not desirable to legislate piecemeal.—Upon division the motion was carried by 123 against 69, and pro- gress was reported. ISCELLANEOUS. —The House went into Committee on the Labourers (lieland) Acts Amendment Bill.—Mr. BRODRICE at once moved to report progress, and the Committee divided on the motien.—For the motion, 47 ; against, 125.--Clause 3 was added to the bill. On reaching clause 9 progress was reported. Mr. JOHNSTON introduced a bill to enable voters in towns and distric's in the province of Ulster to prevent the com- mon sale of intoxicating liquors. The House adjourned at 2-15. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TUESDAY.

'The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter-past four o'clock. PARISH CHURCHES BILL.—The Parish Churches Bill was read a second time. The measure was commended to their lordships by the Bishop of ,Peterbprough as one enacting the the old law declaring the parish churches free for the use of all parishioners. Incidentally the Bishop referred to a time when he had himself been a minister of a Congre7

- _ ..... gational chapel, selling sermons, accoiding to his present view Of his then position, at so much per Sunday. Now, as a Bishop of the National Church whose principle be main- tained to be free religion, he warmly attacked the pew BYS tern. He declared that there was nothing like a competition for a seat in church except a struzgle for a seat in Parlia- ment. There, he contended, human nature reaolied the lowest level of degradation. The Bill was subjected to some lively criticism. by Lord Griinthorpe, who movel its re- jection, and in deference to whose objections their lordships ultimately resolved to refer it, after its second reading, to a Select Committee. . A Women's Suffrage Bill, in the hands of Lord Denman, was promptly negatived without discussion. A number of noble lords were nominated to serve on the Joint Com- mittee of both Houses on the Government of India, and their lordships adjourned at five minutes past seven

div.head: TAILGATE SCHOOLS.
div.p: THE TAILGATE SCHOOLS.

The Schools Committee recommended that Messrs. Col- lins" tender for necessary Alterations to hospital and stores be accepted, it being the lowest. The Superintendent (Mr. Mines) reported that the children were generally healthy and cheerful; about a dozen, however, were sufering from chilblains. Mr. Stevens, the Government inspector, had visited the schools, and found their condition satisfactory.

div.head: CLERK'S ILLNESS.
div.p: THE CLERK'S ILLNESS.

The CALIEMIN said be had a letter from their clerk (Mr. J. C. Sutton) stating that he was still confined to his house. He bad hoped to be present at tne meeting that day, but he found the weather was too severe to turn out.
THE DISIRESB.-THE WAGES QUESTION.-- LE TTER FROM

MR. CHAMBERLAIN. On the accounts of the relieving officers being. proposed for payment, Mr. HARRISON asked hew the relief accounts of that fortnight corresponded with those of the previous fortnight.—The ASSISTANT CLERK said that so far as the cheques were concerned it was £5 more.—Mr. BROADBENT suggested, as so much was being said about the distress amongst the unemployed, that Mr. Harbourne, the relieving officer, should be asked to give some information on the mat- ter.—The CHAIRMAN said he thought the temporary relief at present being administered in Warrington met the case to a great extent, because the increase of pauper relief was very small.—Mr. Harbourne was then called in, and in reply to questioes, said it appeared to him that the distress in Warrington was growing. He had always been able to reduce the amount of the relief at this time of the year, but there was no keeping it down just now. There were many really bad cases of distress, but as yet he did not think the area of the distress was very extensive.—Mr. BROADBENT : In what classes does it principally exist ?—eir. Hia- )OURNE thought it was most fett amongst people who fol- lowed agricultural work, bricksetters' and plasterers' la- bourers, and men of that sort; but among mechanics there did not seem to be anything abnormal in the shape of elistress.—Mr. BROADIIENT : Then you may expect a greae dinsinution as soon as the frost breaks.—Mr. Hennounere : Yes, sir.—Mr. DAR- BYSIIIRE said, with regard to agricultural labourers, that if the labourers would work for a little less wages in accordauce with the price of food, they might get I work better than by sticking up for the late prices of labour He knew that farmers were determined to do with a less number of workmen, and leave work that can be left undone in preference to paying the high wages they had been accustomed to pay, because as a boiy they had not the money to pay them with. The cost of the produce that their farms grew was reduced one half in price, anol therefore it could not be expected that farmers 'would em- ploy hands unnecessarily and give the wages they had hitherto been giving. But if labourers would ask for a little less money they might get work. For instance, two or three labourers had applied to him that week, but because he said they ought to work for less money than they used to get they would not start.—The Cereals- elLe.7 thought there should be serne disposition on the part of labourers to recognise the increased purchasing power of money.—ln answer to a question, Mr. DARBYSHIRE said there were a good many farmers who had been paying the best class of labourers a£l a week. He thought if they would now work for 15s a week instead of a£l a good many more of them would be employed.—Mr. Bnomenrser said that everything seemed to be going down most seri- ously in price excepting the price of labour. (Hear, hear.) These was no doubt that a great deal more work would be done in this country if the price of labour was reduced in the same proportion that commodities had been. There was work now going past Warrington that might be done in Warringtosn if wages were lower. And in fact, to speak cor- rectly wages would not have to be reduced at all, for al- though nominally lower in money they would have the same purchasing power even when reduced as the larger amount had some years ago, and therefore working-men would be in no worse position. Lately the large manufac- turing concerns had really been curiae on for the benefit of the workers, that was to say all the profits had gone to labour. Thy would not regret that that should take place for a short time, because there were times when capital had more than its share, but that state of things Was reversed, and labour had too much and capital little or nothing. In these times of distress they ought, he thought, to say plainly what they thought, because they were not speaking for one class only. It was better that both masters and workmen should recognise the state of things, because if the workmen held out for a rate of wages which capital could not give it would drive trade out of the country altogether, and master and workmen I would suffer alike, whereas by a timely reduction both might be saved and trade in some cases saved from annihilation. (Hear, hem.) It was Mr. Chamberlain, he believed, who in the House of Commons mentioned a case in which 400 men were wanted to sweep away the snow and to be paid 2s 64 a day. But men could not be got, only 25 coming forward, the other preferring to go to the soup kitchen and ether methods of relief. The vicar of St. Jude's (London), a man well known for his untiring efforts to reduce distress in the east of London said that the Mansion House Fund, which was now being distributed somewhat indiscrimi- nately in London, had been the greatest evil with which they had to contend. The mischief caused by the indiscriminate aftinistratiOrt ef the fund was really caus- ing more tell and more pain to those who bad the welfare il of the population in the east of London at heart than the distress itself. His (Mr. Broadbent's) object in rising was rather to confirm that what Mr. Derbyshire had said in re- I lation to agriculture, was applicable also to the other indus- tries of this country, and it was a subject to which Boards I lof Guardians and otherg should not shut their eyes.—Mr. RATCLIFFE said that was a very broad question, because if I wages were to come down rents of houses and other assess- able property in the Union would have to come down also. —Mr. GREENING was of opiniom that that question of capi- tal and labour would right itself. The labourers were per- fectly justified in keeping up their wages if they could, just as it was right for the manufacturers to keep up their prices if they could. But it was also a fact that the manufac- turer, owing to the immense amount of foreign competition be had to contend with, WiS obliged to drop his prices or ,elese his manufactory, and they might depend upon it that the time would come when labour would have to follow in the same direction. That must come as a natural MISS-. quence.—Mr. BA.LHARRY mentioned that the wages of agri- cultural labourers in his district had been reduced 10 per cent recently.—The CLERK then read a communication from Mr. Chamberlain, as Presilent of the Local Govern- ment Board, with regard to the result of the inquiry re- cently made by that authority as to the distress in the country and suggesting certain modes of dealing with it. In this document Mr. Chamberlain stated that this in- quiry unfortunately confirms the prevailing impression as to the existence of exceptional distress among the working classes. The returns of pauperism do not show considerable increase, but the Local Government Board have thought it their duty to go beyond thn returns of actual pauperism, and have made some investigation into the condition of the working classes generally. They are convinced that in the ranks of those who do not ordinarily seek poor law hell) there is evidence of much and increasing privation, and if the depression in trade continues it is to be feared that large numbers of persons usually in regular employment will be reduced to the greatest straits. Such a condition of things, Mr. Chamberlain thinks, is a subject for deep reeret and very serious consideration. The spirit of independeece which leads so many of the working classes to make great personal sacrifices rather can incur the stigma of pauperism is one which deserves the greatest symathy and respect, and which it is the duty and interest of the commu- nity to maintain by all means at its disposal. The present regulations in regard to out-door relief do not, however, meet the emergency. Stone breaking or oakum picking presses hardly upon skilled artisans, and in some cases their proficiency in their special trades may be pre- judiced by such employment. Spade husbandry is less open to objection, and when facilities offer for adopting work of this character as a labour test the Local Govern- ment Board will be glad to assist the Guardians by author- ising the hiring of land for the purpose when necessary. What is really rf quired, however, in the endeavour to relieve artisans and others who heve hitherto avoided poor-law as- sistance, and who are temporarily deprived of employment, is, firstly, work which will not involve the stigma of pau- perism; secondly, work which all can perform whatever may have been their previous avocations ; thirdly, work which does not :compete with that of other labourers at present in employment ; and, lastly, work which is not likely to interfere with the resumption of regular employ- ment in their own trades by those who seek it, The Local Government Board have no power to enforce the adoption of any particular proposals. They recommend the Guardians to confer with local authorities, and endeavour to arrange with the latter for the ex- cntion of works on which unskilled labour may be immediately employed. These works may be of the fol- lowing kinds, among others :-1, spade industry on sewage farms; 2, laying out of open spaces, recreation grounds, new cemeteries, or disused burial grounds ; 3, cleansing streets not usually undertaken by local authorities ; 4, E.A.Y'S COMPOUND or LINSEED, Aniseed, enega, quips. laving out and paving of new streets, &re; 5, paving of ~ with Tolu, &c ' E E Oblrtodyre. 9i4., ls,lid, 2s 9d. of Gheinhts. unpaved streets and making of footpaths in country roads ; —Advt. 6, providing and extending sewage works and works of Four men were drowned at Teignmouth on Wednesday water supply. div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.-MESDAY.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.-MESDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at five minutes to four o'clock. RAILWAY Book STALLS.—At the time of private business exception was taken by Mr. A. O'Cowriou to a London, Brighton, anti. South Coast Railway Bill being read a second time without some prevision for preventing Mr. W. H. Smith's monopoly in the railway bookstalls. This mono- poly he condemned as injurious to trade, and as tending to set up an irresponeible censorship. Conversation on this subj-ct reached excitement beat when Mr. COURTNEY gave au opinion in favour of some general. reetriction on the Power of stall-holders to refuse to sell particular books or newspapers.—Mr. MITEDELLA, however, took the view that interference of any klnd would be a delicate matter, leading inevitably to other demands, such as, for example, the regu- lation of the refreshment-room contracts of railway corn- panics. This opinion evidently prevailing, Mr. A. O'Connor's proposed instruction to the Committee on the bill was negatived. QuEsTipirs.—At question time Mr. Fowl-kk informed Mr. Ruston that Constahle's picture, "The Hay Wain," pre- sented by its owner to the National Gallery, had already been placed on the walls of that institution.—Mr. GLAD- STONE, replying to Mr. de Cobain, testified to a general im- provement In the criminal statistics of Ireland last month.— Mr. CHILDERS informed Sir R. Cross that he had now re- ceived the report of the Royal Commission on Mines, and hoped, after considering it, to introduce a measure which would render the Coal Mines Bills now before the House unnecessary. THE CONTAGIOUS DISEASES ACTS. Mr. STANSFELD brought forward his 'notion declaring that the Contagious Diseases Acte ought to be repealed.—Mr. CAMPBELL-BAN- NERUAN, for the Government, supported the motion "in the interests of health, order, and humanity, as well as of their own political consistency."—The Government were strongly pressed to accept an addition to the motion (pro- posed by Sir J. Kenneway and seconded by Sir J. Pease) committing the House to make provision for the mainte- nance of hospital accommodation in the garrison towns. The amendment was, however, resisted, as unduly tying the hands of the House and likely to restrain local efforts.—Mr. GLADSTONE spoke in this sense before the division, which was taken early, And resulted in the amendment being nega- tived by 245 to 131.—Mr.Startsfeld's motion was than adopted amid cheers.

--- TAXATION OF GROUND RENTS.—Mr. SAUNDERS brought forward a motion in favour ef taxation of ground rents and increased values irm)arted to land by building operations or other improvements.—Mr. MOULTON seconded the motion, upon which discussion had not far proceeded when Mr. LAWSON interposed with an amendment, which was accep- ted by the Government, referring the subject to the consi- deration of the Committee on lown Holding.e.—The CHAN- CELLOR of the EXCHEQUER, in announcing the decision of the Government, complimented the mover of the amend- ment, to whom he referred as one of the youngest members of the House. on his contribution to the debate. Ultimately the amendment with the assent of Mr. SAUNDERS was agreed to. RIVERS PURIFICATION BILL.—Sir E. LUBBOCK moved the second reading of this bill.—Sir H. ROSCOE moved the rejection of the bill on the ground of the great damage that it would cause to manufacturing industrv.—Mr. HUT- TON also opposed the bill.—Mr. CHAMBERLAIN considered it was impossible for the House to acoept the stringent provisions contained in the 6th clause.—Lord C. BIIRESFORD suggested that it should be referred to a Select Committee. —The order for the second reading was negatived without a
The House adjourned at ten minutes to one. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at twenty minutes after twelve o'clock. WRIT FOR ALTRINCHAM,-012 the motion of MY. AKERS DOUGLAS, a new writ was ordered to be made out for the election of a member for the Altrincham division of the county of Chester, in the room of Mr. John Brooks, deceased. CHURCH OF SOOTLAND BILL.--MY. FINLAY, in moving the second reading of the Church of Scotland Bill, declared that its object was to remove obstacles in the way of the re- union of the Presbyterians of Scotland.—Dr. CAMEROIti moved the rejection of the bill, declaring that it was an illu- sory measure which had already been condemned by the three branches of the Presbyterian body.—The amendment was seconded by Mr. BnrcE.—ln the course of the debate which followed Sir R. Anstruther, Sir A. Campbell, Mr. J. A. Campbell, Mr. J. P. B. Robertson and Mr. J. H. A. Mac- donald supported the bill, and Mr. S. Mason, Mr. G. Beith, and Aar. Trevelyan opposed it.—Upon a division 177 mem- bers voted for the second reading and 202 against ; the bill was therefore rejected by a majority of 25. THE REGULATION OF THEATRES AND MUSIC HILLS.— Mr. E. RIDER Coot moved the second reading of the bill promoted by the Metropolitan Board of Works for the regu- lation of theatres and music balls. The bill proposed to give the Metropolitan Board power of supervision over the structure of theatres, so that the Lord Chamberlain might or their report grant his licence with greater assurance of the security of these places of amusement than he could have at present. Before the hon. member could conclude his remarks the debate stood adjourned at a quar- ter to six. MISCELLANEOUS.—The Sporting Lands Kiting (Scotland) sill was read a third time. Leave was given to bring in bills as follows :—Mr. P. Fitzgerald: Bill to amend the Merchant Shipping Act, 1854. Mr. Boyd Kinnear: Bill to simplify the transfer of land in Scotland. Mr. McLaren : Bill to amend the law of compensation for land acquired by compulsory purchase. The House adjourned at five minutes to six. HOUSE OF LORDS—THURSDAY. The Lord Chano,lior, took his seat en the Woolsack shortly after four o'clock. THE LUNACY LAWS—Upon the motion for going into committee on the Lunacy Acts Amendment Bill, Lord SELBORNE urged that no impediment should be pui in the way of the prompt treatment of curable cases, and that they should not move too fast in the direction of the extinction of private asylums 'in view of the magnitude of the inter- eats involved.—Lord CRANBROOK considered that the State should provide the asylums and not the counties, and that great injury would be done to society if private asylums were abolished.—ln committee on the Bill clauses of a con- troversial character were postponed, and it was intimated that the committee stage would be resumed on Monday the 29th inst.
Their Lordships adjourned at ten minutes to eight o'clock.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TuuRsDAT.

The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. QHESTIONS.—Mr. CHAMBERLAIN informed Mr. T. Robin- son that he could not undertake to bring in a bill this ses- sion to repeal the compulsory clauses of the Vaccination Act.—Replying to Mr. Johnston, Mr. GLADSTONE Said the distress in the country was not of a kind to warrant the appointment of a day of humiliation and prayer. NAVAL ESTIMATES.—In Committee of Supply on the Navy Estimates, Mr. HIBBERT made a general official state- ment. He remarked that the policy of the present Board of Admiralty was a loyal adherence to the policy followed and the expenditure undertaken by Lord Northbrook, and to the further expenditure co omenced.by the late First Lord. The estimates, which were for 12,993,000, were higher than they had been in any year since the commencement of the Crimean war, and this had been rendered necessary owing to the large liabilities involved in carryinv out the shipbuild- ing programme of Lord Northbrook and of Lord G. Hamilton. There was no desire after the present large ironclads were completed to go to any ex- cessive expenditure for ships in that direction. We were not so badly off for ammunition as had been re- presented, and in future ships would not be kept waiting for their armament. He should always insist on the im- portance of maintaining the supremacy on the sea which England had kept in the past, and which, he hoped, she would preserve in the future.—Lord GEORGE HAMILTON thought that while we had consented to spend nine-tenths of the sum estinalted to ke necessary to place the navy ih a thoroughly efficient state, we were unwise to decline to spend the remaining sum required to renovate the navy from top to bottom. Several votes were agreed to, and the other orders having been disposed of, the House adjourned.
ANTI-VACCINATION CANVASS AT
EARLESTOWN.

The much-talked ef canvass of the householders of Earles- town and Newton on the vaccination question has taken place during last week and the present week, and the result was ascertained at a meeting of the members of the Earles- town branch of the Anti-Compulsory Vaccinatien Society, held in the Welcome Coffee Palace, Market-place, on Wed- nesday evening. The voting papers were delivered by a staff of canvassers on Friday night and Saturday morning, and were collectui on Monday. They were headed, "Canvass on the Vaccination Question in Newton and Earlestown," and stated, 'You are respectfully requested to record your vote on the compulsory vaccination law by answering the following questions, Yes' or 'iia ' :-Ist. Do you believe in vaccination? 2nd. Do you agree with the law which enforces vaccination upon unwilling parents by flue or imprisonment? " The arrangements for the distri,. bution and collection of the voting papers were made by Mr. Benjamin Harrison, an active 'worker in the anti-vac- cination cause. About 1,800 papers were given out, and of these 1,300 were returned duly filled up. leaving 500 nnan- mared for various reasons. The meeting to ascertain the result of the voting excited some interest among the anti- vaccinators, and there was a good attendance. Mr. John Clarke (president) occupied the chair. The voting papers were counted and classified, and it was ascertained that the answers were as follows : Against vaccination and compulsion tegether 829 votes or 63.77 per cent.; in favour of vaccination, but against compulsion, 253 or 19 46 per cant; in favoni of both vaccination and compulsion, 179 or 1377 per cent; while 39 or 3 per cent. gave no answer to the first question, but voted against compalsion. When the result was announced it gave considerable satisfaction to the persons present, and it was pointed out .that it dif- fered comparatively little from the results arrived at at other places where similar questions have been submitted , for the vote of the householders.

REVENUE GRANTS.'The estimates for the Revenue De- partment were issued on Saturday, and show a net increase of £304,480, the grants for the last financial year having been £10,249,211. and the estimates for the coming financial Year being £10,553,091. The principal item of increase is £304,231 in the Past-office. BARRISTERS—whose professional labours necessitate long in- tervals between meals—nothing will be found so exhilarating, comforting, and capable of sustaining exhausted natu:e as Cadbury's Cocoa, gnaranteed absolutely para.—Advt.
SCHOOL FFIE3 COMMITTEE.
This committee reported that fees had been granted in 39 old and 89 new eases.—Confirmed.
VACCINATION AT EAULESTOWN.

A communication was read from Mr. A. Cooper, vaccina- tion officer for tbe Newton township, in which he steted that having now held the office of vaccination officer foiAhe district for over two years he had pleasure in placirw beifore them a report in reference to the arrears. When he ex- amined the report book on his appointment in January 1884 be found there we le 434 vaccinated, 42 dead, and 586 not finally accounted for. Of these 586 ,here were now 183 vaccinated, 13 were dead, 47 removed to other districts, land the vaccination officers acquainted with the fact, 291 were removed and not feuud, 13 were postponed by medical certificate, 28 whose parents had been fined, and 11 were not yet accounted for. He also found in the birth register 109 not vaccinated which were over four months old. Of these there were now 78 vaccinated, 5 dead, 9 postponed, 12 removed, and 5 had been tined. Daring the period in which he had held the office be had had a considerable 1 amount of trouble not only in reference to the above but in reference to vaccination generally. At the latter end of 1884 scarlet fever and measles were very prevalent, and al- most pitt a stop to vaccination for some months. He had also had a deal of trouble through the opposition of the Anti-yaccination Society, who had carried on their agitation both in public and in private. Another cause of delay and trouble was the amount of ignorance as to the requirements of the vaccination Acts; in fact he had bad to act the part of teacher and instruct the people as to what was to be done. He should like to take that opportunity of removing an impression which be found very general, that was, that he received a great benefit from prosecutions, and that it was to his interest to prosecute people, whereas he did not receive any benefit whatever but must lose a great deal of time by such prosecutions which occupied three days, viz. : One day going to Warrington to take out summonses, another going about the country to find a migi- strate to sign them, and another appearing at the Petty Sessions; and if afterwards it was necessary to take cut distress warrants, then there were two more days extra.— The ASSISTANT CLERK mentioned that at the time of Mr, Cooper's appointment, a promise was made that under certain conditions a gratuity should be granted to Mr. Cooper. He certainly thought Mr. Cooper had done the I work as well as any man in that district could have done.— After a short discussion, Mr. GREENING gave notice that he would move at the next meeting that a gratuity of .£lO be made to Mr. Cooper.

div.head: HOW SCARLET FEVER IS CULTIVATED AT RUNCORN.
div.p: HOW SCARLET FEVER IS CULTI- VATED AT RUNCORN.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, John Roughsedge, of Warrington, was charged with hav- ing failed to comply with a n.tice of the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners to abate a nuisance ex- isting upon certain premises belonging to him in Sutton-street. Mr. W. H. Linaker appeaned on be- half of the Commissioners.—Mr. James Percival, inspector of nuisances, said that he inspected the defendant's property in Sutton-street on the 21st August last. He found the ashpit and privies in an insanitary state. The ashpit was deeper than was allowed by the Local Government Board, while a wall of only Jour and a half inches thick divided the privies from the back kitchen of one of the houses. The defendant was written to in respect of the pro- perty, and he (the witness) told him that the ashpit was too deep, and that it should also be covered in. ' A final notice was served on the defendant on the 'llth November to abate the nuisance,--Tbe Iffpflant cioss-examined the witness at some length, with the view of showing that he had done all that was possi- ble to abate the nuisance.—The Inspector: The house is not fit for a pig to live in.—The defendant: Not fit for a pig to live in! If that is the case with this property, what about other property in Runcorn—in Duke-street for instance—which is in a much worse state? The defendant proceeded to state that he had made every endeavour to comply with the wishes of the Commissioners. He had been to the Town Hall, and had been put off time after time, as they said the matter was being dealt with by a com- mittee. He could not get any satisfaction at all.— Dr. MacDougall, medical officer of health for Run- corn, said on the 22nd September last he received in- formation that there was a recurrence of scarlet fever in Sutton-street, and that there had been two deaths in one house; and he felt it his duty to dis- cover what was really the cause of the disease, and to find out whether there was any nuisance contigu- ous to the premises that might have eggravated it. On the same day he visited the premiees,and found the ash- pit to be much greater in depth than any person with a grain of common sense would allow. There was nearly three feet of water in them, and a seething mass of fermentation was going on. In the back part of the place there was a cottage which had been allowed to be occupied, which was only divided from the privy by a 4i.inch wall. On the inside of the wall in the kitchen the plaster was much discoloured, showing that percolation had taken place from the outside. He said, without hesitation, that no civilised community, having a regard for the health of the i district, would allow such a nuisance to go on for 48 hours. He pointed out to the Authority the seri- ous nature of the nuisance, and the necessity for abating it, as no fewer than three deaths from scarlet fever had taken place in one house which had the use lof one of the privies in question. He pointed out to the defendant what was necessary to be done in order to abate the nuisance, and he I promised faithfully that his instructions should be attended to. None of those promises had Ibeen fulfilled to the satisfaction of the Authority. The 'nuisance was one which was injurious to health, and Ithe matter was really so serious that it would be a tquestion whether the Authosity would not take into ; consideration the necessity of closing the back cottage altogether.—Cross-examined by the defendant, wit- ness said that two closets adjoined the one house, but they were in different yards.—The defendant said he had done all that could be done to make the ashpit I dry. He was quite willing to make the ashpit shal- -1 lower. He had provided spouting, but the people living in the neighbourhood had used it as firewood, and he had now put up iron spouting. There were i , many nuisances n Runcorn to which the Commis- sioners might direct their attention, and his was no exception.—The Bench, after some consideration, said 'that the defendant had failed to show that a nuisance I did not exist. The evidence before them showed that I a serious nuisance existed, and they had decided to make an order for its abatement within 30 days. They also ordered the defendant to pay the costs of Ithe prosecution, which amounted to £2 ges defendant gave notice of appeal, and said he should not pay the costs.—The Bench expressed the opinion , that the notice served on the defendant for the abate- ment of the nuisance should have stated explicitly what was required to be done.

A REMARKABLE CURE OF EPILEPTIC FITS ErFECTED BY "GORDO:VS EXTRACT."

D. Teomes, 74. Hoxton-street, Bralford, writes July 24th. 1885.—Gentlemen,—Permit me to attest my unsolicited and husnble teatimeny to the healing and curative properties of your EXTRACT, not only in rest oringthe weak and debilitated but in the curing of Epilepsy in its most aggravated form; not only do I speak from Information, but personal observation in one special case--viz , that of a woman subjected to the above disease for upwards of twelve years; not so severe at first, but as time went on the fits became mare frequent, until %be patient was seldom a week without the recurrence, until she was reduced to sheer helplessness, and almost to a state of Idiocy; for over three years not able to do her own household work, and the fami'y had tried anything and everything that doctors and patent, medicines could do without effect; in fact. she gradually became worse, untiii the doctors said there was no cure. and the patient could net sur- vive long. They had tried many patent medicines, one preparation to the amount of £7. This for a time seemed to have a little effect, and the family had hopes of a cure, but so soon as the system became used to the medicine, the medi- cine beoame meets Rad a)1 hopes vain blighted. Tne family, in fact, becsme seriouly impoveri-bed in expending moaey with hope of a cure, but all to no purpose; besides, the hus- band's health became enfeebled for want of rest for such a length of time that lie was laid aside for long, until the family was redue.,d to a Tani condition indeed. However, as the last effort your EXTRACT was resorted to, and with surpris- ing effect! six or seven bottles regularly taken succ,esdvely until the fits became less frequent and the health became im- proved, until the woman was enabled to attend her household , duties; and now, though she has not used the EXPRACT for many months, she Ips not had fits for twelve months, and is now in her usual health. Any party writng me for proof, I will gladly unswer and-give the fuil name and address of suf- ferer. and at my expense; they will most gladly reply to any luquiry, but for reaoons which are justifiable, they would rather not have their name come before the public. Yet you are at perfect liberty to make what use of my statement you like, ?..e.d, beli,.ve me, yours respectfully,

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, MARCH 23, 1886.

AT the Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Mon- clay, there was quite a revelation of the way 'ln which it is possible to cultivate scarlet fever. It seems that the fever having been Prevalent in Sutton-street, with the result that lo one house there were two deaths, Dr. Mc- 120uoALL, the Medical Officer of Health for Runcorn, set about searching for the cause. Going to the back of the houses in the street, he soon -came upon a nuisance of the worst kind—deep ashpits with "nearly three feet of water in them, and a seething nlass of fermentation going on." More than this one co:tage was so close to one of the ash Pits, that the kitch-n was "only divided from the privy by a four and a half inch wall," Which furnished evidence in its discoloured plaster of percolation from the outside. Can We wonder that the attempt to live under such c.rOnditions should result in fever and death ? The owner of the property in question, Mr. J °RN ROUGHSEDG F. of Warrington, was ordered to abate the nuisance ; this was as far back as November last; but he did nothing that could be regarded as satifactory, and was therefoie brought before the mai! is- , trates at Runcorn on Monday last. Dr. Mc- PotrsAu. was emphatic in pronouncing upon the nuisance; it was one, he said, which no civilised community should allow to go on for forty-eight hours. The defendant re- , sorted to the shallow plea that there were 4‘ tnany nuisance in Runcorn," and that 'his was no exception." zupposing the Case were so, it would go to show not that ;he defendant was guiltless of breaking the Jaw, but that the authorities were not as ac- tive in enforcing it as they ought to be. Cotnnany in distress may make trouble less, but "two wrongs can never make one right." The defendant may congratulate himself on having got well off with payment of the costs 'of the prosecution (22 16s 6d), and an exten- , tsion of time to abate the nuisance. It is pre- Supposed by the law that every house for 'Which rent is paid is in a fairly habitable con- ; and it has been decided that a ten- , era may not only break his tenancy, but ustain a claim for compensation, if 11, e can show that he has suffered injury in nealth through a landlord neglecting to abate a nuisance. As a matter of fact, • tenants are altogether too easy about affairs of this kind ; they frequently tolerate bad smells from defective drainage ; and it is °illy when there is serious illness,fr actual death, that they insist upon steps being taken to remedy the evil. " Health," as EMERSON has it, "is the first wealth ;" and to the work- ing-man it may be said to be everything. The poorest of the poor suffer the most from insanitary surroundings; and it would be 'well if they could be made to understand that, however little they may pay in the shape Of rent, they have a right to insist that any uisance which may arise shall be removed

_ or abated. We should like to see Nuisance Inspectors troubled a little more than they are with Complaints. They are only mortal,and , are too apt to think that because nothing is said , there is nothing to be done. In this case at ' Runcorn, bad as it was on the face of it, there Was no complaint from the tenant, so far as ~ We can learn; the initiative was taken by the Medical Officer of Health, through the matter coming under his • notice when death had done its work. It is to his credit that he has ' spoken so plainly; and we think with him that it is the duty of the Authority to consider , Whether a cottage which is separated from t an ashpit by a +IA inch wall only should not f be closed altogether. But Authorities are always tender towards vested interests, being composed for the most part of men who have vested interests of their own to protect. Not long since, society was shocked by revela- tions as to the awful, insanitary condition tinder which a considerable number of people are living in well-known slums within a stone- throw of Windsor, Castle—the greatest resi- dence of the greatest Monarch of the age. It was urged that nothing could be done; that when the Prince Consort Was alive he had exerted himself to oring about a change for the better, but in vain, Proposals, it is said, have been made for buying the landlords out; but the pro- Perty, wretched as it is, brings in, in the

aggregate, a large rental, and a price is demanded which is abstlreity high. Of course so long as the game is profitable un- scrupulous landlords will not hesitate to keep 'it going. But surely the matter in such cases is not one to be dismissed by saying nothing can be done. Something ca x be done. Authorities have power ziven to them to close dwelling-houses which are in their judgment unfit ,for habitation; and it is a power which they ought to exercise more frequently than they do. Some Corporations have done their duty in this respect, and have thus raised the standatd of living where; there was most need of its being raised. Landlords should be made to feel that it does not pay to have their property in an insani- tary condition. Mr. ROUGHSEDGE is being taught a lesson; perhaps when he has paid , the costs of the present prosecution, and the costs of the appeal which he proposes to make, he will perceive that the money would have been better spent in improving his pro- perty and abating the nuisance as required by the Runcorn Commissioners. He has much to learn yet, and it is to be hoped that he will not be alone in taking to heart and applying the maxim that property has its duties as well as its rights.

THE death of Mr. JOHN BROOKS, M.P., happening, as it did, so unexpectedly, and whilst the young politician had before him what promised to be a useful career, has ex- cited more than common expressions of re- gret—even from those who a few months ago worked hard to prevent his being returned to Parliament. Liberals have united with Conservatives in votes of condolence; but, as his demise has left a gap in the representa- tion of Cheshire, both parties are now called upon to take steps for securing the vacant , seat. The Liberals met last evening week, and unanimously decided to ask Mr. I S. LEADAM, who fought the battle at the last election in opposition to Mr. BROOKS, to again become the champion of the Liberal cause. Looking at all the circumstances of the case, we do'not see how they could do otherwise. Mr; LEADAM was, it is true, de- feated by a majority of 752; but it was generally recognised that he gained ground the longer the campaign continued, and that the Conservatives owed their success to the exceptional circumstances of the time, and to the local popularity of the late member. Mr. LEADAM will commence, as to the ground he has won, where he left off; and, although it is not to be denied that the Conservatives have a good candidate in Sir WILLIAIef CUNLIFIE BRooKs, it is thought that, as he was beaten at the last election in the Macclesfield Divi- sion of Cheshire, he will not fare any better in retreating to the Altrincham Division of the county, During the contest in November , last, the Conservatives traded on the under- standing that had been come to with the r Parnellites • to drop the Crimes Act; but I since then Irishmen have had their eyes ' opened. They are now disgusted with , politicians who, after using them as a! cat's-paw, were preparing to push them I into the fire ; and we cannot therefore doubt that the votes of this class in the Altrincham Division—not a large class it may I be admitted—will be given, under normal conditions, to the Liberal candidate. Mr. LEADAM showed at the enthusiastic meetingl which was held at Altrincham on Monday night that he is utterly opposed to coercion, and that he has faith in Mr. GLADSTONE being able to propound a scheme for the settlement of the Irish Question upon a satis- factory basis. The Liberal candidate speaks l as one who has some special knowledge, for he wrote some time ago a history of coercion,: and the result of his inquiries is that repres- 1 sive measures fail, as a rule, in their object; their tendency is to increase crime rather than diminish it. He has watched the move- ments of the Tory party in playing fast and loose with Mr. PARNELL, and speaking on ! Monday night of their recent action he guaged the feeling of his audience when he said " he thought they would be disposed to I say that action so cynical, and betrayal so ; mean, had never disgraced the annals of poli- tical life since the time of the unprincipled adventurers of the Restoration." On Tues- day evening, Mr. LEADAM addressed an en- thusiastic meeting at Lymm, and took occa- sion to expose the hollowness of the claims of the Tory party in professing to be the friends of the farmer. Referring to Sir W.CuN- LUTE BROOKS as his opponent, he some- what astonished his hearers by making it known that, in 1815, the baronet who was i seeking their suffrages took part in birt.26 out of zis divisions. A matter of this kind should be brought to the knowledge of every elector in the. Division. There are already , too many men in Parliament who look upon ; the House ot Commons as a high-class club ' to be made use of just as it suits their conve- nience. If the electors are wise, they will send such people to the right-about, :Ind return men to Parliament who have given 1 some proof that they are able and willing to I look after their interests. An opportunity is now afforded of giving further freedom to Cheshire, and we trust that the best use will be made of it by electing Mr. LEADAM. To this end Liberals must work ardently and unceasingly. They are first in the field, and they must see to it that on Friday next they are at the head of the poll.

IN the House of Commons, last evening, , the PRIME MINISTER, in reply to a question put by Sir MICHAEL HICKS-BEACH, sounded a note of warning to which politicians of all shades would do well to pay heed. After intimating that he had no change to an- nounce with regard to the proposed measures for Ireland, he said he hoped to be able next week to fix the day when he would make his statement on the question. Meantime he advised "prudent reserve and wholesome scepticism as to the proposals to be made." This is timely advice, for, as it seems to us, it is not only premature, but ridiculous, to attempt to come to a conclusion, as some people are doing, as to the merits or demerits of a scheme of which they know as yet little or nothing. It is amusing to see folk shaking their heads because they happen to have heard some big figures named in connection with the suggested buying out of Irish land- lords. It is ominously urged that it would never do for England to be heavily taxed in order that Irishmen may obtain land upon easy terms. As if it were possible for Mr. GLADSTONE to propose anything so absurd! Whatever the scheme may be, we may be quite sure that, whether the country will be prepared for it or not, it will not violate any sound principle of finance. It is simply incredible that the greatest financier of the age will in his proposals with regard to Ireland overturn a reputation that he has been building up for more than half a century. Should Mr. GLADSTONE fail, it will be with a leaning to virtue's side; it willibe because he is disposed to he more trust-

ful, more generous, and more magnanimous than the rest of his countrymen in dealing with the sister isle. We are on the eve of a great crisis—a crisis without precedent in this generation—but that is no reasan for rushing to conclusions upon insufficient data. Let us possess our souls in patience until the case is before us, and have the decency to refrain from deciding until we are in a posi- tion to decide.

COST OF THE SIIIP CANAL BILL.—The return with respect to the expenses and other particulars of the Manchester Ship Canal Bill; moved for in the House of Commons on the 24th of February by an hon. member, has just been received in Manchester. The return shows that in the session of 1883 the Commons Committee sat, with respect to the bill, 39 days, and the Lords Committee 10. In the two following sessions the Commons Committee sat 20 and 35 days, and the Lords Committee 41 and 30. The total of the promoters' expenses were-1'3,557 4s—in 1883, £1,423 14s; in 1884, £1,216 11s 6d ; and in 1885, £9IQ 18s 6d. The opponents of the bill spent altogether £5,099 15s 6d, made up as follows i-1883, £1,432 19s 6d ; 1884, £2,139 8s; and 1885, £1,527 Bs. The number of witnesses ex- amined in the three years were 204, GO, and 40 re- spectively. Several oi the witnesses appeared twice in the same session—once before the Committee of the Commons and once before the Lords, or vies rersa. In 1883 the Commons Committee found the bill proved, but the Lords. expressed an oppo- site opinion. These . opinions were exactly i reversed in 1884, whilst n the last session- 1885—they were agreed that the preamble had been proved.

PATRICK'S DAY AT WIDNES.—The festlval of the patron saint of Ireland, which in former years was charac- terised by outrage and disturbance, passed off very quietly in Widnes. The "wearing of the green" was al meat usii- versal amongst old and young of the Irish pepulation, whilst in many instances there was the added adornment of 1 a sprig of shamrock. In the morning mass wee said at the. Catholic chapels, and in the afternoon the children of St. Mare's Catholic School. the members of the total Abstin- ence League, and the Young Men's Society paraded the main thoroughfares of the town, headed by the brass band of the Young Men's Society. Banners were borne in the procession, which attrected much attention from the numerous persons who assembled in the streets. The Irish National Foresters celebrated the de' on Satin-dare after- noon, when, to the number of 100. they walked in proces- sion through the town headed by the band sf the Order.
