WortK .IN WARILINGTone.--4t is to be regretted that there doee not appearlo be at present:any signs of improvement in the trade of the town, but that, on the contrary, all the changes that have recently taken place seem to be for the worse. During the I present week:a:large nuralser af ironworkers have ' White- cross -talrniepawnyo. works Messrs.been thrown into enforced idleness through the The ltieomnikiazrytia closingll and c of cross Works, although not entirely- closed, I are ,producing ,on a much :reduced scale, . dan conse- quently work is short and precarious. Almost all, if not all, the ‘wireworks in the town ,are also on short time. The fustian,entting •trade is likewise extremely dull, though it is hoped that the ap- proach of spring will ha.ve the effect of bringing in Lome. orders, PRUDENTIAL ASSURANCE COMPANY, IJIMITED.— The thirty-seventh annual meeting of the share- holders or this company was recently held at the 1 •offices, :Holborn Bars, London; under the presidency of Mr. Edgar Horne, chairman. The report of the directors, a cam of •which appears in our .advertis- ing columns, was taken as read. - The Chairman said , that as that was the fourth year .of the quinquen- , ilium, it would be interestinw to compare what the [society had done in the past year with what it did lin 1881, in order to show what progress it had Jasale. Their total assets may amounted to .£s,7o2,B62—(cheera)—whilst four 3-ears ago the amount was \.£1,580,001. In 1884 it was -c4711,462. 1 He wished °particularly to draw their attention to the ordinary branch a the seciety's business. They ' found that in 1881 they were doing a new business of £31,000 a year in premiums, which was a hand- some addition to their income, but nay they had a new premium inconw of of £85,060 a year— (cheers)—an increase upon last year of £27,000. In 1881 they had an income in the ordinary branch of £142,000, as compared with £303,000 at the present time. They also congratulated themselves in 1881 of having an insurance fund of £700,000, but that fund now totalled £l,4oo,ooo—(applausej —and the increase in premium receipts on the pre- , vious year had been .004,000, against the increase in 1881 over 1880 of £20,000. Those facts would show the progress the society had made, and he was happy to state there was every indication that the same rate of progress, or even greater, would he made during the present year. With respect to the , industrial branch, notwithstanding the depression 1 of trade, the average rate of progress in that de- partment had been considerably increased, the re- sults having exceeded £2,750,000 (an increase of £150,000 on the previous year), as compared with . £1,750,000 in 1881, when the insurance fund stood at £1,700,000. \ The latter fund now amounted to about £4,000,000. They had nearly 40,000 free policies, a p,ivilege which they hoped to extend as soon as they could find it safe. The report was adopted. The retiring directors, Dr. Fraser, Dr. Cross, and Mr. H. A. Harben were re-appointed, and ' Messrs. Allanson and Warrie were re-elected audi- tors. Votes of thanks having been accorded, the meeting terminated.

A DAIRY SCHOOL OR CHESHIRR.—Mr. Rigby, secretary of the Cheshire Chamber of Agriculture, is receiving -very encouraging promises of support , from landlords and tenants in the appeal on behalf' of The Dairy School for Cheshire. About £2,000 are required before a start can be made, . .

and that it is proposed to raise by shares. It is probable that premises at Tattenhali will be secured for the school,this being the centre of the cheese- making district. . NEW LOCOMOTIVE WORKS.—The Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway Company are at present engaged in building enormous Locomotive Erecting Shops at Horwich, which lies about midway between Bolton and Chorley. The building is no less than 1,519 feet long, and is proportionately wide and high. The massive beams, and other ironwork to the extent of 2,800 tons, are being supplied by Messrs. Pearson and Knowles' Coal and Iron Company.- Mr. Birtles, of • Warrington, has recently been engaged in photo- graphing sections of the building whilst in course of construction. TILE REGULATION OF MINES.—The Home Secre- tary was waited upon on Thursday by a deputation representing the colliers of England and Wales, I who desired to urge the Amendment of the Mines Regulation Act in the direction recommended by the Birmingham Conference. Mr. Burt, M.P., intro- duced the deputation, and in the course of his speech he begged the particular attention of the Government to the question of the appoint- ment of check weighmen. Mr. W. Pickard, M.P., advocated the appointment of a Minis- ter of Mines, and Mr. Rowland (North York- shire) called attention to the insufficiency of the inspection of mines. Mr. Childers, in the course of his reply, elicited from the deputa- tion-an expression of opinion that the miners were unanimously opposed to the employment of women about collieries. He said the report of the Royal Commission reached him only this week. In his consideration of that report he would pay careful attention to facts now laid before him. He was anxious to pass a bill on this subject in the present session.

Thu THEFT OF £3,000.—A scene such as -is not often witnessed occurred at Nantwich, on Saturday, in -the course of the examination of the 'prisoners , who are charged with stealing £3,000, the property gf Mr. Samuel Blud, fellmonger, of Stapeley, near Nantwich, under circumstances of a somewhat ex- traordinary character. Blud, who was the first wit- ness called, gave his evidence in such a curious way as to confirm the suspicion his appearance had pre- viously created that he was much the worse for drink. This conclusion fairly forced itself on the court before he had finished his evidence, with the result that he was ordered to leave the box. He left the witness-box smiling complacently, as if he regarded the incident as rather amusing than other- wise. Blud's wife, apparently in even a more ad- vanced state of intoxication than her husband, was afterwards ordered out of court. After some of the witnesses. had been examined the prisoners were remanded till Monday. On Wednesday the pre- liminary inquiry was concluded. One of the men in custody, William Hesketh, sem, was discharged; the others—Thomas, /William, and Charles Hesketh and John Astles—were committed to thA quarter sessions for trial.

BANKRUPTCY Of A PRESTON BROOK WrlEEL- wßiorrr Warrington County Court, on Thurs- day, Edward Pennington, wheekffright, Preston' Brook, appeared before his Honour judge Ffoulkes on his public examination in bankruptcy. Mr. Worsley, deputy official receiver, questioned the bankrupt, who said that he commenced business in 1870, but had then no capital. He had only kept one account book, which was at .the office of the official receiver. Ile kept .no memoranda of moneys borrowed from people. He was expecting £25 by reversion on the death of an aunt. The debtor was examined at some 'length as to moneys borrowed by him from his brother, and the answers that he had made to the questions submitted to him when making his statement to the official receiver. The debtor attributed his failure to bad trade, sick- ness, and being too fond of company. He could not say what his personal expenses were, as he had not kept any account in figures. It would be•four or five years since he began to be too fond of com- pany. For the last two years he had been spending as near as possible all the money he had got. The examination was adjourned until the 15th of next month, his Honour remarking that Pennington must in the meantime exert himself to assist the official receiver.

THEFT OF A Honsii —At the St. Helens Police Court, on Saturday, before Mr. J. C. Gamble, a youth named James Bibby, who lives in South- lane, Bold, near St. Helens, were charged with stealing a horse, value £8 10s, the property of Mr. George Fox, farm bailiff. About twelve o'clock on. Thursday night a constable of the Warrington diti- sion was on duty in Bold-road when he met the pri- soner with the pony. ifs stopped him and asked him where he was going. Prisoner said the pony belonged to Mr. • Warburton, of Warrington, for whom he worked, and he was taking it home. Not believing his statement, the officer took them to the Penketh Police Station, and subsequent inquiries proved that the animal belonged to Mr. Fox, of Bold, and had been stolen. Mr. liox stated that the animal was safe at nine o'clock on Thursday night; and that the prisoner had no right to take it. Ile was remanded until Monday, when he was again brought up before Dr. E. P. Twyford and Alderman J. Harrison. Mr. Fox and Constable Slingsley, of the Warrington police,. gave evidence. Prisoner was committed to the Sessions for trial. The father was asked if he wanted his, boy out on bail, as the Ses- sions would not be until the 20th April. He re- plied, *“ He had better stop where he is, sir."—Pri- soner was removed to the cells.

WILWRINGTON AND DISTRICT ELGHWAY BOARD.— A general.meeting of the members of this Board was 'held at the office, in Sankey-street, on Wednes- day afternoon. The chair was occupied by Mr. R. Houghton t(Lowton House), and there were also present Messrs. John raireleugh (Burtonwood), James Wright (Cuerdley),Wiiliam B.‘ Kerfoot (Great Sankey), 'Samuel Bent (Lowton), 'William Royston (Poulton); James Houghton (Woolston), John Grounds .(Orford), Henry Wolff (Rixton), and R. Owen (Croft).—The Deputy-Cierk reported that with reference to an encroachment at Hollins Green they had written to Mr. Sankey, who, he believed, :had communicated, with the surveyor. ' —The Surveyor said that be had seen Mr. San,key, and ihadmo doubt but that the encroachment would be set back as, soon as the weather was more settled. 'The subject then dropped.—With reference to the bridge crossing the canal at Sankey Bridges, the Deputy-Clerk said that Mr. White had found that he had not the information in his office that he thought he had, as to the liability of the London and North-Western' Railway Company to maintain the bridge.—Mr. Kerfoot said that a better bridge was required. There should also be a better ap- 'roach ,and more protection., as was the case with the bridges over the Weaver..—The surveyor's report on the subject said that on dark and foggy nights the bridge was dangerous, it was objectionable be- cause of the great vibration under traffic, and it , was also inadequately lighted. A new and well- lighted bridge should be put down to remedy the defect, It was decided that the clerk write to the ' Railway Company, calling attention to the danger- ous state .of the bridge.—Mr. lierfoot mentioned the danger caused by a ditch close to the footpath in the district of Woolston, and the Surveyor remarked. , that pipes would be laid and the ditch made up; for the present the danger had been stopped.—A discussion took place relative to the practise of posting placards on sign posts, and it was resolved to write to two firms giving them notice to discon- tinue it.—The balance in hand was reported to be £1.017 odd, out of which acf..,ouiits amounting to £957 odd were passed for payment on the recom: mendation of the Finance Committee.—This was all the business of interest.

! there had been criminal neglect on the part of the husband —The jury, whilst expressing strong disapproval of the course adopted by the husband and his lodgei a, did not think this serious step called for, and returned a verdict of acci- dental death. •

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."
The change in the weather is hailed with delight by the starving poor. It is in itself a Relief Fund and a blanket thrown in.

The House of Lords is, occasionally, in a rational mood.. • Last night their lordships decided by a majority of 14 in favour of opening London Museums and Art Galleries on Sunday. There have been six divisions on this question in the Lords, but this is the first time the motion has been carried.

The Liverpool opponents of the Manchester Ship Canal Bill have all but given up the ghost; they have withdrawn their petitions ; and the bill will now pass the Commons as an unopposed measure. It is suggested that the House of Lords may make a strong stand against the bill; but this is "very like a whale."

Mr. Wiggan who has, along with Mrs. Wiggan, been conducting successful evan- gelistic services in Widnes and Warrington, would do well to drop the title of "weeping preacher." It savours of sensationalism and " the penny dreadful " to say nothing of its not being in accord with the scripture phrase as to "wiping away all tears from their eyes."

A Charity Organisation Society is being formed in St. Helens, although the trade of the town is in a normal condition. The idea is to get the fullest information, so as to be able to cope effectually with really deserving cases. The police report that there are a large number of tramps in search of work ; but it will scarcely do to put a premium upon their visits to St. Helens.

Sane little imposition is inevitable in the distribution of relief; but the per centage* in Warrington is small. Recently an old woman applied to a clergyman in the town for is- sistance—telling a pitiful 'tale. The wide awake cleric requested that the rent book should be shown him. He wised to see what tale it would tell. Thus put to the test, the applicant produced what she believed to be the rent book; but she had made a slight mistake; it was the bank book, show- ing a balance to the ,good of about £3O. The old sinner didn't succeed that tithe.

The Roman Catholic Bishop of Notting- ham has forbidden his flock to have anything to do with the Primrose League. He says that "the majority of the members of. the League. in professing to maintain religion, simply mean defence of the heretical sect of the English Church and maintenance of the Protestant ascendancy." The Bishop is evi- dently not colour blind; he can see that the Primrose League is mere Orange than Prim- rose.

People are beginning to ask questions. Thcv want to know where Sir Gilbert Greenall was when the House of Lords was was put on its trial in the Commons; and where he was when the Ship uanal Bill was being discussed and Voted upon. Our `• P. D." says people shouldn't deal in conun- , drums.; and then, with impish inconsistency, he puts the following, and answers it in the same breath :—Why is Sir Gilbert like a policeman? Bez)2.use he is never there when he's wanted.

The watchmakers of Prescot are suffering. as Sheffield workers are, from the fraudulent practices of foreigners. English watches being in good repute, cheaper and inferior watch, movements of foreign 'make have been placed in English Hall marked cases, ardd then sold as .English goods. The British wisrkman has a right to " protection " agaimst fraud of this kind ; it should be stamped out alike in the interests of morality and of trade.

At the Liberal ball the other night, at New- ton, two Tories turned up with one pair of white gloves between them---,one figuring as a right-handed., the other as a left-handed in- dividual. These are they, a correspontecit informs us, "who on the day of the date election caused a large amount of diversion by driviag to the poll in a barrow drawn tandem fashion by two donkeys." Can it be that they wish to cast a reflection upon tkeir leaders; or do they desire to place it beyond doubt that they are themselves asinine?

The Newton Improvement Commissioners should rend, mark, learn, and inwardly digest that portion of the report of the Medical Officer of Health just issued) which relates to the sewage of Earlestown (East) and War- grave, which is "flowing .over the land below the cemetery preparatory to its being passed through settling tanks about to be con- structed." This primitive way of disposing of sewage may be cheap, but it is certainly nasty ; nd it may prove to be dear in the end. " Whilst the .grass grows—but the provecb's somewhat musty."

It is some satisfaction to observe that the Warrington Highway Board are making a move with a view to getting a better bridge across the canal at Sankey Bridges"; but it would be more satisfactory if they would move a little quicker. It is not long since a Warrington gentleman had a pony badly in- jured through being thrown down at the bridge ; it had stepped into a hole in the structure. If the London and North-Western Railway Company are responsible, it is dis- creditable to them that such a dangerous bridge should be in existence on the highway between Warrington and Liverpool.

div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.
RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

RUNCORN FREE PUBLIC LIBRARY.—DariRg the past month there hay. been 1,659 books isued to borroware, be ing an increase of 249 in the corresponding month of last year. NELSON STRBET itAPTTST CIIATBL, WIDNES.—To fair con- gregations the Rev. R. Yeatman, the pastor, on Sunday de- livered special discourses. In the morning his subject WAM "The Christian combat," and the evening "The power of Jesus to forgive sins." STEALING COAL AT WIDNES.—Annie McCormick, eleven years of age, was brought up at Widnes Police Court on 'Monday chargcd with stealing 171bs. of coal from the canal bank, the property of the London and North-Western Rill- way Company. The prisoner, who was caught in the act by P.C. Murray, was fined 103 and costs, or to go to gaol for seven days.

ST. JOHN'S PRESBYTERIAN CHAPEL, RUNCORN.—The an- niversary sermons of this place of worship were preached to good congregations on Sunday morning and evening by the Rev. Dr. Lewis, of Shrewsbury. A. service was also held on Monday afternoon, when the Rev. Thomas Evans, of Pres- ton. was the preacher. In the evening the rev. gentleman lectured in Bethesda Schoolroom on "John Bull's sympathetic excellencies and failings." Mr. R. Shaw pre- sided. MILTON CONGREGATIONAL CAPEL, WIDNES —On sun- day evening the Rev. R. G Hughes preached a special ser- mon with reference to the death of Mrs. George Warner. of Albert-road. Although comparatively a stranger, and of reserved and modest demeanour, he said she made a deep impression on all with whom she came in contact. There was an influence and power about her that was uncommon. The chapel was well filled, and the service was a most im- pressive one. SPITEFUL SAILORS'AT RUNCORN.—B,Ifore Mr. J. Brundrit and Mr. G. L. Davies, at Runcorn Police Court on Satur- day, Charles Grandin and Philip Carcand, sailors, were charged with wilfully damaging a stove and breaking some crockery on board the brigintine Magic. The men had been diestharged from the Magic, and en order to spite the cap- tain they visited the vessel when the crew were at dinner and damaged the stove and smashed the crockeiy. They were apprehended at Southampton and brought to Run- corn.. The prisoners were sentenced to a month's hard labour.

WATERED Run AT RIINCORN.—At Runcora Petty Ses- sions on Monday, John West, landlord of the Duke of Wel- lington public-house, Percival's-lane' was charged with sailing adulterated rum. On the 16th February Supt. Leah sent P.C. Barber into the Duke of Welliogton for a small rum. He was supplied by the defendant from a bottle which stood on a shelf in the bar. P.C. Wallace then went in and asked for half a pint of rum. The defendant went to draw the rum from a keg, but after some objection he sup- plied half a pint from the bottle. The analyst had col-titled that the rum contained 54 per cent of war. or 29 per cent more than was allowed by law. A tine of Li and costs, £1 3s 3d was itnposed. TRH BAPTIST CHAPEL, RUNCORN.--IlleSara. Marsh and Son, auctioneers. on Tuesday evening, offered for sale at Wilson's Hotel, the chapel in Bridge-street formerly used by the sect known as the Particular Biptlsts. The chapel is leasehold for the residue of a term of 999 years, from the let May, 1845, and was subject to the yearly ground rent £5 .I7s. The cellars of the chapel, which are used as shops, brought in a rent of £l6 18s per annum. The bidding was carted bv Mr. W. Farrell at £BO, and concluded at £435 by Mr. W. Littler, who acted on behalf of the Lily of the Valley Lodge of Oddfellows. The auctioneer teen declared that there a reserve ,of £5OO on the building, which was withdrawn. There was also a reserve of £2O upon the or- gan, and this too was unsold. RECHABITES ecr•RUNCORN.—The financial report of the "Union" Tent of Runcorn 1.0. of Rechabites has just been issued. it appeared that during the peet rear the con- tributions amounted to £134 Sc 6d, and the District Tent for funerals contributed £4B, the total receipts being £l9O Is id. There had ben £76 16s paid in sick allowance, £26 8s 21 to the District Funeral Fund, and £lB for , funerals. The total payment amounted to £l5l 7s 2d, the balancl on the year's workines heing £3B 13s 11.1. The funds of the society amount to £329 Is 5?,d, of which £2P6 18s Ills invested in the Runcorn Savings Bank, The number r.f members on the 31st December last was 157, and the worth per member £2 is 11d. The average Amount of sick pay per member at. 12s per week for the year ending December laet was Os 9L-cl, and the average for the past tea years 6, qd. MArine FUEL or Moira r AT We'Dieas.—On Monday, Mrs. Goff, wife of Air. A. Goff, pork 'butcher, carrying on 'busi- ness in Waterloo-road and Widnes-road, Widnes, made an exceedingly unpleasant discovery. On Saturday night, in consequence of the cash box being in an insecure condition, Miss Caroline Goff placed a tag containing £l2 amongst a , lot of paper and rubbish in the tiregrate fn the apartment adjoining the shop As the night became very.coltl, Mrs. Goff, unaware of the teresence-ef the bag an-1 its comtenta, lit a -gre in the grate, with the result that the money, which was nearly all gold, was melted into an indistinguishable mass. The loss was not discovered until Mr. Got was ge- ing to the market on Monday, when on asking for the Satur- day night's takings, his daughter recollected where eke had placed the bag, and on searching amongat the *ekes was horrified to find that it was -coneumed aad itscontents re- duced to a shapeless mass._

Amman)) FRAUD SF A SAILOR AT RUNCORN.—kt Run- I corn, on Saturday, Tern Tomson, a foreign sailor, was ) .charged with obtaining by false pretences from Mr. WJ! Phillips, clothier. Church-street, a suit of clothes. a shirt, ti and a muffler. The prisoner was boarding at the -Sloop Inn, r and 'represented to the landlord that he had Eft due to him from the vessel .upon which he wasersployed. On the strength of this foseph Itegg obtained the prisoner the ' clothes from Phillips' shop. It afterwards transpired that no money was due to Tomson, and on int:prides being made it was found that he had pledged the coat beloneing to the suit-at the shop of Mr. W. Craddock, Ct.urch-street. The prisoner was fogswed to Liverpool and brought back to Runcorn by Joseph Pegg, &tad given into custody.—The vessel on which the prisonet was last employed haxing lett theport, the charge of fraud against the prisoner.could not be-sustained, and be was discharged. •OK/CORY FOR COFFEE AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, Sam uOl Blair, grocer. Bridge-street, FM 4 charged with selling half a lb. of coffee, which woe not Of , the•quality demanded. Mr. Hitchen defended and pleaded not guilty. 'On the 6th February Constables Bar- ber ,and Wallace were supplied with half a lb. contained in a tin, no mention beizg made that Anything was mixed with the coffee. Supt. 'Leah Pro- duced a certificate-Showing that the,coffee was adulterated ? vrith'fo per cent of chicory. Mr. Hitchen made technical objections, which the Bench overruled. He then contended that his client was fatly protected by the fact that the tin , was labelled with a proper description of its contents. He , called Edward Evans, manager for Mr. Blair, who otated , that be told Barber he had Otely French coffee in canisters at 10d per lb. He put down the tin on the counter. The ' Bench imposed -a finely( 5s and costs, c£l.l3'3d: Mr. Hitehen intimated his intention of giving notice of appeal. WIFE DESERTION AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Police Court on Monday, Richard Jones was charged under a warrant with neglecting to maintain his wife, who was chargeable • to the comsnon fund of the Prescot Uuion.—Mr. Scannell, the relieving officer, stated that the prisoner was a labourer at the works of Messrs. Golding, Davies, and Co., and earned on an average 30s. per week. He bad net contr'.huted to- wards his wife's maintenance for a long time, and declined to do so. he prisoner calied witnesses to prove that his wife deseired him. After a fortnight's search he found her, and promised to pay her so much per week, but she never turned up,and he could not find leer. She had been re- moved to the Workhouse. The case was adjourned for a fortnight, the prisoner in the meantime to pay 295., the charges of the Guardians, and KA 61 the cost of the war- rant.—Walter &Isbell was charged with running away from 1 Widnes, and leaving his wife and two children chargeable to the COMRIOR fund of the Union. Mr. Scannell said the cGuardians had gone to a deal of trouble in finding the prisoner, who was a fiatman. The cost of hi a family to the Guardians was £45 12s. He was sentenced to a month'. hard labour.

A RUNCORN GROCER AND HIS BREAD. At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. C. Reynolds and Mr. James Handley, Mr. Edward Johnson, provision dealer. St. Helens, who has shops in Runcorn, and many other towns in the district, was summoned for selling bread otherwise than by weight and which was also short of weight. Mr. F. A. Lake, solicitor, defended —Superintendeet Leah said that on the 6th lust, from something which came to his knowledge, he sent for a loaf of bread to Mr. Johnson's shop in church-street in order to see if he sold his bread by weight. A girl named Clara Spencer paid Ad for a 41b. loaf, but it was not passed over the scales at ali, as should have been done. When complaint was made that the loaf was not weight some excuse was made that the messenger did not ask for it to be weighed. When put on the scales its actual weight was found to be thrce ounces and 10?2 drachms short of 41b. Mr. Lake, on behalf of his client, pleaded guilty to the breach of the act, but contended that as the messenger was not charged the full price for the loaf there was no intention to defraud the public. Under these circumstances he asked the Bench to inflict as light a pen- alty as possible.—Mr. Reynolds said there was already a conviction against the defendant's name for a similar thing —selling bread otherwise than by weight, and then there was another conviction for selling adulterated butter and other things that were infringements of the act.—Mr. John- son said the case was a very hard one for him, as he was in the hands of his manaors.—Mr. Reynolds: We have de• cide4 to fine you 203 and costs (153).
FATAL FALL DO WN STA IRS AT WIDNES.

Yesterday afternoon, Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner, held an inquest at the Rose and Crown Inn, Moss , 13”1:, touching the death of Mary Casey, 34 years of age, wife of Patrick Casey, labourer, who lives at 51, II loss Bank-road, Widnes. About half-past ten on Tuesday night Mrs Casey was going upstairs to bed, and baiting reached the ton she fell oackwards head first. She was picked up, in an unconscious state by John Faßon, a lodger. She was bleeding from the nose, mouth, aud a wound on the back of the head. The husband, who had been in bed about three hours, was awakened, and sticking plaister was applied to the cut on the head, and the woman was taken to bed. No doctor was sent for. About four o'clock she recovered con- sciousness, and was evidently in much pain. About eight o'clock the husband went for Dr. O'Keeffe, . wito was not \at home, and Dr. licCambridge Iwas also away: Dr. McCambridge was, however, , found About two o'clock and brought to the house. Death ensued about half-past two on Thursday morning, the woman haying been sensible for a very short interval. Evidence bearing out the above facts was given by the husband, John Fallon, Bridget Duffy, and Peter Earring- ton.—The jury questioned the witnesses at some length as to why they did not summon medical assistance immedi- ately after the accident. The answers were to the effect that they did not think they could get a doctor at that hour, and that they thought the woman would be better in the morning.—The Deputy Coroner pointed oat that the , jury could return a verdict of manslaughter if they thought

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF ar UARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF ar UARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday, under the presidency ot Mr. John Weir. Present—Revs. J. W. N. Tanner, J. Lockwood, J. J. Bryant; Messrs. W. Handley, T. Speakman, Parr, Aaron, Higbfield, Hadfield, Mclntyre. Stokes, Hamilton, Wilkin- son, Hewitt, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk).

div.head: MR. BRUNNER, M.P.
div.p: MR. BRUNNER, M.P.

The folloring letter was read 132, Palace Chambers Westminster, S.W., March 9, 1886.—Mr. U. Linaker, clerk Runcorn Union.—Dear sir,-1 am directed by Mr. Brunner to acknowledge the receipt of the petition in favour of the Manchester Ship Canal. He duly deposited, it yesterday, and it appears among tbe records of the Private Bill Office in the Parliamentary papers issued this morning.—Truly yours, TMCMAS E. Elam."

div.head: SURCHARGES.
div.p: SURCHARGES.

"I am directed by the Local Government Board to state that Mr. Dolby, district auditor, has reported that at his [audit of the accounts of the Runcorn Union for the half year ended at Michaelmas last, he surcharged Mr. Davenport, assistant overseer of the township of Appleton, with the sum of 26 13s 7d; and Mr. J. Whitfield, assist- ant overseer of the township of Walton Inferior, with the sum of is 3P. The Board request that you will inform them whether those sums have oeen paid to the treasurer of the Union, as required by section 32 of the 7 and 8 Viet., c. 101."—The Clerk said the amounts had been paid.

div.head: LIiTAID CALLS.
div.p: LIiTAID CALLS.

Tbe Deputy Clerk read a list of the calls due on the sth February, but which were still unpaid :—Aston Grange £l6, Frodsbam £62, Newton-by-Frodeharn £l6, Preston- e'-th'-klill £5B. Whitley Inferior.X3o, total £lB2.—The Clerk asked what proceedings should be taken, but the Board deferred taking action.

div.head: ESTIMATES AHD COUNTY RATE.
div.p: THE ESTIMATES AHD COUNTY RATE.

The basis of contributions required from the everseers for the Ensuing half-yenr ending Michaelmas, 1886, was =O- mitted for consideration. Tile total capital for the current half-year ending Lady Day amounted to £7.971, and the nett probable expenditure was estimated at £5,281, which *hewed a probable balance in favour of the Union at Lady Day of ,f 2,684. The expenditure during the ensuing half- year ending Michaelmas was estimated as followe:—School fees for non-pauper children. £l6; county rate, £2,400; in maintenance, £700; out relief, £2,000; lunatic accoent, £394; salaries account, £551; Assessment Cemmittee ex- pauses, £120; vaccination, £72; registration, £73; with other items, total £6,875. There was an estimated credit of £420 from commote fund, reducing the amount to £6,455. The balance and contingency fund ef £2,020 would bring the estimated expenditure to £8,476. Alter taking ccedit for 1 the probable balance at Lady Day, the amount required from the overseers was £5,702. The rateable valuation of the Union as per valuation lists in force was £213,375, being an increase of £1 621 as compared with the corres- ponding period of last year. A rate .of 614 in the £ would produce £5,778 1831 d, being a decrease of 1d ia the L as compared with the corresponding period of last year. and a , decrease of a penny in the £ as compared with the calts for the current half-year ending Lady Day.—The estimate of Dee expenditure of the School Attendance Committee for the Michaelmas half-year, 1886, was submitted. There was a probable balance of £4 at Lady Day, and it was estimated that the expenditure would be school attendance officers SA clerk's salary £35, books, post Ages, legal exte'enses, itca £2O, balance and contingency fund £5O, total amount re- quired £l4B. less balance of £4. The rateable velue was £105,560, and a rate of five-sixteenths of a penny in the L would produce the sum of £137 8e 9d.—Mr. W. Handley moved the adoption of the estimates carefully prepared by tine clerk, and remarked that the county rate was £5BB 15a fa less than it ' was the corresponding quarter of last year; the amount being last year £1,050 9s, this year £461 13s Bd. This was a very satis- factory decrease, and had made a reduction of id in the £in the rates necessary for the ensuing half year. Provision bad been made in the estimates for an increase of in maintenance and out-door relief if this severe weather should continue. He dwelt with satisfaction npin the low rate necessary for educational purposes.—The Rev. J. Lock- woad said he supposed the succeesful application of the Board for a re-assessment of the county rate was the cause of the reduction.—The Clerk replied that that was one rea- son, no doubt. Another was that the Weaver Trustees bad Paid to the credit of the county £15,000 last year.---Mr. Handley pointed out that there was a great increase in the assessments for county purposes; but they were on a fairer basis than they had been for many years. The townships in the Runcorn Union were on a fair basis compared with the rateable value, and the union had benefited by the equalisation of the basis for the whole county. The con- tribution from the Weaver Trust was £5,000 more than they had paid for some lime.—Mr Hadfield: When the Ship Canal stops the Weaver traffic they will stop that pay- ment.—Mr. Aarcn : We shall get treble that amount from the Ship Canal.—The estimates paest.d.—The relief busi- ness was then taken.

div.head: RUNCORN RURA.L SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: RUNCORN RURA.L SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday. Preeent—Messrs. Mclntyre (in the chair), Weir, Hadfield, Parr, Aaron, 13ighfield, Stokes, Revs. J. W. N. Tanner, J. Lockwood, and J. J. Bryant, with Messrs. H. Linakee (clerk), W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk), and J. Far- rington (inspector).

div.head: WESTON POINT SEwk.RAGE SCHEME.
div.p: WESTON POINT SEwk.RAGE SCHEME.

The Deputy Clerk read a letttr from the Pablic Works Loan Commissioners making an inquiry as ti the applica- tion to borrow meney for the Weston Point sewerage scheme.—Mr. Aaron said thera was a bill passed its second reading last week in the House of Commons to make the owners of property make the sewers, and he did not see why under these circumstances the Authority should spend about £3OO in making a sewer at Weston.—The Deputy Clerk: That is for the Urban Authorities and not for the Rural Anthority.—Mr. Aaron: I saw it in the Standard.— The Deputy. Clerk: You can see what you like; I have got the bill.—lt was mentioned that the Local Government, Board would compel the Authority to carry out the scheme.. —Mr. Aaron said if the Local Government Board hs:d to rule and dictate what the Authority must do they might as well give over meeting. The medical officer said the present sewer was quite sufficient for the present pro- perty that was in Westoa Point. Why should they i the face of these bad times spend £3OO of the ratepayers' money just to satisfy the Local Governrpent Baard.—Rev. J. .1.. Bryant said the doctor stated that the sewer was sufficient for the present time.;—Mr. Aaron: For the present property. —Rev .1. J. Bryant said there was a great deal of difference of opinion. It was a horrid place. There was no legal out- let for the sewer, because the Weaver Trustees might turn the Authority out at a moment's notice.—The Deputy Clcrk suggested that the Public Works Loan Commissioners should be informed that-the Authority had divided the work in three parts, and had accepted two tenders but deferred the third.—Rev. J. J. Bryant: That is putting off the evil day.—Mr. Aaron moved, and Mr. Hadfield seconded, a resolution in accordance with the suggestion.—Rev. J. J. Bryant said they were spending £3OO in sewering one part of Weston Point. The sewer would strain only about 40 houses, and leaving a block of about 30 houses compara- tively unsewered. This particular spot had always been the very centre of the disease.—The deputy Clerk said this discussion was entirely out of order, as the Board bad de- cided that two lengths out of the three should be made Mr. Aaron Etated that an endeavour was made some time- ago to deprive the ratepayers of Weston Point of their sewerage rates, and they had now put that matter right for .£3OO. At come future time it would have coat thousands of pounde.—The resolution was passed without dissent.

div.head: MEASLES AT APPLETON.
div.p: MEASLES AT APPLETON.

Dr. Adams, the medical officer of health, reported a slight outtneak of measles at Appleton. Four cases had oc- curred altogether, and the disease had been of a very mild type. He had issued the usual oreventitive directions. He ordered the families to be detain.d from school. The re- port was adopted.

div.head: NUISANCE AT KELSEY.
div.p: NUISANCE AT KELSEY.

Mr. W. Fairish, of Hill Side Villa, flelsby, wrote com- plaining of 'a nuisance in Robin Hood Lane. on property owned by Mr. Mark Smith, contractor, Widnes. The nuis- ance was a cesspool, which was a receptacle for all the filth from the small farm of Mr. Thomas . Atherton. The stench was simply unbearable, and how they ha i escaped an epi- demic was something wonderful.—The Inspector WAS in- structed to investigate the matter.

div.head: NUISLNCE LICSPECTOE'S REPORT..
div.p: NUISLNCE LICSPECTOE'S REPORT..

The Nuisance Inspector presented a statement of the sani- tary wotk done daring the year ended December last. There had been 52 nuisances reported, and the inspector bad made seven special reports. Sixty-five notices had been served to abate nuisances, and four had been abated without notice. Five cases of over-crowding had been, dealt with, and fifteen certificates for the occupation of new houses had been granted. There bad been 82 yards of main sewer extended. There lad been 25 eatnples of water collected, and sub- mitted for analysis. Sixteen persons had been convicted_ for infringements of the Canal Boats Acts, anctsix convic- tions for other offences.
ESTIMATED E.SYENDITVRE OF TEE FRODSHASI WA'TF_JI SCHEME.

The estimate of the general expenses of the Authority for the Michaelmas half year was presented. There was a probable balance at Lady Day of £702. The amount re- quired for general expenses was £515, and sus- pense account £855. The latter included Weston drainage £174, Frodsham Trial Wells £504, Five Crosses water scheme £177. After deducting the Probable balance, there was left the sum of £668 required. A. rate of id in the £ would produce the aim of A 4372 13s, 6d. There was the sum of £35 16a 4d required for special extoenses.—ln answer to Mr. Stokes, the Vierk said £640 was already spent on the Frodshatn Water . Scheme, and it would have to be paid by the Frodsbam ratepayers. Be recommended that , they write a strong letter to the Local Government Boald and point out that although there was a good deal said about favouring schemes that would find work for the unemployed nothing had been heard from the London Board about the Frodsham Water Scheme for eight weeks, when their in- spector held an inquiry. They were keeping back a scheme which would give employment to many persons.—Mr. Weir moved, and Mr. Aaron seconded, the suggested resolution, which was carried unanimensly.—The estimate was also approved.—There was no other business of • public in. tercet.

div.head: POLICE INTELLIGENCI4I
div.p: POLICE INTELLIGENCI4I
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATCIMAY.—Before Aldermen Burgess and Holmes.

The only case before the Court is reportett in another coin mu. MoNDA.Y.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), Alder- man Davies, and Councillor Greening. MrscELLANEous.—Creorge Gerrard, charged with being drunk in the Market-place, on Saturday, was dismissed, and Maria Knockton, a hawker was fined 2s 6d, including costs, for being drunk and disorderly in Irlam-street, on Saturday night —Maria Shields was sent to prison for a month, and John Hoare was fined Ns and costs for disorderly conduct. —James Leslie, charged with trespassing upon, and refusing to quit, the passenger station at Bank Quay, was fined 5s and costs, Mr. Ferrand, on behalf of the company, stating that defendant was one of S gang of loafers who were in the habit of loitering about the atation.—Patrick Dooney was fined lOs and costs for keeping lodgers without having his bouss registered, and a similar charge against John Glynn was adjourned —A fine of is was imposed on Arthur Wil- liam Baker and Michael Maher for permitting the chimneys of their hose s to b 4 on fire.

ONE OF THE UNEMPLOYED.—George Pritchard, iiho when sear:lied had a begging book in his possession, \vas charged with being drunk and disbrderly in Sankey-street, on Saturday night.—Chief CoostAble Hunt stated that de- fendant was a recipient of relief from the soup kitchen.— Defendant replied that be had not been near the kitchen himself, but that his wife and children fetched the soup.— Defendant's wife said that the beer had been given to her husband, who had not worked since Christmas.—The Bench
dismissed him. TUESDAY.—Beforr Councillor Broadbent, Councillor Green- ing; and Mr. Monks. DRUNSENNESS.—NIatiIda Carlisle was fined for drun- kennees.

THEFT BY A SERVANT—Robert Appleby (20), of New- ton Heath, near Manchester, was charged with stealing a silver wa'ch and chain from the house of Henry Bithell, chimney sweep, 83, Mersey-street. He pleaded guilty. Pri- soner was in the employ of Bithell, and on Friday was left in the house while Mr. and Mrs. Bithell were out on busi- ness. On their return he had disappeared, and the watck and chain, a coat and vest, and a hair albert chain were missing. Prisoner afterwards offered the watch and chain in pledge at Salford, but the name of the prosecutor being engraved on the watch, the pawnbroker's suspicions were roused, and he gave prisoner into custody. Sentence of three months' imprisonment, with hard labour, wai passed.

div.head: W2DNASDIY.—Before Mr. John Fairclough,
div.p: W2DNASDIY.—Before Mr. John Fairclough,

SLEEPING OUT.—Edward Percival and Thomas Fleming were charged with sleeping in a stable at the Eagle and Child yard, the same morning, without visible means of subsistence, and were each sent to prison for seven days. TETIRSDAY.—Be fore Alderman Holmes and Mr. Z. Armitage. A VIOLENT TIZAMP.—Thoma3 Jackson was charged with refusing to perform his task of work whilst a casual inmate of the vagrant ward at the Union Workhouse.—Mr Curry, the warder, said that prisoner threw a stone at him, which, had it hit him, would prooobly have killed him. He behaved like a madman, and in the cell wounded witness on the head. When prisoner was dealt with Mr. Armitage had not taken his seat on the Bench, and prisoner was therefore only committed for 14 days, one magistrate not having power to send him for a lengthened period. THErr yA. GlRL.—Margaret Plinston (17), daughter of William Ptinston, marine store dealer, pleaded guilty to stealing nix ounces of wool, yalue 2s, from the shop of Herbert Peace, small-ware dealer, 75, Buttermarket-street, on the previous day. She purloined the wool while in the shop making a purchase.—She was sent to prison for 14 days. FRlDAY.—Before Captain Reynolds, Mr. John White, Mr. R. Garnett, and Dr._Gornall.

WIPE AS 17 LT.— A man named Kane was charged on a summons with assaulting his "wife, who said that he had abused her for the last eleven years. On Saturday he knocked her down and kicked her on the face. The magis- trates ordered him to be bound over, himself in £5, and one surety of £5, or go to prison for fourteen days. VAGRA.NCY —Richard Jefferson was charged as a rogue and vagabond with begging in Orford-lane and Battersby- lane on the previous afternoon, he having been previously convicied of the same offence. He was sent to prison for two months with hard labour.
WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. P. Stubs and Mr. Tinsley.

ISCELLINEOLS. —Thomas Monaghan, for being drunk at Rixton, on the 2nd inst, was fined 5s and costs, and Wil• ham Hill, charged with being drunk and disorderly, on the 16th of Fehruary, on the Manchester-road, was similarly dealt with.—James Harrison and George Travis were charged with committing a breach of the peace in Manches- ter-road, Axton, on the 7th inst. They were each bound over to be of good behaviour for six months, and ordered to pay the costs.

div.head: LYMM PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: LYMM PETTY SESSIONS.
FRlDA.Y.—Before Messrs. G. Devrhurst (in the chair), P. Stubs, W. Long, T. P. .Norris, and C. Lister. _

POACHING.—Two men, neither of whom appeared, named John Drink water and Uohn Madox, were charged with poaching at High Leigh on the 11th ult.—P.C. Ardhern spoke to having seen the defendants hurrying along a road at High Leigh on the day in question. They ran when they saw him following, but he overtook them, and got hold of a net containing a hare which they had in their posses- sion. They refused to let the net go hut the constable blew his whistle, and as soon as the defendants saw some- one coming to the officer's assistance they gave up the net and hare, and each gave the name of John Adams, which were afterwards found to he false names.—Sergeant Turner, stationed at Marston, near Northwich, stated that one of the defendants threatened to knock in his windows some night because he let their real names be knawn, and said he would get something that would make him gc on a wooden leg.—A fine of 40s and costs, £1 Gs, was imposed in each case, or one month's imprisonment. CRUELTY TO A HonsE.—John Ditchfield was SUMMOIIei for having cruelly ill-treated a horse on the 13th inst by working it whilst in an unfit condition; and Richard Cook, greengrocer, Lymm was summoned for causing the animal to be worked. Mr. A. Browne, of Warrington. defended. P.C. Dutton speke to having seen the horse worked whilst lame on one leg, and Inspector Greenwell, of the BeS P * C.A , said he had been told by Mr. Cook that the horse had been lamed by an accident in October. It had had little to do, but he thought it would do it no harm to send it out with the groceries on the day in question.—Mr. W. W. Hill, veterinary surgeon, of Altrincham, said he had examined the horse and found it totally unfit for work.. He was of opinion it would never be in a condition to worle.—A fine of 205 and costs, 2s. was imposed on Mr. Cook. ALLEGED TREFT.—Jovph Heath, a lad seven years of age, was charged with having stolen an overcoat, valued at 75 6d, the property of J. Southern. The defendant atte.nds Lymm National School, and it was alleged had stolen the overcoat of the complainant's son, who also attends the same school. The case was, however, dismissed. Doo CASES—John Frangleton, Fanny Winstanley, David Molyneux, and Alfred Swanwick, were each ordered to paw 5s 6d costs for allowing unmuzzled dogs to be at large.—W. H. Barrow was fined 5s and costs for a similar offence at Rol- liogton. It was stated that in this latter case the dog was of a ferocious disposition, and had made attacks nieon several individuals.
WIDNES POLICE COURT.
MONDAT.—Before Mr. H..Gaskell, junr., and Mr. T. S.
Timmis.

DRUNIEENNESS.—Tbe following were fined 5s and costs for Eirunkenness :—John Cotesworth, John Callan, John Egan, William Baines, W. Moorcroft, and James Tierce. Michael Dudley, and Thomas Kelly were each fined I.os and Costs; and John Starkey, who made his 33rd appearance before the Bench, was fined 20s and costs, or a month, for being drunk and disorderly. STONING CONSTABLES.—Thomas Sullivan and Patrizk McCreese were charged with committing a breach of the peace on Sunday morning. The man were kicking the doors of houses in Oxford-street, and stoned Constables Savory and Thompson when they appeared. Thompson was struck on the chest by a dead cat thrown by McCreese. The prisoners were bound over to be of good behaviour.

WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. TH,RsDAy—Before Messrs. H. Gaskell and J. C. Gamble. MISCELLANEOUS.—John Miller, Edward Sweeney, Patrick Kennedy, Michael Madden, and John Murray were each fined for drunkenne!s.--LWilliara Cain and Jane Cain, man and wife, who did not appear, were charged with fight- ing in Mary-street, Moss Bank, on the 6th inst. A fine of 5s and costs was imposed.—William Wallace and Edward Wild, young men, were bound over to keep the peace for SIX months for fighting in Church-street, katnworth, on the 6:h inst. MAINTENANCE OF A SON.—John McCann, a labourer, was ' ordered to pay 133 arrears of contributions towards the maintenance of his son in Stockport Indutrlal School, and also Pz 6d costs.

div.p: FOOTBALL.

div.head: RUGBY RULES.
div.p: RUGBY RULES.

RrNCOItN V. SALE.—Played at Sale on Saturday, when, Runcorn, though short of Woods, Johnson, ifotHand, and Dea•z, won somewhat easily, scoring two goals4twe tries. and four minor points, to Sale nil. • WIDNES v. ST. HELENS RhCREATION.—This match was played at Widnes on Saturday, the home team winning by one goal and six minor points, to two minor points. Owing to a rapid thaw, play was of a scrambling nature. J. ii. Smitll got the try by good following up. itidyard also got over, tut the point was disallowed.

WESTON SHANTBRS v. RrNOORN WATERLILIES.—This match was played at Weston on Saturday, and a one-sided game ended in an easy victory for the home team by two' goals, three tries, and ten minor points to nil. Moores dropped a goal, and the tries were obtained by Hollings- wortn, Pendlebury, Speakman, and MolinQaus, and from the latter Tudor kicked a goal. _

FRODSHAM ROVERS V. RuNCORN FREE WANDERERS.— This match was played at Frodsham on Saturday, and ended in a victory for the home team by two goals, three tries, three minor points, to one minor point. The tries were obtainnd by F. Thomas and Tickl,2. The latter played a splendid game throughout. T. Rogers, by a splendid rut! and drop, landed a goal. All the backs played well for the visitors, and Darlington, Abrams, and Helsby played well for the borne team.

RUNCORN RECREATION V. WIDNES RECREATION (IST TEams.)—The above match was played at Runcorn on Saturday last, and after a pleasant game, the home team won by 2 tries and 1 minor point to Widnes' 1 minor point. In the first half the visitors had hard lines in not scoring, being continually on their opponents' line ; the score stan- ding one minor to their credit. In the second half Run- corn had the game a little more in their favour, Clarke and Stubbs each scoring. RUNCORN V. Sr. HELENS RECREATION (SECOND TEAMS) —The return fixture between these teams was decided at Runcorn on Saturday, when the borne team woo easily, simply penning the Recreation on their lines all through the game, who were forced to save no fewer than fifteen times. in addition to three tries which were scored by H. Cawley (2) and W. Riley—Woods kicking a goal from one of Caw- ley s tries A Cawley and Riley played a grand back game. Clare nessed splendidly, and Raffe, Orme, and Andrews played a grand forward game. WEST LANCrISHIPE CUP.—FIRST ROUND.

ST. HELENS RECRVTIGN v. BLIINDELLSANDS.,---At Eun- dellsands these teams met in the above competition. on Saturday. During the first half the Recreation team scored 3 tries, besides which, Blundollsands had to save no les3 than five times. During the early part of the second halt, Dean, one of the forwards got his eye severely cut, and had to retire, which materially weakened the team. In this portion of the game the Recreation had matters pretty easily, and secured 2 more tries (Hankinson and Pyke) and 8 minors, the latter try being converted into a goal by Lang- ley. When time was called the visitors were victorious by 1 pal, 4 tries, and 13 minor points. Teams :—Recreation: W. E. Taylor, back; R. Langley, J. Peachey, and J. Greg- son, three-quarter; J. liankinson and A. Smith, half-backs; W. Parr (captain), W. Cook, T. Green, J. Pyke, James Han- kinson, W. Dean, J. Gaskell, H. Gregson, and J. Pilkington, forwards. Blundellsands: F. Ronghley, back; P. Leonard (captain), Freeman, and T. Wilkinson, three-quarter backs; Leadbetter and Chadwick, half-backs; J. Leonard, Hiddies- ton, Spenter, Hill, Kirby, Rimrner, Rotnwell, Alloy and B. Wright, forwards._

PAGEFIELD V. NRIVTON.—This match was played on Saturday on the ground of the Wigan Football Club (kindly lent for the occasion), before a moderate number of specta- tors, not a few of .vhom came with the Newton team fully expecting their favourites to win. The Newton forwards seerns.:l no match for their light opponents. Tne score at half-time was Pagefield 2 tries and 10 minors to n Page- field were ultimately the victors by 2 tries and 12 minors (20 points) against Newton 1 try and 5 minors (0 points). WARRINGTON v. MANCHESTER RANGERS.

Walton haying cancelled their return fixture with War- rington owing to their having to play a cap tie, tne War- rington committee got the Manchester Ringers to play their return match a week or two earlier to fill up the vacancy. Saturday last being the time appointed for the match. The visitors had whipped together a strong team, Warrington on the other band being far from renresentative, such good men as Warren, Gilbert, Jolley, and Dillon being absent from their ranks. A goodly number of the home sup- porters thought that their boys had an easy task in hand, but in this they were mistaken, for a much better game has not been played this season on the club ground, the game not being half so one-sided as the score implies. The ground was in good condition, and some 1,500 spectators witnessed the proceedings, and, according to some of their talk, were quite satisfied with their three, six, or nine pennyworth of amusement. Whittle, Boardman, and E. Dillon were picked to play in the absentees' places, and showed that they have had a good grounding in the ranks of the" chicken's team "by the manner is which they acquitted them- selves, the score at the call of time being 1 goal, 2 tries, 8 minors to nil.

About 3-30 the teams arriveron the field, and hostilities commenced by Fair. Turner starting the leather from the town-end. The return was a very poor one, and the home forwards dashed up, thus confining play to the vieiters' quarters. Whittle was first to the fore by a good pass to Barnes, who repassed to Boardman, this player gaining ground, but Radcliffe saved by a well-timed kick into touch. Some severe scrimmages now took place, the home forwards trying hard to score, their attempts being frus- trated by the tactics of Harrison, who saved by kicking dead, three touchdowns being the only result, Frank Turner all but scoring after a fine break through and dribble, whilst his brother nearly got over after a dashing ran. The visitors now seemed to exert thernsSives, for by fine forward play the leather was taken to the centre, Sabin and Hasleham at times putting in good work. From the quarter, Sabin received the ball from Tay- lor, and seemed likely to score, but Barnes put a damper to his hopes by making him kiss mother earth. Aehton, Heyes, Povey, and Frank Turner, by a lively dribble, took the leather within a few yards of the goal line, but Harrison was equal to the occasion, saying finely. The brothers Turner were next to the front, the "small boy" by a strong run, and Frank by a dribble, Harrison only just saying in time. The trio, Whittle, Asbten, and Fair. Turner, now dribbled to the line, but Harrison picking up nearly ran round the posts and kicked into touch at the other side of the field, a performance deserving all the shouts of approbation such play deserved. The forwards now followed up this slight advantage, for by a combined dribble they took the ball to centre; but Buxton was equal to the occasion, re- taliating with a fine punt to touch. The same player shortly afterwards showed that he was as good, if not better, than the visitors' full back, for on obtaining the leather he got in a good run, kicked, and followed well up, collaring the visitors' back with the ball in his possession— a really good performance, and a piece of play which was evidently to the taste of the spectators. The home forwards now kept play for some time on the goal line, Heyes struggling over, but being overpowered by numbers, he was pushed into touch-in-goal. Massey, how- ever,on fromtheo tshpeer aski side, ,whaes gotnot, over, r, bedenled Speakmanfo g r kriecckelinvi n g the ball a bga neo aod uci et i play xa yto just n goal.w h o beforeilaal ll f-oossubenod by yl y afterwardsEo axrcahmani ‘nyvactiaei ends. ted! des beingt gainedme w i wastrag Povey first led off by a smart dribble, and for scene time play was very even. After some severe scrimmageq, of which Warrington had the best of it, Ashtoe got hod, got in a short run, and then transferred to Barnes, who 'got over, scoring try No. 2. Fair. Turner made a good attempt, but failed to convert it into a premier point. From this period of the game for a long time nothing was scored, the play being pretty evenly balanced, the oval sometimes be- ' fle. at one end and sometimes at the other. Whittle, Snea kman and Barnes on the one hand, and Sabin, Rad- eliffe, and Taylor on the other playing grandly for their respective sides. Eventually, Speakman put in a sharp pass Barnes, who seemed .all over a scorer, but unselfishly to f "Ind aru " dto Massey, this piece o bber bounding passe over we. • the greatest of ease, but again Fair. Turner's ,la judgment at goal proved wrong. The visitors now strove hard to get in a point, but the home forwards were top se ' watchful for them, and from now until the clo of the game, nothing but minors were scored, and these were in favour of the home team, t quarter of an hour Rigby, Po'yer, and During the last Frank Turner had hard lines in not scoring. Whittle also got over, but Graham coming up at fun speed threw him into play again. bl The referee shortly afterwards blew his whistle, and brought to a conclusion one of the fastest pleasantest, and best passing games ever witnessed by .eed b thea Spectators on this ground. Commenting on individualplhiy; it may be said that Buxton never played a better game, tackling and following up being one of the principal fea- tures of the game. The three-quarters acquitted . them- selves in a very creditable manner, the play of Barnes betne, a treat to witness. He passed most unselfishly, and if he adopts this practice with the same success es last week, he will acquire more fame as an unselfish player, as he has dens in the past, as a goal-kicker. Wreittle'e first appear- ance was a decided success, playing up to expectation, his I partner, Speakman, also playing a sterling game. Coining Ii
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY MARCH 20, 1886.,

to the front division, Povey, Rigby, and Ashton were very prominent in the loose, whilst Fair. Turner and Reyes tackled splendidly. Frank Turner's play deserves special mention, being quite good enough for county honours. Of the visitors Sabin, Radcliffe, and Harrison played a good game behind, whilst Haslehava, Barrow, and Wilson were the pick of the scrimmagers:

The teams were : Warrington: Back, Burton; tree- quarter backs, Boardman, Barnes, and Massey; half-backs, Whittle and Speakman ; forwards, F. Turner, Fair. Turner, Rigby, Dillon, Ashton, Ifeyes, Povev (captain), Davies, and Hough. Manchester Rangers : 'Back, Barrison •' three- quarter backs, Sabin, Radcliffe, Graham; half-backs, Taylor and Dawson ; forwards (captain), H. Elasleham, E. Plasle'•iatu, Wilson, Jones, Pollard, Dail, Galley, Barrow, and Bainbridge.

NOTES BY THE WAY. Great excitoment is being caused in Warrington and the sarrouni:ing districts Or the meeting of the Widnes and War- rington clubs to-day in the second round of the West Lan- cashire cup tie. Both sides will be strongly represented, but Warrington will again be without the services of War- ren, their captain. Each club is confident of winning, both being in grand form, but we venture to predict that victory will rest with the Wat,:ugtonians by a few points. Saturday last ought to lave witnessed the conapetiion of the first round of the Border Union Cup ties. However, king frost again ruled, and in consequence one fixtsre, that of Walton v. Bootle, had to be postponed. A very even game proved how equally matched are St. Helens and Wavettree, who met at the latter place. After the expira- tion of 2 mica. 40 secs. the Saints bad scored 3 minors to 2, and after an additional 20 mine. The game was drawn. The teams will have to meet again at Wavertree probably next Saturday.

' Wigan faced Blackrod on their own ground, and as the visitors only beat Blackred at Wigan a few weeks ago by 1 try, an even game was anticipated. During the first half the home team bad the advantage, recording a try and several minors, but fell off considerably in the second por- tion. Banks and Smith, both ran in, and in each case the points were converted into goals. Aspuli well nigh sustained a reverse at Southport, the Olympic showing that their defeat by the same club a short time ago by 2 goals and 1 try, to 1 try, was not their true form. According to the statement of an eye-witness, if the home players had been better supported by their full back, result would have been altered. Lund, the three quarters, who played against West Cumberland at Warrington, was somewhat off colour, but his partner, Price, showed capital form. Pagefield sat on Newton•le-Willows. The match was played at Pagefield, and at the termination a protest was lodged against two of the Pagefield players on account of professionalism. The protest was squashed, as was also one from Blackrod against Binks, of the Wigan Club. Music bath charms, but apparently it had very little effect upon Kirkdale, as Leigh, comfortably nilled them, recording five goals, two tries, and ten minors. A band met the visitors at the station aed escorted them to the dressing- room, playing seine lively airs. Reports speak of the atten- dance numbering 3,000, but this is too tall. The Leighites have not lost a single match this season, and naturally are very confident, but it is thought that the chances are that Runcorn will spoil their splendid record next Saturday. As Widnes did not feel inclined to be idle, a match was arranged with the Rec's. from St. Hens, the Chemicals proving the victors by one try. This form of Widnes must be materially improved to dispose of Warrington. The " mashers " from Sale had to take a back seat, when they opposed Runcorn at Brooklands last Saturday. Manchester Rangers played a capital game at Warrington. Their quick long passing at Vie opening of the match served to stimu- late the cup favourites to follow suit. This they did throughout, and it was about the best exhibition of the Rugby rules ever seen in the town. If they perform as well against Widnes, they are certain to come off with fly- ing colours. The international match at Raeburn-place, Edinbergli, proved a draw, after a grand struggle. There were nearly 10,000 spectators.
