and then an army of people would find employment all over the country. He asked the people of that division to support Mr. Leadana, because in so doing they would be as- sisting Mr. Gladstone, the purest and soundest-minded man in the House of Commune. (Cheers.) Mr. LEADAM, who was enthusiastically received, said the expressions which the chairman had used, in relation to their late lamented member, Mr. Brooks, bad. he was sure, found an echo in the hearts of all who had heard him. Deatk was al ways terrible, but most so when it cut short a career of promise, and he thanked God that between Eng- lish political opponents there did not yet eiist that acrimo- nious venom which should forbid them conveying to their Conservative friends from the bottom of their hearts an ex- pression of btotherly sympathy in the lose which had befal- len them and the constituency. Mr. Brooks, he knew, both during the late contest and after the election, rapidly en- deared himself to the constituency by his gracious and kindly bearing, and be was happy to remember that only about a month ago he had the pleasure of meeting Mr. Brooles in London, and of exehanging with him some words which showed that any trifing asperities which might have arisen during the contest had been swept out of recollection. (Cheers.) He would be doing less than justice to his poli- tical allies and to himself if be were not to say that they env and all deplored as men might the unhappy occasion which hal led to the present contest. (Hear, hear.) The chairman had remarked that some changes had taken place in the main features of politics since last he addressed them in that hall, and amongst those changes there was ens which had particularly riveted the attention of the public, he meant the change in the attitude of the two politieal parties towards Ireland. In November last, when be spoke there, there existed an alliance between the Conservative party and the Parnellitea. Since then the Irish elections had been declared, and declared with a very remarkable re- sult—a result that had been followed by a new departure on either side. Taking first the position of Mr. Gladstone, he had held out unquestionably a certain olive branch to the Home Rulers, and in consequence of that he bad been, per- haps, considering the circumstances, not unnaturally, hotly denounced by his political adversaries. But what if Mr. Gladstoue had held out that olive branch immediately prior to the general election? (Hear, hear.) They could picture to themselves what the probable language of the Conserva- tive party would have been. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) They could imagine how Lord Randolph Churchill— (laughter aid hooting)—with his hands in this Irish matter so immaculately clean, would have denounced the man whom the Conservatives were fond of calling a hoary- headed traitor for being anxious to barter his country for the sake of place and power. Since Ireland bye majority of some five-sixths of her people had declared her fixed determination to enjoy Home Rule, what had Mr. Gladstone's language been? On the 21st of January in the Vous() of Commons be quoted and reaffirmed the words which he uttered in September. He had then facing him the constitutional fact, which must never be absent from their minas, that for the first time in history the people of Ireland, a largely extended electorate, bad with most singular unanimity declared its wishes. On the 4th of this month Mr. Gladstone said that,iconsidering the state of Irelend, his Government had arrived at the conclu- sion that at the juncture at which they stood they would not be justified in proposing to supply the defects of social crier in that country by means of sp4cial repressive legis- lation, but that it was their duty to*searcle out more posi- tive, substantial remedial measures. (Cheers.) Passing from Mr. Gladatone'e position, which he thought had been unfairly and unjustly attacked, let him consider the general aspect of the Irish question. We had been for 600 years past endeavouring to govern Ireland according to our own English notions. (Hear, hear.) Some of them might be aware that a few years ago he wrote a history of coercive measures in Ireland, and he investigated from the Blue Books the success which had attended them. He found that, roughly speaking, some fifty coercive measures had been passed since the beginning of the present century, and he further found, from the returns of Irish crime, that al- most without exception the effect of them had been to in- crease rather than to diminish crime in the country—(hear, hear,)—because the moment they had a coercion act in Ire- land, such was the temper of the people that a sort of politi- cal halo gathered round social disorder, and even about the most brutal, the most common, and the most despicable misdemeanours. And their position in regard to this qaes- tion. was made stronger by the line which the Tory party had taken. The Conservatives made the most of the Irish vote, though how many seats they gained by it was perhaps a little difficult to compete. When January came round, there was a sudden betrayal of their allies. One Saturday night Mr. Smith was sent to Ireland on a mission— (laughter)—and on Monday morning he declared that he bad found coercion to be necessary once more—(renewed laughter)—and the Conservative Go- vernment had the face to meet Parliament and their late allies with the announcement that their one prescription for Irish ills was the enactment of a new coercion law. What was the cause of that ? Was there anything he the condition of Ireland to justify that sudden chance of frcnt. They might judge of the condition of Ire- land by the amount of agrarian crime that prevailed, and also by the extension of that new feature of Irish politico, the unhappy practice of boycotting. In May, while the Liberals were in office' there were 227 cases of boycotting. In September, when the Conservative Government had been in office for some time, there were 879. That, he supposed, constituted the abundant justification of which Lord Ran- dolph Churchill spoke. (Laughter.) Coming to January the number was 900, so that, though the previous increase of 600 was not sufficient to shake Lord Randolph's confidence, the addition of 21 cases when the general election was safely over made all the difference. (Laughter and cheers.) Then with respect to agrarian crime, in October there were 106 agrarian crimes in Ireland. In November there were 84, in December 89, in January 96, and in February, he believed, 71. The 106 were he October, when to dispense with coer- cion was a proceeding abundantly justified. Why, then, was it necessary to have a coercive measure to deal with 71 cases in February? They would have to come to the con- clusion that coercion was an absolute heal-all for the woes of Ireland or that it was not. If it was needed in January it certainly was needed in October, and therefore they might present to their Conservative friends this dilemma, that either they betrayed the national interests for the sake of getting the Irish vote, or they were now proposing a policy which they knew to be uselesseand which they themselves bad discredited for the sake of cloaking their own political barrenness. (Cheers.) Whether they regarded their con- duct to this nation on the one hand, or to their Irish allies on the other, he thought they would be disposed to pro- nounce that action se cynical and betrayal so mean had never disgraced the annals of English political life since the time of the unprincipled adventurers of the Restoration. (Cheers.) During the course of the next few days he would have several opportunities of entering more at large into this matter of Ireland. At present what he wished to im- press upon them was that whatever measures Mr. Gladstone applied he had already affirmed he would apply, subject to the substantial unity of the empire and the supremacy of the Queen. (Cheers.) It was-a great problem of construc- tive politics, a problem in the !wee of which the Conserva- tives by their own admission stood paralysed and impotent. They had no shadow of remedy, to propose, and therefore it was the duty of the country to commit the problem to the only man who could face it—(cheers)—and whose prac- tised genius and fruitful experience would command, he believed, the confidence of hie fellow-countrymen. (Cheers.) Mr. JESSE HAWORTH moved :----" That this meeting con- siders Mr. 1. S. Leadam a proper person to represent this constituency in Parliament, and pledges itself to use all legitimate means to secure laiareturn." Mr. Gladstone had come forward in his old age, when he had no ambition to serve, and no personal end to gain, and the Liberals of Altrincham could best assist him by returning to the House of Commons Mr. L S. Leaden), Mr. H. T. GADDIIM seconded the motion, and said he was sure Mr. Leadam would worthily represent the division in Parliament.

Mr. M. PEKE supported the resolution, and as a Church- man expressed the opinion that the Established Church was in no danger from Mr. Leadam. Mr. GEORGE BOWEN (Mayor of Altrincham) also sup- ported the resolution, and expressed confidence as to the result of the election. He said the Liberals now were in a better position than they were at the last election. On this occasion they had started in good time; they were well organised, and they had a candidate of whom they might well be prwd. Mr. B. J. LEACH further supported the resolution, which was carried unanimously and amid loud ckeering. Ques- tions were invitq, but none were asked. Mr. LEADAM briefly replied, and was received with re- newed cheering. A Ite of thanks
then

. vote of .lanks was . passed to the chairman-, on the motion of Mr. THOMAS STEPHENS, seconded by Mr. C. Mon- los, and supported by Mr. WILLIAM MILNE. The CHAIRMAN briefly replied, and the meeting was brought to a close.

In a speech which he delivered at Bollingten last July, he quoted the opinion of Lord Salisbury on the subject of agri- cultural reforms, which he advocated, and penned out that they had little to expect from the Conservatiyes. He thought he ought to take out a license as a prophet—(lar:oe ter)—for everything be had said had come true. (leonewed laughter.) After commenting ow the action of Captain Cot- ton, and the Hon. Alan de Tatton Egerton, Mr. 'Leadam referred to the conduct of Messrs. Barclay and Balfour, who had for years been working with him on the Executive Com- mittee of the Farmers' Alliance. It was, he said, a slap in the face for the faithful farmer, and on the 26th of January the Conservatives determined to give the labourers a clap in the face. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Jesse Collings introduced 3R amendment as follows:—"This House humbly expresses its regret that no measures are announced by Her _Majesty for the present relief of theoe classes, and especially for affordi ing facilities to the agricultural labourers and others in the rural districts to obtain allotments and small holdings on equitable terms as to rent and security of tenure." That amendment was seconded by Captain Verney—(loud applause)--and was opposed by Mr. Chaplin on behalf of the Government, but there was not a'word in his speech about Ireland. (Hear, bear.) They must deal with the hypothesis. Where would Sir William Cunliffe Brooks have been in the House ? He had taken the trouble to look at the attendances of Sir William where he was a member of Parliament, and he found that when two very important measures for farmers were brought forward, and Sir William sat a member for Cheshire, he did not find it possible to be present, although the measures had reference to the Agri- cultural Holdings Act and the Ground Game Act. (Hear, hear.) Sir Cunliffe Brooks was in l'arliament in 188'5, and although there were 225 divisions he did not find it conve- nient to be present at more than 26. (Laughter.) He (Mr. Leadam) asked those present where would Sir Cunliffe be if .he was returned ? (Laughter.) He answered the question by stating that he would be absent. The British termer was a patient being, accustomed to buffets, and Came up smiling afterwards. (Laughter.) The labourers had notions, and would not be humbugged by fair trade, and could not see how tkey would be benefited by paying more for their clothes, food, dic. (Hear, hear.) The Conservative party had shown that they would ride roughshod over farmers, but he thought after the way in which Mr. Collings' proposition was entertainee, they would see that they must be cautious how they aroused the labourers. (cheers.) _

Mr. BREWTNALL proposed, and Mr. J. HOLT seconded, " That this meeting considers Mr. Leadam a fit and proper person to represent the Al trincham Division in Parliament, and pledges itself to use every legitimate meats to secure II his return." (Cheers.) Mr. Barniernu, M.P., who was received with loud ap- plause, said that the question they had before them in that division was not /be difference between the "Golden Pippin," as Sir William Cunliffe Brooks was called, and ; Mr. Leadam, but it was the question of whether England was going right or wrong. It was "Were they going to keep on the same bad old road? "—k" No ")—and it was not only a bad road for Ireland, but for England also. (Hear, hear.) A great deal had been said, and would be said, about the money that Ireland cost us, and the money that Mr. Gladstone wanted us, probably, to guarantee for Ireland; but let him tell them that they could hardly put their hands deep enough in their pockets when on one side it was a question of Claristian kindness, and on the ether of black hearted tyranny. He recommended them to make up their minds before hand that, Caine what might, and come what sacrifice should be put before them, they would be men enough to stand it. There were a good many things to consider besides Ireland. Taxes were not laid on fairly, and agricultural gentlemen present would understand hiel when he said that there was not a man in the country who was as hard hit and as unjustly treated on the rates as the farmers, unless it were the small shopkeepers. But the Irish farmers were treated far worse in this matter than the English farmers. There was not a thing that was wrong in England, but was worse in Ireland. Until they got the question of Ireland out of the way, and left Irishmen to settle their own questions of rating, they would not get their own matters put right. They had not that day to choose between two men, but between two sets of plinciplee. Tbey wanted a man who would work for them—(applause)—and he could recommend Mr. Leadatn as a man of sound commonsense— (renewed applause)—and of industry. He wanted them to send Mr. Leadam to Parliament in order that he might help all the men of commonsense and industry in the work they had get to do on behalf of the people. Mr. Leadana would vote for the amending of the Employers' Liability Act, and against working railway servants too long hours. They of the Liberal party desired to make every man equal before the law. (Cheers.) Mr. HOWELL, M.P., on rising to address the meeting, was also received with cheers. The rule of the Tories, be said, was one of mistrust, and that of the Liberals one of trust, which was the great distinction between the two. The Liberal party was always attempting to make progress, and the Tory party were always blocking %lee way, and when- ever they gave a measure of reform it was because they dare not block the way any longer. (Applause.) After touching upon the Irish question, Mr. flow.ell said that the English land laws required considering, and they wanted the very best men that could be sent from Cheshire to help them through with the land question. If they would only back up Mr. Gladstone in his scheme for remodelling the land laws of this country, then, depend upon it, the farmers and farm labourers, and artizies of our ' towns' would no longer be led astray upon the question of fair trade or protection. (Cheers.) The resolution was then carried, and a vote of thanks to the chairman concluded the proceedings. MR.. LNADAM AT TIMPERLEY. Mr. Leadam was present at a meeting of electors on Wed- nesday evening aleTimperley, and delivered an address, in which he expressed general approval of the views which Mr. Gladstone is said to entertain in regard to Ireland. He asked the voters in that constituency not to be humbugged by the fables which the Tory party are circulating to the effect that Mr._ Gladstone is about to aek them to provide 150 millions sterling for the purpose of buying out the Irish landlords, for the proposal simply was that the money which we now spend on Ireland in one direction should in future be spent in another.

MR. LEADAM AT CHEADLE HULME. On Thursday night, Mr. I. S. Leadam, the Liberal canc;i7 date, addressed a meeting of the electors at Cheadle Huhef, in the Congregational schoolroom. Mr. Alexander Boyd presided, and among those dn the platform were Mr. Cameron Corbett, M.P. Mr. Leadam contrasted the Liberal and Tory principles of government, and discussed in detail the Irish question in somewhat similar terms as at his pre- vious meetings. Mr. Whittington moved a resolution pledging the meeting to support Mr. Leadam. The resolu- tion was seconded by Mr. Ward, and supported by Mr. Cameron Corbett; M.P., who said he had been sent down from Ole House of Commons as an expression of the earnest desire on the part of their leaders that Mr. Leadam should secure a victory. Such a victory would be of immense ser- vice to the party.,--The resolution was carried with enthu- siasm.

A meeting in support of Sir W. C. Brooks, the Conserva- tive candidate, was held at Altrincnam on Wednesday evening. A vote of confidence in Sir William was carried. Sir William had not then returned from France. The nomination for the Division has been fixed for the 22nd, and the polling for the 26th inst.

div.head: FAMOUS
div.p: FAMOUS
Ma. I. S. LEADAM AT LYMM.

On Tuesday evening Mr. I. S. Leadam addressed an en- thusiastic meeting of his supporters at the Plough Hotel, Lymm, he and his friends being heartily cheered on enter- ing the room.. The chair was occupied by Mr: W. Long, I who was supported by Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., for the Northwich Division : Mr. George Howell, M.P., Mr. E. Brewtnall, and Mr. Swanwick. The CHAIRMAN said that before passing to the business • of the evening be wished to express their unfeigned sorrow and sympathy at the event that had called them together. He was sure that they all ,regretted. the untimely removal from a position of public usefulness of a man like their late antagonist Mr. Brooks. But they must remember that they had a duty to perform to themselves and they entered upon that contest with a feeling of determination that if possible they would carry still further the victory they obtained at the last general election in wresting four of the seats of Cheshire from the Tory party who had so long dominated. (Applause.) Mr. LICADAM, whose rising was the signal for continued applause, after a kindly reference to the death of Mr. Brooks, proceeded to speak at length on the Irish question. 'the Conservative party proposed to catch a wolf by the ear and then did not know whether to hold on or leave go. (Laughter.) To act in the way the Conservative party had done was to betray their entire political impotence. (Ap- plause.). The time was come for some more positive, sub. etantive, and remedial measures. Mr. Gladstone said that , INA- must preserve the right of minorities, the unity of the empire, and the supremacy of the Queen, and upon these principks, and that a concession can and must be • made, he was prepared to take his stand in that election. (Applause.) Passing to the internal English policy of the Cons,rvative Government, Mr. Leadam re- ferred to Mr. Barclay's motion in the House of Commons.

div.head: 'VACANCY IN THE ALTRINCHAM
div.p: THE 'VACANCY IN THE ALTRINCHAM

SELECTION OF THE CONSERVATIVE CANDIDATE. On Saturday afternoon a meeting of the Conser- vative Association of the Altrineham. Division of Cheshire took place at the Conservative Club, Altrincham, and was largely attended. In the ab- sence of Lord Egerton (the president of the Associa- tion), who sent a telegram expressing regret that lie was unal4le to be present, the chair was occupied by Mr. T. H. Sykes. The following resolution was adopted, on the motion of the CHAIRMAN :—" That this meetingof representatives of the Conservative party in the Altrincham Division expresses its deep sense of the irreparable loss the division has sus- tained in the death of Mr. Brooks, M.P." It was also decided to send an expression of heartfelt sym- pathy to Mrs. Brooks, the wife of the late member. Mr. P. STUBBS (Lymm) afterwards proposed that the meeting should request Sir William Cunliffe Brooks, Bart., to become the Conservative candidate for the representation of the division in Parliament. —This was seconded by Mr. S. CHRISTY (Stockport), and after being supported by Mr. Alderman Griffin and Dr. James, was carried with much enthusiasm. —During the meeting the CHAIRMAN announced that he had received a telegram from Sir William Cunliffe Brooks, who stated that he was willing to contest the vacant seat in the Conserva- tive interest. MR. LEADAM AT ALTRINCHAM. An enthusiastic meeting was held on Monday night in the British School, Altrincham, in support of the candidature of Mr. I. S. Leadam, who has been selected to contest, in the Liberal interest, the Altrincham division of Cheshire,. a vacancy in the representation of which was caused by the death of the late Mr. John Brooks. Sir Joseph Lee presided, ' and the la-ge room was filled in every part, while many people were unable to obtain admission. Among those on the platform were Mr. J.l'. Brunner, M.P., Mr. T. H.Ver- non, Mr. A. Evans, Mr. A. A. Atherton, Mr. E. Potts, Mr. James Robertson, Mr. J. H. Haworth, Mr. Thomas S. Haworth, Mr. James Russell, Mr. Wm. Johnson, Mr. W. S. Adams, Mr. Jesse Haworth, the Rev. E. Armitage, Mr. H. I T. Gaddure, Mr. George Davies, Mr. W. H. Johnson, Mr. James M'Kean, Mr. Abel Heywood, Mr. A. Kendal, Mr. A. • Hogg, Mr. W. M. Johnson, -Mr. A. H. Ambler, Mr. C. J. • Morris, and Mr. T. Stephens. . When Mr. Leadam entered the room he was loudly cheered. Die CILIIRMAN said they all knew of the sad event that had called them together that night. They all would de- plore that a life which seemed so full of promise should have been terminated so soon, and would agree in expres- sing condolence with the bereaved. The fact that it would be impossible for the Conservative party to bring forward another such a candidate convinced the Liberals that they would not be doing their duty i!ither to their party or to the constituency if they did not again enter into the fray with new zeal—(cheers); lend on Friday the Liberal Council unanimously decided to ask Mr. Leadam to fight the battle for them., .(Cheers.) The Conservative party bad signally failed in their attempt to deal with the Irish difficulty, and therefore the Liberal party was entitled to ask for the con- fidence and support of the country in their efforts to deal with this perplexing question. Mr. Gladstone would no doubt gain some strength if the Liberals of Altrincham returned Mr. Leatam to the House of Commons, and that they could do so if they worked hard he (the chairman) was convinced. (Cheers.) Mr. J. T. BRUNNER, M.P., who was received with loud cheers, then addressed the meeting. He said we stood to- day at the threshold of a crisis as great as any man among us had seer. The question of the relation that is to exist between England and Ireland must be settled, not only for the sake of England, but for the seke of Ireland as well— (hear)—and he had every confidence that Mr. Gladstone of all men was the best to provide a safe solution of the diffi- culty. He hoped Mr. Leadani, if returned to Parliament, would advocate for England a homestead law by which every man would have his household furnitere secured to him. In the United States and in Germany the law was such that no creditor could take a man's furniture and leave him in ellen a etate that he Ltd to seek assistance from the rates. Anether reform needed for EnglanO, was that the land should be freed. Mr. Brunner went ma to speak of the depression in trade and said the remedy for it was not to be found in doing trade, trade, but rather in doing more. The Tories suggested as a remedy for the preeent state of trade that import duties should be put upon tnanufactured articles which came from abroad. This was all 'nonsense. In deal- ings between ceuutries goods were paid for not by cash but by goods, and if England bought less from foreign countries she would most assuredly sell lese to them. He recom- mended the people to buy where they liked and not where the manufacturers in Manchester suggeeted. The real cure for the depreesion in trade was in the first place to give se- curity to every farmer in the Country, and in the next place to enfranchise every ease in the country wherever possible,

Her Majesty Ithe Queen arrived at Buckingham Palace on Wednesday morning from Windsor Castle, on a visit to the Duchess. A neighlsonring farmer stopped the train, and savad the man's life by improvising a danger signal with his hat and Mrs. Weldon's action against W. H. The Lord Chief Justice remarked that Mrs. Weldon had behaved very gener- ously, Mr. Parnell was not present at the St. Patrick's Day ban- quet in London en Wednesday evening. "Indisposition is mentioned as the cause of hie absence. Mr. E. D. I Gray, M.P:rpresided, and proposed the toast of "Ireland a I nation."

A FATAL Dar.—Two young artillery sergeants garri- soned at 'Vincennes, France, have fought a duel with p:•s- tols in one of the rooms in the barracks no witness being present. Both were shot in the heart. 'Jealousy was ths cause of the duel. %% bile about 100. persons were upon the ice on the large lake at Black Park, Langley, the estate of Sir Robert Har- vey, on Sunday afternoon, it suddenly gave way, and two, persons, a youth named Langton. of iver, and a Mr. Dunton Baker, Uxbridge, were drowned. SWING BOAT ACCIDENT.—Mary Matthews, factory opera- tive, has met with a shocking death at Newtown, near Wigan. She was in a small swing boat with the landlOrd of an adjoining public-house, when she screamed loudly and immediately fell over the side, alighting on her head. She died shortly afterwartb. ARMY ESTIBIATES.-1 he Army Estimates issued on Wed- nesday, after deducting appropriations in aid, amount to ' £18,2.33,200. as against £17,750,700, with a supplementary estimate of £lOO for the year which is about to close, the net increase being £482,50a The number of officers and men on the establishment of the regular army, exclusive of India, is 151,867, as against 142,194 at the beginning of last year. Saunders says :—.* I have I often lirnitedinfeetious diseases to the room occupied by the sufferer by nailing a sheet saturated with dilute Condy's !I Fluid over the doorway." Caution :—Condy's Fluid beais the name of Coudy and 'Mitchell at foot of every label. Beware , of worthless colourable imitatilons.—Ativt. JUST So.--Whatever ()the:, tax may be remitted in the coining Budget, it seems certain that the carriage tax will Ibe continued. Sir William Harcourt received a deputation t of carriage builders on Wednecday, and though he c,uld not I agree that the tax was destroying the trade, he said the : question of a remission might be well considered in more prosperous times.

_ APPLYING "THE SCREW " TO MICHAEL DATITT.—After delivering his lecture on Home Rule at Oxford on Tuesday night, Mr. Michael Davitt became the guest of an under- graduate, and slept within the University College build.- logs. His presence appears to have been objectionable to certain persons, who during the night screwed up the door of the room so firmly that cri Wednesday morning Mr. Devitt was obliged to leave by the window. His brief "resi- dence" bad been sanctioned by the authorities. MR. BRADLAUGH, M.P., ott•lnitE IRISH QUESTION.—Mr. Bradlaugh, speaking on Sunday. at Liverpool on the Irish question, suggested that Mr. Parnell. who was the leader of nearly 90 members in the House of Commons, ought to pos- sess a policy, and ought to state in Parliament what he wanted. Tne task Mr. Gladstone had before bial was not easy, as he would have the whe4e *court influence against him,; but if anyone could settle the Irish question it was Mr. Glacittone, and to those Irishmen who mig'ut think the Prime Minister did not go far enough ha would say," Take all you can." SO6IALIST DEMONSTRATION IN,GLASGOW.—The Glasgow section of the Social Denaocratio Federation convened a meeting of the unemployed and others at Glasgow Green on Sunday afternoon. The bills announcing the meeing asked " Why should men starve .?" and also stated that John Burns, "the great Sociatiot orator," now under Gov- ernment prosecution, would attend. All the night and day constables were on duty and stationed in detachments 50 strong in the neighbourhood of the crowd, which numbeFed from 40,000 to 50,000. There were a good many of the dis- orderly class present. IPSWICH ELECTION PETITION.-.—The hearing of the Ips- wich election petition was resumed-on Saturday. Mr. Nash, secretary of the Liberal Associajon„ stated that he engaged Gunn as a messenger at the county election. did not Gunn was a bankrupt publican.—Gase proceeding.—On Monday, Mr. ,:ustice Denman remarked that in all prob- ability the judges would report some eight or ten persons, and at the conclusion of the learned counsel's speeches ad- journ the case to some future day. Evidence was soon afterwards closed, and, on the conclusion of the ad- dresses by counsel, their lordships adjourned the case for a fortnight

M. BRIGHT ON SECOND BALLDTS,—Mr. John Bright, re- plying to a correspondent who suggested a second ballot in all Parliamentary elections in which no candidate receives an absolute majority of the votes- polled, suggests that the remedy proposed might produce an evil greater than the correspondent wishes to remove. The evil is, the right hon. gentleman thinks, rather temporary than permanent, and he believes that the experience of- the late election will do much to prevent a repetition of the folly and blunders which we all regret and condemn. He is afraid that if we had a second ballot, as in France, we should have far more cases of too many candidates, and that we should have more vain and foolish and selfish men offering themselves to con- stituencies than we have now, or are likely to have if our present system is continued. .

THE UNEMPLOYED IN LtiAIVaRESTER.—The unemployed in Manchester had another demonstration on Thursday, and some of them acted in a very disreputable manner. -Being informed that they could not be allowed to hold any more meetings in Albert-sqaare, part of their number marched to New Cross. Whilat proceeding along Oldham-street, one of ; them hurled a stone through the window of the shop of a firm of drapers. Later in the day another attempt was made Iby a numerous body of men to congregate in Albert-square for the purpose of' holding a meeting there, but it was de- feated by the vigilance of the police. Three persons out of employment were arrested during the morning on a charge !of obstructing the streets, and were brought before the city I magistrates, who remanded them for a week, the men being I liberated on their own recegnisances. e, I THE ALLOTIZENT QUESTION.—Mr. Jesse Collings, elev., has written a latter to a gentleman at Wareham in reply to a communication respecting his efforts on the labourers' behalf, and th 3 laying out of allotments by Tory landowners. In the letter Mr. Collings- states :—"I can assure you that ; any service which I have been able to render to my friends the labourera has been a labour of love, and I trust that the I tune is not far distant when the hard lot of the rural la- ' bourers of this country will be lightened and made brighter for them. There is no doubt that one result 0: our efforts- its relation to allotments and small holdings has been, as YOU say, to make the Tory landowners move in the direc- tion of supplying the wants of the men in a manner that they would not have done but for those efforts, and for the fact that the men new possess the vote." FATAL GAS Emostcne : THREE PERSONS KILLED Tuesdaet afternoon a gas explosion occurred in a three- storied house in Coppul-lane, Wigan, blowing out the front of the building, and killing two children and injuring six other persons who were in the street at the time. An escape of gae.had been noticed for some time past, although the house was not supplied with it. The gas must havd found. its way into the house from the street mains. It was ignited under the kitchen fire. None o 2 the Inmates of tho house were injured. On Tues- day. night Thomas Wilson, lamplighterr, one of those injured by the explosion, died at the infirmary, where he was removed after the accident, Wilson was passing the house when the explosion occurred, and was knoeked dawn and buried by the falling debris. When removed hi 3 head was found to be badly hurt and one arm almost tern away. The deceased was about sixty yea's of ago. THE BELT CasE.—On Monday,the Attorney-General replied on the whole case, and said the previous histories of the par- ties concerned,which had bean dragged into the case, had nothing to do with it.—Mr. Justice Stephen then summed up, pointing out that it was a false pretence to say that the diamonds were very pure stones, or that they had belonged • to a Mrs. IVlorphy, who had been mistress of the Sultan, and if the jury believed that Sir William Maly had been in- duced to purchase by these representations, they would be justified in finding both prisoners guilty. Tele case against Walter Belt was much weaker than that against his brother Richard.—The jury returned a verdict of "Guilty" against ' Richard Belt for obtaining money by false pretences, and "Not guilty" against Walter Belt, —The prisoner convicted was sentenced to twelve months' imprisonment with hard labour.

A WARRINGTON LADY KILLEIi ON THE RAILWAY LINE. At about ten o'clock on Sunday morning Mil Cooper, of Warrington, who tin to recently carried on business in Norsemarket-street, was knocked lown by the Southport express when crossing the line ay Irlam Station, and cut to piece & Death was inst,l4' taneous. Miss Cover had gone to Irlam to viBil some friends who live at Cadishead. Mr. F. Price, district coroner, held an inquest re- lative to the sad affair on Tuesday afternoon, at the Ship Inn, Irlam, when Ur. F. Simpson, chief of the Cheshire Lines police, watched the proceedings on he' half of the company. The Irlam stationmaster, gr. Hutchinson, was also pressant —Richard Taft, tobac- conist, Lb Horsemarket-street, said that the deceased was his sister-in-law, and had resided with hire' About two years ago she earned on business as a toY dealer, but had of late assisteelwitness in his business- On Sunday morning she left home to visit a friend at Cadishead, and soon after noon on the same day be heard of her death, and went over to Irlam, where he saw the remains. The body was so mutilated that he onl7 recognised the remains of his sister-in-law by the dress.—John Williamson, Hayessroad, Cadishead, a letter carrier employed delivering letters between Warrington and Cadishead, said that on Sunda," morning he travelled by the train whit+ left Warring' • ton at 8-56- o'clock. He went to Glazebrook in th° same compartment and there they had to-change- ee saw deceased again at Liam, where she was endear' ourhag to go across the up-line. She was walking in the four-foot when he heard a porter named Elliott call out to her to keep hack. She would then be in the six-foot. She turned her head towards Fli%ton and started to run across the down-line. The express train was approaching the station at a rapid speed, and before deceased could cross the line she wasstrurk by the right-hand side butler on the side of the head- Her head was knocked off her shoulders and carried towards the platform on which witness was standing. Her body was rolled up by the engine and the whole of the train went over it. Witness saw no one but the deceased attempt to cross the line by the level. A notice on each side of the station requested pa3sen" gers to cross the line by the bridge. The porter gave warning to those on the platform to stand back whet, the express was approaching and had deceased stoons still when he called out to her she would have been safe.—Th &fleas Elliott, Liverpool-road, Cadishead, porter at the station, gave evidence of a confirmatorl nature. He was the only porter there.—The Coroner saitl, that he did not think there was any blame to be attached to anyone, but asked whether one porter wee' suffelent to attend to the- station.—Mr. Hutchinson,' the stationmaster, said that there were two porters?, but only one was engaged on Sundays. He consider& one porter was sufficient. —The jury returned a vexa diet of "Accidental death."

PRESCOT BOARD OF GITIRDIAIS- The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians was held at Whiston Workhouse on Thursday forenoon- Present—Mr. J. Leatherbarrow (in the chair), Re. Father Finegan, Rev. J. Barnacle, Messrs. J. Griffiths, T. DobeD, W. G. Ashton, Jackson, E. Syder, H. Hu!me, W. Tyrer, T. Hall,. R. Leigh, J. Kenwright,.J. Ellison, W. Newsome, W. Birchall, W. Swift, P. Longton,.J. Fisher, W. Gerard, J. Matthew, T. Eatock, W. B. Longton, and S. H. HartleY (clerk).

EitE7.—The Workhouse Master reported that there were 533 inmates in the Workhouse this week, 533 last week, and 456 in the correspozding week last year 43' vagrants had been relieved, against 54 in the corresponding week of 1385. ALLEGED THRASHING —The Workhouse Master reported that P.O. Palmer, of Rainhill, had brought a boy named Twist to The Workhouse, whom he had found wandering about the street. The boy stated that his father had stripped him and beat him with small rods and twigs, and afterwards with an umbrella. The Beard postponed- consideration Of the matter until the close of the meeting, when the lad IVO brought to the room, and it was fou'ild that his back was almost covered with " stripes " and bruises. The Board directed the Clerk to make further inquiries into the matter.

VACCINATION AT RAINFORD.—The Local Government Board wrote acknowledging receipt of a schedule of the arrangements proposed for public vaccination in the Rain - ford gistriet, and stating that they were prepared to approve of a contract with Dr. Murdoch drawn in accordance with the schedule.—on the motion of the Rev. J. Barnacle, seconded by Mr. Fisher, it was resolved to send a draft coPY of an agreement to the Local Government Board. THE DISTRESS AND UNEMPLOYED, WATCIHISIAKERS.—The Clerk read the circular letter referred to in another column signed by the Right Hon. Joseph Chamberlain res- pecting pauperism and distress. Mr. Newsome said he thoroughl7 agreed with the spirit of the letter, whicb deserved the consideration of the Guardians. He sugges- ted that a committee be formed to employ any unemployed men, or consider what steps should be taken in the matter. —The Rev. Father Finegan said it was important if any- thing was to be done it should be done immediately. Ile moved that a committee be formed at once.—Mr. Fisher seconded :he motion, which was carried. The whole Board was appointed a committee, and the first meeting was tir;ed for Monday after- noon next—The Chairman remarked that a deputation of unemployed from V idnes were anxious to see the Board. - Do-aell aid not think it necessary after the action the Board were about to tase, and Mr. Matthews said he had taken it upon himself to say to the deputation that he did not think it was necessary for them to wait as the Board would do everything for them that they possibly could.--* The Cler:z intimated that with regard to the depression ill the watchmaking trade, which greatly acts Prescot, the Herologioal. society was moving in the matter of placing foreign watch naovements in English Hall-marked cases, and were about to promote a bill in Parliament to make it penal to pass off such watches as I:nglish made. It was for the Guardians to say whether thy would assist the Horological Society in their efforts.--Mr. 'Newsome thought a vote on that subject would be unanimous.—Mr. Tyrer moved that the Clerk draw up a form of petition as suggested.—Mr. Newsome seconded the motion, and from his personal knowl,dge of watchmakers iv the district could endorse what had, been said. There was far more distress amongst ' them than was generally known, and he hoped the petition would ha.drawn up as strongly as possible to express Os feelings of the Board.—The motion was carried pnani•- tnously.

THE 7NION AUDIT.—The Clerk reported receipt of notice that Mr. George Haelehurst, the district Gevernment auditor, would audit the accounts of the, Prescot Union for' the half-year ending June next on the sth April. THE WATER SUPPLY.—Regarding the,extra water supplye to the Workhouse in case of fire, Mr. Timmins, of Runcorn, who had been asked to report upon the question, was of opinion that it would be possible to get such supply from, Mr. Longton's quarries, at a cost not exceeding £2o.—Mr. Hill, after some cliscueeian, moved that the suggestion of Mr. Timmins with respeet to Mr. Longton's ability to pro- vide the increased supply at a cest4 not exceeding £2O he - carried our.—Mr. Tyre:, seconded the.motion, which wag. carried. - CIiARGE AGAINST D 3. COOPER.—The Clerk read a let- ter from Dr. Cooper, of Widnes, with reference to the death of a person named Whitfield, who died at Widnes, and uponr whose body an inquest had been held. Dr. Cooper submit- ted a statement of the bets, in the eetirse of which he stated that it was exattly 25e minutes to. two o'clock, as be was sitting down to dinner that Mrs Burke, with whom deceased lodged, came to his house and asked him to see Mrs Whit- field who she thought was in a fit. He told her what mea- sures to take immediately on her return home and that-he would follow her in a short time, which he was preparing to do, after having dinner, whee, at five minutes to two, scarcely 15 minutes- from the time Mrs Burke had quitted his surgery, a messenger arrived to say that Mr a Whitfield was dead ; in fact had died just as Mrs Burke entered her own house on her return. He merely called at four o'clock lie inquire whether notice- of the death hadilbeen given to Inspector Wood, as he knew nel was at lirescot. He could produce four wit- nesses to corrobeeate his statements if necessary.—The Clerk also read a letter upon the same subject from Edward Atherton, of Longton'e-row, Farnworth, brother of the de- ceabed woman, who complained of the action of Dr. Cooper with reference-to the case, and said be had given them a lot of trouble in the matter. The letter continued: "The per- son (who went for the doctor) told the jury what the doctor said to her, and „t hey crie6 shame on him for such treat- ment. On the Saturday became down to the house with a solicitor and tried to frighten the woman, but she stuck to what she said before the jury. I will leave- it to your judgment if such treatmeet is to be used towards the poor, hoping you will look further into it."—The Clerk intimated that Dr. Cooper had sinus called upon him and explained that he could not possibly have arrived at the house before the person died.—Mr. ilall thought the explanation a very satisfactory one, and that Dr. Cooper was not blameable in the case. He moved that the report be considered satisfac- tory, and that Dr. Cooper had not been negligent in the case. The Rev Father Finegan, in seconding the motion, said he thought it hard that professional men like doctors should be censured without hearing what they had to say. The same coroner had condemned one of their relieving eXcers, but when the officer gave his emplaeation it was unanianousle resolved that he was not to blame at all. Now the same coroner was making a se- rious charge against the doctor at Widnes.—The motion was unanimously passed.

-- MR. CHAMBERLAIN AND WELSH DISESTABLISHMENT.— Certain Mold electors baying written to Mr. Chamberlain expressing regret that he did not take part in the debate or division on Mr. Dillwyn's motion for the disestablishment of the Church of England in Wales, the following reply has been received:—'• 40, Prince's Gardens, London.—Sir,—Mr. ebamberlain is unable to recognise any right on your part to question his actions as a member of Parliament. you appear, however, entirely to misunderstand the position. The Government are not able—partly in consequence of the pressure of other business, and partly owing to statements before the election by Mr. Gladstone and others—to attempt the final settlement of the question of the Church Estab- lishment during the present Parliament. Mr. Chamberlain has frequently stated that he is personally in favour of Dis- establishment, not only in Wales and Scotland, but also in England, and whenever the proper time comes to give prac- tical effect to his opinions he will be prepared to take his part In the setttement of this great question. In the mean- time he does not consider it necessary either to vote or speak on the occasion of an abstract resolution, which can have no immediate practical effect —Yours obediently, WILLIAM WOODINGS." "All flesh is grass," but some people display more green- ness than others. Why is it absurd to talk about the "apple" of your eye ? 1 Because, having two, they are a pear. A shoprnan recommending a piece of silk to a lady for a gown said, "Madam, it will wear for ever, and make a petticoat afterwards." "What are you in here for?" asked the visitor at the penitentiary. "'Cause I was put in," growled the prisoner, savagely. " Yer didn't thiek I come in here 'cause I liked it, did yer ?" Old Farmer (to young ditto) : What do you feed your pigs with ?—amateur Farmer: Corn.-0. F.: In the ear ? A. F. (in disgust) : No, in the mouth. When a man reaches the top of a staircase and attempts to take one step higher, the sensation is as perplexing as if he had attempted to kick a dog that wasn't there. Rich uncle to his physician: "So you think there is hope for me ?"—" Not only that, but I can assure you that you are out of danger."—" Very well; I wish you would inform my nephew, but break the news gently to him." THE IRREPREBSIBLE AGAlN.—Bobby: You've got a cold in your head, have you ?—Dude (making a call on Bobby's sister) : Yes, a verwy bad cold—B.: Then sister told me story.—D.: ft Told you—ah--a storwy ?—B.: Yea; she said you hadn't nothin' in your head. SHE DIDN'T HEAR HIM SAY IT.—" Does your wife talk 1 in her sleep ?" asked one married man of another one day when they were comparing notes. "I don't lie awake to see," replied the heartless husband; "but she talks all the rest of the time, so I rather guess she does." A GOOD, KIND SISTER.—SmaII brother: Where did you get that cake, Annie ?—Sruall sister: Mother gave it to me ? —Small brother: Ah ! she always give yam more than me.— Small sister: Never mind; she's going to put mustard plasters on us when we go to bed to-night, and I'll ask her 1 to let you have the biggest. Nice young man, lecturing to a Sunday school: Now is there any little boy or little girl who would like to ask any questions?. Well, little boy, I see your hind ; you needn't snap your fingers. What question would you like to ask? —Small boy: How much longer is this jawin' going to last? Two INTERESTING TIME PIECES.—A lady who has been , abroad was describing some of the sights of the trip to friends. "But what pleased me as much as anything," she continued, "was.the wonderful clock at Strasburg." "Oh, how I should love to see it," gushed a pretty young woman in pink. "I am so interested in such things. And did you see the celebrated watch on the Rhine, too ?" A WomAtes QunsrioNt —" Did you say or did you not say, John, what'l said Ton said? Because Walt said you said you never said what I said you said. Now, if you did sly that you did not say what I said you said, then what did you Fay ? " "What are you reading, Mamie ?" said Mr. Clamwhooper to his daughter, aged thirteen. "Only one of these French novels, pa." "You should not do that." "0, I'm not reading it for my own amusement. It's my painful duty to examine it. I'm just looking through it to see if it is a proper book to have lying around where mamma might pick it up and read it."—.Texas Siftiays. ELEGANCE OF SPEECII.—A teacher at an evening school had before her a class in which were many very rough lads. "Suppose," said the teacher, "I should. say, 'Look out, boys—here comes the police!' Would that be proper?" There was a silence. Finally a little fellow said, " No'm— that wouldn't be right." " Well," inquired the teacher, "how should it be said? " "Cheese it, cullies ; here comes a cop ! " was the reply. Sheridan was one day annoyed by a member of the House of Commons who kept crying out every few minutes, "Hear, hear!" Daring the debate he took occasion to describe an opponent who wished to play the rogue, but had only sense enough to act the fool. "Where," he cried, with great em- phasis—" where hall we find a more foolish knave or a more knavish fool than he ? " " Hear, hear! " shouted the troublesome member, as usual; whereupon Sheridan turned round, and, thanking the honourable gentleman for the prompt Information, sat down amid a general roar of laughter. It was a case of breach of promise. ?The defendant was allowed to say a word in his own behalf. "Yes," he said, " rkissed her almost continually every evening I 'called at her house." Lawyer for plaintiff : "Then you confess it?" Defendant: "Yes, Ido confess it; but I had to do it." Lawyer: "You had to do it! Whet do you mean ? " De- fendant: "That was the only way I could keep her from singing." The jury gave a verdict for the defendant with- out leaving their seats. It is said that the average Texas landlord usually manages to secure the toughest beef in the market. "Is there a carpet-beating establishment next door ?"1 asked a newly- arrived guest at an Austin hotel. " Not that I ever heard of," said the landlord. Well, then, you must have a black- smith's shop in the cellar. Do You shoe horses down in the cellar ?" pursued the guest. "Why, no, stranger! What makes you think so?" asked the landlord. "What's all that pounding, as if there was a boiler factory in full blast, or some coopers were driving down the hoops of a wooden cistern ?" said the guest. " Oh, that ? Why, that's the cook pounding the-beefsteak for breakfast !" answered the landlord. " Rooza ME !"—A brave little Scotch lad, about eight years old, had misbehaved himself so far as to strike a lad nearly double his age, for which he was taken into custody. The next day he was brought before the bailie. On the lad's mother being called, she was asked if she could not keep her boy from such disgraceful acts; to which she re- plied," Weel, your worship, I'll look better after him in the ' time to come; but at the same time I canna see hoo my laddie, only eight years old, could beat a laddie near as mild ; again." The eight-year old, thinking his mother was Making him out to be of small account, convulsed the Court with laughter by exclaiming, "Reese me, mither, rooze me, and I'll thump twa softies like him ! ' A PHILADELPHIA CANARD —A New York shoeblack attracts trade by distributing cards that tell how nicely he shines shoes in the following simple Bostonese language: Pedal teguments artistically illuminated and lubricated for the infinitesimal remuneration of five cents. Antiquated teguments (pedal or superpedal) expurgated judiciously and resuscitated with expedition for nominal compensation. Of the innumerable foretastes of heaven enjoyed by every patron I would simply state: From the eventuation of the operation even to its ultimate successful completion the patron reclines superincumbent to cushions which a Sybarite might envy, in a superlatively luxurious attitude in which the horizontal and perpendicular are gracefully blended." Last week a strapping negro woman was up before an Austin judge, charged with unmercifully beating her boy, a I saddle-coloured imp. "I don't understand how you can have the heart to treat your own child so cruelly." "Jedge, has you been a parent of a wafiess yaller boy like dat ar cub of mine?" "Never, no never," ejaculated the judge with great vehemence, getting red in the face. "Den don't talk." There was such a sensation in court that the judge had to ' call "next" four or five times, and to find a man who said "hardly ever" five dollars, before order was restored. "Do TOR know this woman ?" asked a lawyer of a negro who had been summoned to give evidence. "Yes, Bah, I knows her." "Do you know her very intimately?' "No, I sale, karn't say dat I do." "How long have you known , her." "Wall, I got 'quainted wid her short time before I married her." "She's your wife, then ?" "Yes, sah, , sorter." "Thought you did not know her intimately ?" " Dat' a what I jaekerlated." "I don't understand, then, how she can be your wife." "Wall, yer see, sah, she longs ter de chat oh, de singin' s'ciety, de sistors o' de sacred I broom, de daughters o' Ham, an' two or three little side- shows. Er 'oman what is kep' so busy, sah, ain't got no time tor fool er roan' home."

ALLRGED FRAUD EY A VISCOUNT.— At the Old Bailey, London. on Saturday, before the Common Sergeant, Vis- count Hinton George Alcock and William Wright were charged with oonspiracy to defraud various tradesmen and to (Main goods by false pretences. Mr. Montagu Williams, in opening the case for the prosecutian. said it appeared that Lord Hinton had taken a place called Grove House, Lewisham, and had thence, with the other defendant, sent orders to tradesmen in all directions for goods of every de- scription.—On Monday, further evidence was adduced for the purpose of showing that all the defendants were-acting in concert. The Common Serjamt said he should tell the jury that the counts imputing fraud had not been supported, and he should only leave the conspiracy counts to them. The jury were afterwards addressed for the defence, and the trial was adjourned. AN Emenßse TRAIN HORBER.—A DESPERATE ENCOUN- TER.—New York telegrams report a desperate affray upon the Rock Island Railway on Saturday night. The train was near Joliet, Illinoie, about midnight. when the conduc- tor entered the United States Express Company's car, and was horrorstruck by the sight that met his eyes. The Ex- press agent was lying dead, having been beaten to death with a poker, after making a terrible struggle with his murderers, evidence of which was afforded by the confusion of the con- tents of the car. The furniture and fittings were broken to pieces, and the floor and sides of the car were bespattered all ever with blood. The dead man's bands were tightly I clenched • one held a lock of black hair, and tbe other a lock of red hair. The thieves had evidently feared to raise an alarm by firing a revolver, and had, therefore, recourse to a poker They had taken twenty thousand dollars out of the cash boxes, and forty peck-ages of jewellery, and with this booty bad leaped from the train while it was in metion; and so made their escape. MARRIED WOMEN AND TRADESMEN. IMPORTANT CASE. A somewhat important case to tradesmen was heard by the St. Helens magistrates on Monday. A married woman named Ann M*Clory, of 8, Twyford-street, Parr. appeared to answer a summons charging her with obtaining goods by false pretences from Saul Tuinin, a general dealer. carrying on business in Shaw-street. alr. 'Ailey appeared to support the. information. He re- marked that it mieht be an ungracious task to prosecute the mother of a fafnily for an offence which might end in her separation from them, bat that was an offence which was rapidly on the increase, this obtaining geeds' by married women, who represented that they were authorised by their husbands. but when the payments fell in arrear and the husband appeared in the County Court his plea was invari- ably that he had not authorised his wife to pledge his credit. Early in December last the defendant went to Mr. l'umin's shop for a pair of blankets and a quilt. The pro- secutor had had earlier transactions with the woman, and was not altogether satisfied, and declined to let her have the goods unless her husband was present, or until he received a note from him. The defendant then went away, but she returned with the following note, purporting to have been written by her husband 8, Twyford-street, Parr. Mr. Tumin,—Please let use have a pair of blankets and a quilt, and send the bill by my wife, and obljge, Thomas M`Clory." The prosecutor let her have the goods, and later on. the payments falling into arrear, the husband was summoned to appear at the County Court to answer the prosecutor's claim for 325, the value of the geode supplied. At the court, on the 24th February, the defendant's husband swore on oath that he had not written the order, nor had he au- thorised anyone to write it. The judge adjourned the case for a fortnight for the attendance of Mrs. M'Clery. The defendant then admitted that the note was not written ley her husband, but that she got one of her boys, alto named Thomas, to write it. This fact, Mr. Riley contended, would not exculpate the accused. A summons had also been issued against Thomas M'Clory, jun., hut it was very doubtful whether there was such a pereon in existence. That, how- ever, was not material to the case, as the order was not written by the defendant's husband with the intention of authorising Mr. Tnenin to part with the goods.—Mr. Tnmin then gave evidence corroborating Mr. Riley's statement. He added that at the County Court the defendant's husband said on oath that the note was not written nor authorised; to be written by him ; and that Mrs. M'Clory on a later 1 occasion swore that it was not written by her husband, and I that she got the goods without his knowledge. Had it not been for her bringing that note and representing that it came from her husband he would not have let her have the goods.—Defendant : Didn't I tell you that the goods were not for me, but for my son Thomas and his wife ?—Prose- cutor : You never said anything about your son Thomas, nor did I knorr that you had a son.—lsaac Plumbeig, Mr. I Tannin's partner, deposed to being present when the defen- dant came lute the shop and preserving the note purporting to come from her husband.—P.C. Ratcliffe stated that when he served the summons upon the defendant he asked her where her son was and she replied that he had got married and gone away. He asked her where he had gone to and she said she did not know. He had been on duty in the neighbourhood of the defendant's house far nearly four years, but he had never heard of the son Thomas referred to.—Defendant was committed for trial at the sessions.— The Clerk : Do you want ta go out en bail P—Defendant (indignantly) : No, sir, I don't want bail. I will go. I have never reaped the benefit—She was then removed below. As the sessions do not commence until the 20th prox, the ac- cused will be incarcerated for five weeks.

One of Mr. Gladstone's proposals A WORKING-MAN. is to bay out all the lastdlords at a cost of something , --- like £150,000,000 sterling, which money is to be raised on a loan guaranteed by England. That is the proposal which Mr. Chamberlain cannot approve. He will not see the honest British tax- payer saddled with this cruel burden for the benefit of the Irish landlord. Therefore he retires from the Cabinet. All this:is very well, very clever, delights the Times, and raises the spirits of the Tories. Last night the Speaker entertained at dinner the members of the late Government, and 'Subsequently Mrs. Peel held a reception, at which there was a mixed assembly of members of the House of Com- mons. Lacking the glory of the gold braided uni- forms of Ministers, the scene was a little less gor- geous than that of a fortnight ago. Notwithstand- ing that, ir R. Cross, in spectacles and the red rib- bon of his order, did his best to lend grace and colour to the scene. Still it was very striking, and the gathering comprised some of the best known faces in the House of Commons.
OUR NATIONAL CHURCH.

Sr,—l ask the favour of a little space in your valuable journal to reply to Mr. liix's strictures upost me with re- spect to " Our National Church and Dieestablishment." Mr. Dix considers a lecture upon ,Church reform—as opposed to Disestablishme,nt—not the happiest occasion on which to give an cpinion on the subject, and that the seconder of the vote of thanks " went some little out of his way " to state that he favoured the scheme of the lecturer, and why. I think that the occasion was most happy, and in my direct way. However, since Mr. Dix could listen to Mr. Tuck-well and remain ignorant of his views, I cannot be sur- prised at ray being beyond Mr. Dix's comprehension, just as lam also beyond that of the Church. Can Mr. Dix imagime a Liberationist advocating Mr. Tuckwell's plan? If he can, I cannot, any more that I cin imagine Dogmatic Christians, putting their Dogmas into a secondary place in order to make their religion first arid foremost. The National Church is fore. d to do this practically, but not theoreti- c illy. by the simple historical accident that three" schools of thought," as Mr. Dix euphemistically puts it, or three sects, as they are, in fact, have grown up together within her borders, viz, the Catholic, the Calvinistic, and the liberal Thinkers, or High, Low, and Broad. The same different ,chools of thought exist outside tile Church as Roman Catholic, Calvinistic more or less diluted, and Unitarian or (to borrow a title from the Chris- tian World) unattached. Inside the church, Mr. Dix and I, with many others, keep them in something like harmony through the strong arm of the law. They hold the "National Church," and must obey the national will. Out- side the church their intercourse is almost nil, and Mr. Dix and I have no control over them to make them keep the peace. Inside the church, where Christian feeling is not strong enough, gentlemanly feeling (often a fair substitute or at least imitation) makes a Calvinist, eg , much more civil than his creed. The creed announces 13 times every year that the heretic will "without doubt perish everlast- ingly." The Calvinist established priest, when reading the burial ssrrice over the heretic, expresses a charity which cantradicts the creed. The Celyieist outside the church has no such restraining influence. If he abstains from open udeness to the heretic, he quietly' boycotts him none the less, and does his best to give said heretic some taste here of what he is going to get there. Now, Mr. Dix wants me who now, with many others, am a ruler of the church, to make the bigots inside the church as free as those outside the church, but with a much greater endowment. To me it is a simple rule of three sum. If the Irish church secured ten million?, having hut a fraction of the people at her back, how many millions will the English Church secure, having more than half the people in more or lees active sympathy with her? (Mr. Gladstone says 90; Mr. Arnold 61 ; "Reformers' Almanac," page 64.) When freed, she will still be the richest church in Europe. Bigotry will run riot, and under it her religion will be trampled out. If Mr. Dix deuhts this, let him read the Huddersfield chapel case, and he will doubt no more.

It is to be hoped that the Earl of Poulett will live yet another year. Should he die before March, 1887, very disagreable circumstances would arise. In such case it would be necessary to go to one of her Majesty's prisons in order to hail the heir of this ancient earldom. The present Viscount Hinton has been sentenced to a term of one year with hard labour, upon *conviction of a charge of obtaining money under false pretences. The sentence is a very heavy one, for with these shorter terms of im- Drisonraent the labour is increased and the food is less generously: supplied. The whole story, apart from Lord Hinton's latest adventure, is a very remarkable one. The present 'Earl of Poulett married nearly forty years ago the daughter of a pilot at Lamport. Tho marriage took place on the 23rd of June, 1849, and on the 15th of December in the same year a son and heir was born. The young Viscount was sent to college, but does not seem to have taken kindly to the opportunities provided for him. Honourably desirous of earning his own living, he dropped his title, assumed the name of Mr. Cosman, and ob- tained an engagement at the Surrey Theatre as a clown and professional pantomimist. Here he made the acquaintance of a Miss'.Shippey, a ballet dancer. whom he married, and who in due time provided the illustrious earldom with another heir in the person of the Honourable William Henry George, *born 1870. When the present Lord Poulett dies, the unhappy nobleman now languishing in prison will be privileged to sit in the House of Lords and make laws for us. Mr. Horace Davey, the new Solicitor-General, is like the late Conservative Attorney-General, a teeto- taller, and is a shining example of what teetotallism may do for a man. As I incidentally mentioned the other week, he has at the bar the reputation of be- ing the most tremendous worker of the day. lie. can do with an incredibly small amount of sleep. Lord Brougham had this faculty, and living to be eighty-seven really existed much longer as compared with men who require eight hours sleep of the twenty-four. Mr. Horace Davey, drinking only water or tea, has been known to work forty-eight hours at a stretch. How much longer he could keep it up supposing he took a little wine no one can say. In a few days more—unless in the meahtime the political question should become not merely burning but scorching—we shall find ourselves tangled in the silly web of "the divided skirt." Lady Har- berton has made up her mind that she will teach ladies how to make up their materials, and that petticoats must henceforth be worn cleft. She and her supporters 'are to have a great meeting next week. There will be an interesting lecture, which 'will be the more interesting because model cos- tumes will be exhibited at it. They will not only be exhibited but they will be worn. The divided skirt will be filled. But Lady Harberton, appar- ently brave, is after all timid. No men are to be admitted to hear these counsels of wisdom, or to see these models of costume. This is surely a mis- take, for if the costumes pleased the men they would soon enough please the women. If the ladies who support this measure are too timid to appear in the dresses they advocate, Lady Harberton ought to engage costume models to wear these model costumes.

• Mr. Dix may now perchance understand why I should sympathise with Mr. Tuckivell's plan. If the church can he brought to do what our congregation (e g.) at Cairo. street has done for two hundred years, viz., live an unbroken religious life with modified ritual and changing creed—and this is Mr. Tuckwell's ideal—l should much prefer it. It is true Christian feeling translated into true Christian deed. Love of God and love of one's neighbour make up the Christianity of Christ. And to this Mr. Tuckwell will hive to convert not only the three sects within the church, but their correlatives outside. I gladly own that the religious influence of the church has increased of late years, and that her dogmas are kept much more in the second place than they used to be. I sympathise too warmly with that re- ligious influence lightly to wish to disturb it. At all events, it disturb it I must. I prefer approaching the question of disestablishment, kc., as a politician pure and simple and not as a member of a society the bitter spirit of which be- trays too much the taint of former rivalries defeated, and of former wrongs resented and unredressed.—l am, sir, yours truly, RICHARD FILCHER.

ALARMING ?AA' LWAY ACCIDENTS AT GLASGOW —The Glasgow Underground Railway, which runs beneath the city from east to west, and was only opened on Monday, was on Thursday the scene of a serious collision. A passenger train drawn up at .Finnieston station was run into by another passenger tram which, by a supposed failure of the "block" system, had been allowed to approach. The trains were not mach damaged, but several passengers received in- JOl2lCe being cut about the head and greatly shaken One case is regarded AS serious. Abcut the same time another but ?lighter collision occurred between a passenger train end some goods waggons at the junction of the Under- ground and North British lines.

SOCIAL EQUALITY.

Sir,—T am afraid I was a little too positive when I expressed the opinion that evolution is utterly fatal to communistic theories. I ought, perhaps, to have added "or communism is utterly fatal to evolutionary theories." Evolution affirms that living things, human beings included, because of their tendency to increase in numbers, so press upon the means of subsistence that a dire struggle for existence takes place in which inferior types and races are gradually elimi- nated and those better adapted to their surroundings are preserved. Communism, on the other hand, asserts that if men would only live together in the communistic fashion, each would be supplied according to his wants. Nothing 'could be snore contradictory than these two theories of human life. If the Communist is right and has his way, the " struggle for existence" ceases and each is supplied according. to his wants. If the evolutionist is right, it is impossible for each to be suppliel according to his wants, because there is a struggle for existence in which all are nbr umeo7lt ti nessif usa that gs is lellls.s minde qiu- eatl abnormal,esM r esrdo. ebelievesrnCeccheeapptioirinvacebonc4 with, evolutiona f l ex andi bil i ct vo mo anntrdarciaetsh.olTicrtuhlyattihtisadis- th the latest product of evolution. In his last letter Mr. Chapman condescends to give proof. In order to accurately appreciate the value and force of this proof it would be well to keep clearly in mind the nature of the case Mr. Chapman is endeavouring to make out. It is not that it is only possible but highly desirable that human beings should live in a state of communism, each working according to his or her ability, and each sharing of the produce of that work according to his or her needs. The vast majority of men, taking into consideration their own nature and the conditions under which they live, scout the very possibility of such a mode of life, and amongst the hundreds of millions of inhabitants of the earth not a single nation, large or srnall, with any claim to civilisation, has adopted it. Surely, under these Circumstances, all must agree that proof of a most convincing character is required to substantiate a case like that of Mr. Chapman. And what is his proof? That in the State of New York there is a small society, numbering 145 males and 161 females, living according to the principles of communism and practising the mysterious art of "stirpiculture "—in other words a community little more than half as populous as a local insti- tution in which:the inmates labour according to their capacity and receive according to their wants, namely, the WO. house. Was ever so mighty a superstructure raised upon so minute and frail a foundation? If Mr. Chapman, with proof of this kind, Can convince anyone that it is possible for seven or eight hundred millions of human beings, or even thoie of a single nation, to live after the communis- tic fashion it would say much for his persuasive powers. After that he would not hive much difficulty in demonstrat- ing bow a Pyramid might be made to stand on its apex, or a church on its weathercock. But having, as it were, put himself into the witness bex it is pe9niseible to cress-examine Mr. Chapman. One would like to know, for instance, how it is that this "Oneida Community" has only increased its numbers by about 150 pets)ns in .30 years. Is it because outsiders ao not take ,

It is quite a trite aphorism to say that there is no greater mistake made than that of indiscriminate alms giving, for to that the increase of pauperism and mendicity is largely due ; therefore no relief should be given without due investigation, unless under circumstances of great emergency. it is believed that if this course were universally adopted, the professional beggar and the here- ditary ptuper (although they will ever form integral parts at the human family) will rapidly diminish under the fierce surveillance of some such organisation—but there are many generous, thoughtful people, who are of opinion that the existing parochial and congregational machinery for the distribution of alms would, if strengthened, prove quite equal to present and prospective emergencies, instead of cal- ling into existence an "Organisation society" with a high- sounding name and its repulsive machinery of red tape, and inquisitorial officialiem, creating difficulties and delays which would materially mar the apparent usefulness, and consti- tute no adequate) substitute for the active exeecise of that personal charity which does so much to soeth and bless mankind. div.head: TORY PARSON.
div.p: A TORY PARSON.

Sir,—From time to time the question as to whether par- sons should interfere with the politics of the day comes to the front, and has before now been diecus4ed with no incon- siderable amount of feeling. We in Warrington have at last got so used to the article that not a man amongst us but would be sorry to lose the gem we have in our midst. It is not at all necessary that the cobbler should stick to his last, or that the parson should be confined to his pulpit. Let them both strike out boldly ; a fert may be gainers thoreby. I, for instance, consider myself indebted to the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton for his most recent enunciations. lie has contrived, most innocently, I should think, to firmly ground me, in one or twe questions wherein, I am afraid, I was somewhat weak.

I have been labouring for some years to reform the church ; of course, as one " outside her borders." This Mr. Carleton tinds " gratifying." Of the " Church's Catholicity " we all lave ample testimony, and, as if to make doubly sure of all that "The Church Review " says when it charges everybody " with "screaming for re- form," he rushes into print in loving and endearing terms respecting the Radical parson, Mr. Tuckwell, dreading lest this gentleman's utterances are "calculated to bring religion itself into contempt." I thought there was something amiss the night we had Mr. Tuckwell here. The church with so " catholic " a disposition, whose "ancient creed " has so "wide a basis of comprehension," had evidently decided to boycott the Radical parson, for not a local clergyman was present to greet their fellow-worker in their Master's Cause.

By the way, Mr. Editor, it is rather strange that all our Church parsons in Warrington are Tory. There must be something peculiar about the air; Tory parsons, Tory pub- licans, Tory brewers, and a Tory M.P. brewer, and all in the bargain. Perhaps "vested:interests" has something to do with it? Who can say? To return to our own particular Tory parson, Noncon- formists will be surprised to learn that tkey have " elected to build upon a much narrower and more exclusive founda- tion" than the one offered to them by the Church of Eng- land. A statement like this is calculated to take away one's breath. Does the rev, gentleman know anything about Church history? I should recommend him to have five minutes' conversation with any tolerably well educated lad In the town, and it may help him to got rid of his "crot- chets and "cultivate breadth" himself.

The only sensible passage given by Mr. Carleton is the one that so signally proves that, intolerant in the past, the Church will be intolerant in the future' should it have the power. It is "illusory" to suppose that it "would be pos- sible so to construct the Church of England that any, and every body, whatever their views and opinions, might find in it common ground and equal membership." Tiue enough, it is illusory to suppose that a Church ministered to by the " dregs" of our Universities, a Church that missss no opportunity for fulminating its decrees against all and every attempt at placing before the people truthful and helpful intellectual enjoyment, can ever find "common ground" for the "constituent elements" of which society is made of to meet upon. It is possible Mr. Tuckwell may not be so much " in the clouds on ecclesiastical matters" as Mr. Carleton thirks. The "writing on the wall" was plainly to he discerned during the last election, and but that the parson and the squire used their base influence to intimidate the agricultural labourer, the result would have been more striking than it is in the present House of Com- mons.

Mr. Carelton is pleased to point to Mr. Tuckwell "as the gentleman who advised the working-man to make promises, and then plei.se themselves whether they kept them." This is quite true; it is also true that such advice would have been worthless, had the working-men loved or even respected the church parson. Can there be any doubt that such advice was needed ? I have now before me numbers of cases, culled from the public press, of Liberal Church of England clergy- men boycotted because of their out-epokennes3. A Lincoln- shire rector, the Rev. J. C. Edwards, writes Owing to my views and writings on Chnrch mattlrs, I ant as lonely as my sea-girt parish, ostracised by Tory squires and clerical bigots." When Mr. Carleton talks of "breadth of creed "he should not forget that the people are sure he and his church are lacking in breadth of humanity. In Warrington at the present time a poor man walks the street because he could not say " yes "to his clerical employer. Another, a known supporter of Mr. Bradlaugh, had to make his choice between canvassing for a Tory brewer and losing his situation. Worse than all this even;the trade depression is made to minister to the bad, brutal desire of the Church to gain adheremts. Money subscribed by the philanthropic is guided, wherever possible,:into channels leading to the pas- sive support of the Church and State.

I would ask Mr. Carleton what has he or his party to place against the educational lectures of the Ce-operative Society ? As a truthful man, he must answer—nothing. The Co-operative Hall is open to them; let them bring something different than Church Defence lecturers down. Surely they have men amongst them, men able to refute Mr. Tuckwell's Utopian ideas, and who could lay- bare the fallacies contained in the lectures. If this were -done, then Mr. Carleton could again invite the clergy daugh- ters, and would feel at liberty to release his brother clergymen from the painful position of having to boycott a fellow Christian. Mr. Tuckwell in his advice to working-men accepted the least of two evils. In his lectures to working-men he sketches his colleagues as they are. Bishop Ryle tells us the parson goes through "a cold formal round of Sunday services,' and that the people are neglected; they "are like sheep without a shepherd." As Mr. Richards says, the parson's time is taken up with "the perversion of Dissenters." CLIFFORD DIX.
