filir,—The Ladies Sewing Class met every day during the week in the Council Chamber at the Town Hall, where they have been engaged in cutting out and making up gar- ments of various kinds for both men' women, and children, and by so doing have made many a heavy heart light, and many a poor half starved shivering creature warm com- fortable, and clean. The recipients attend at the Drill Hill three times a week at fotr o'clock to take away the clothing, being first regaled with a wholesome tea. The following garments have been made and distributed t—Frocks and skirts, 135 ; underclothisg, skirts, cite., 'U; 30 pairs of stockings • four large woollen shawls ; two- boys' snits ; a quantity of left-off clothing; and 24 pairs of clogs. Contri- butions of left-off clothing and material hare been received from the following ladies :—Mrs. T. Carter, Palmyra-square, 24 yards of flannel, 24 yards of calico, and a parcel ot chil- dren's left-off clothing ; Mrs.. Clare, of Lovely-lane, baby's clothing ; Mrs. Mclver, left-off clothing; Mrs. a Craig, Wilderspool, ditto ; Mrs. J. B. Green, Wilderspool, ditto ; Mrs. Green, ditto ; Mrs. Knott, ditto ; Mrs. Bearnont, 80 tickets for coal. The following ladies have sent subscrip- tions for the sewing class :—Mrs. Jones, The Elms, £5 ; Migs Malie, £2; Mrs. J. M. Edelsten, £1 ' • Mrs. Adams, £1 is ; Mrs. J. And at this point I would wish most respectfully to warn the charitably disposed public against giving credence to certain preposterous statements which are being freely dis- seminated (as I have the best reason for believing) mainly by Oisappoioted and undeserving applicants for relief, who , could not themselves survive the crucial test of the " Relief Committee" and the Inquiry Officer, and who have re- venged themselves by making unfounded statements to the effect that they were relieving imposters ; and an illustra- tive case I hereby submit. A woman who had been refused relief by the Inquiry Officer came to me, and coreplained, that while she had been refused, she knew a woman who had been supplied with soup, bread, and clothes, whose husband was in receipt of £3 108 weekly wages. I at once promised , to give her £5. alld keep her confidence, if she would give me the name and ctdress of the inculpated woman and her hus- band. I think I need hardly say:that she utterly failed either to give the names or to identify cne or the other; and four other cases, not so bad as this appeared to be, which I have perseeaLiy investigated, and found to be also utterly desti-
It is stated that the Hon. Lyulph Stanley has taken Mr. Mundella's place on the Education Commission.

SCALDED TO rJEATH AT SUTTON. - Mr. HuBban3, deputy-coroner. held an inquest on Wednesday, at St. Helens Junction, on the body of Jane Giloohlv, three years of age, who lived with her parents in Rolling Mill-lane, and who died from the effects of being scalded. The child was left sitting in a chair near the fire while the mother went upstairs. be got off the chair, and in trying to get on again caught the handle of a pan of boiling water, which went over her. She was fearfully scalded, and notwithstand- ing the efforts of Dr. Casey death ensued. A verdict of " Accidenbal death" was returned.

A return just published *bows that the volunteer force numbers 224.012, an increase of 9 000 upon last year, C.E.T.S., HUTTON QUARRY BRANersr.—On Monday even• ing, the last meeting a he spason of this branch took place at the Mission school. The Rev. Canon Penrhya occupied the chair, and the capital programme was got to- gether by Mr. E. B. Williams. The room was thronged, and the proceedings opened with a piano solo by Miss Florence Wilde. Several songs were given by Miss Wilde. Miss Isabella Williams, Mr. E. B. Williams, and Mr. Henry Price, and were encored. There were twe duets, piano and violin, by Messrs. John Johnt3on and John Crosby; and Mr. Joseph Gydiatt gave two readings. An excdlent address was delivered by the Rev. W. Hunt. of Ravenhead, urging; all to join the total •abstinence Section of the :misty.

THE Snip CANAL BILL. OPPOSITION WITHDRAWN. On Wednesday boring operations in connection with Om Manchester Ship Caeal were conducted in the district known as Boardman's; Orchard which is situate near the Irwell between Xccles sad Barton. The opponents of the Manchester Ship Canal Bill have withdrawn their petitions in the Commons. The Bill passed the keferees on Thursday, and goes to the Chairman of Ways and Means as an unopposed measure. A. Londt.n correspondent says:—The threatened opposi- tion to the Manchester Ship Canal Billby the Corporatren of Liverpool, the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, and the London and North-Western Railway Com- pany has come to an end by the withdraws) of the petitions, deposited by them in the House of Commons, praying to be heard by counsel against the merits of the bill. This decision on the part of the oppo- nents was come te, it is believed, in consequence of the recent division on the second reading of the bill, and the hopelessness of inducing a committee to reject the bill after the decided opinion expressed by the House. It is, however, pnderstood that this action on the part of the petitioners will in ro way prejudice their right to oppose in the House of Lords, where every opposition will be offend to the passing of the bill. As these three petitioners were the only opponents to the bill, it will now pass unopposed its remaining stages in the House of Commons. The question of the loom siamdi of the petitionere to oppose the bi3l in any form which was to have been argued before the Court of Referees, will now be raised before the Select Committee in the House of Lords,

A Special timed/rig of the Liverpool Chamber of Com- merce was held at the offices, on Wednesday, the president (Mr. Elisha Smith) in the chair. After the re-election of the eice-presidents, treasurer, and committees, with the excep- tion of the Colonial and Foreign Committee, which it was agreed to abolish, as its duties were simply of a formal character, the Secretary read a letter which bad been re- ceived from Mr. Mundella, thanking the Chamber for the copy of their report whieh had been forwarded to him on the question of the Manchester Ship Canal.--The Chairman said the promoters of the bill bed waited upon Mr. Mun- della, and he 1)14 asked for information on the subject, and that Charntier had sent him a copy of their special report, the receipt of which he now acknowledged. After that a deputation was formed to wait upon Mr. Mundelln, of which be (the chairman) was one, and Sir Win. Forwood anether, besides fouhteen members of Parliament. After putting forward their views, they came away with the impression that they bad gained nothing, an circumstances very soon told them that they had made no impression) unan Mr. Ail undella, because be had taken the precise course which they preferred be should not.—Mr. Coke asked what the result was, because he found there were different opinions about it. How did the matter stand now ?—The Chairman: That they were beaten on the second reading, and it was a donbtful matter whether they would have a lerus stowli before the committee as petitioning parties.—Mr. Coke said this was not refused as yet, and it appeared to be generally understood that the whole thing was passed and settled.—The Chairman said the bill had yet to go to the House of Lords, where he believed a very strong opinion was held on the Subject—This concluded the business.

THE MINISTERIAL CRISIS. The Press Association, telegraphing on Wednesday night, says :—There is very little change in the political situation. Up to the time of writing Mr. Gladstone had failed to convert either Mr. Cham- berlain or Mr. Trevelyan to his views in reterence to Ireland, and a compromise is as remote as ever. There has been much speculation as to the position of the President of the Local Government Board and the Secretary. of State for Scotland. The fact that both Ministers continue to perform their usua departmental duties is. adduced as proof positive that they have no intention, of leaving Mr. Glad- stone, and. much reliance is. placed on state- ments elicited from them, in their official capacity to the effect that they have not resigned. It is quite true that 'in the official. sense they have not resigned, but, as already. intimated, they have taken a step which. must almost inevitably lean to their early retirement from. the Ministry. It is more than probable that neither Mr. Chamberlain's nor Mr; Trevelyan's letter to Mr.. Gladstone con- tained a direct mention of. resignation. Of one !thing, however, we are assured—that an intimation was given in the clearest language that it was im- possible for the writers to support the Irish scheme shadowed forth by the Premier at the Cabinet Coun- cil of Saturday. • An intimation of this nature is capable of no other interpretation than that they cannot continue to hold office.. Either Mr. Glad- stone must abandon the proposals to -which Mr. Chamberlain and Mr. Trevelyan take objection, or they must consent to waive their objections, neither of which contingencies is at present prob- able. Mr. Charaberlain.ha,s been busily employed conferring with his political,friends. In the course of the afternoon Mr. Jesse Collings put in an ap- pearance at the House for the first time since the adjournment of the Ipswich election petition in- quiry, an had a long interview with his chief in his private room. Sir Charles- Dilke was also in , consultation with Mr. Chamberlain for a consider- able period. We understand that Mr. Chamberlain will attend the 7/aext Cabinet Council. If a modes vivendi has not been arrived: at in the meanti me the acceptance of the right hon. gentlernarks resig- nation may be expected; immediately afterwards. , Mr. Chamberlain and -Mr,..Trevelyan had conversa- -1 tions with the Premier .on Thursday. We are infor- med, however, that so far all attempts at a compro- mise have 'failed. In the course. of the afternoon : the President of the Local Government Board had an interview with Mr. Bright._ The President of the Local Government Board and the Secretary for Scotland. were in their usual places on the Treasury. Bench on Thursday evening. During questions Mr. Trevelyan crossed to where Mr. Chamberlain was sitting; and the two Ministers entered into an earnest and' animated conversation, which lasted half an hour. Afterwards Mr. Cham- berlain proceeded to his private room, where he was closeted for some time with Lord R. Churchill. Several communicatiOns have passed between the Premier and his two colleagues, but none of them has yet been induced to alter his decision. The in- terview between Lord Randolph Churchill and Mr. Chamberlain, was mach commented on. After leaving the President of the Local Govern- ment Board, Lord. Randolph Churchill. remained in the lobby some minutes in. conversation with Mr. Marjoribanks, one of the-Liberal whips. Ml... Chamberlain subsequently had a consultation ,in his private room with Mr. J. Powell Williams • and Mr.Williamlienrick, members for the Southern and Northern Divisions.o£Birmingham. When these gentlemen left he was joined by Mr. Jesse Collings, accompanied by whom he: left the House shortly before his usual dinner hour. Mr. Gladstone remained indoors the greater part of the day. He received no visitors, and proceeded about four o'clock to the. House of Commons. After question time an informal meeting of Ministers was held in the Premier's private room, to attend which Lords Spencer and Granville walked over from the Upper House. The Daily News understands that 120 millions is the' sum which figures in Mr. Gladstone's scheme as the amount of the guaranteed loan projected for ' the purchase of the interests of the Irish landlords. , Mr. Gladstone had hoped to have been able to make his statement expository of his Irish scheme next Thursday, but circumstances that have recently arisen will probably engender further delay. There was no change last night in the situation. ,
The Princess of wales appears to be gaining health and strength at Torquay after a relapse from which she suf- fered.

CHAMOR OF STBALING £ss.—Williaen Kennedy, ahas Captain Donaldson, a gentlemanly-looking middle-aged man, of military appearance, was charged at St Helens before Lieut.-Colonel W. W. Pilkington, at the Town Ball on Thursday, with stealing £55 from a dwelling-house at Rainford, the moneys of Dr. Andrew Murdoch. Dr. Mur- doch stated that about eight or nine weeks since, when be we* living at Bootle, prisoner and his wife went to take charge of the house; and three weeks mince they moved him to Rainford. On the 11th lost. witness went to the trunk in which he kept his money, and took out Me sovereign, leaving at least -.F.55 in the linen bag. He lecked the box and put the. key on the desk in the surgery. On Saturday he wanted his keys to take more money from the box, but they were not ,to be found. He broke open the box, and then foeand.that ' the bag and cash were gone. He then gave information to the police. When prisoner was at his house he had a full beard. Evidence was then given by P.S. Alexander Smith and Inspector Whittaker with regard to the ap- prehension of the prisoner at 51, Botanic-road, Edge-hill Liverpool, where he passed off as Captain Donaldson. Hero he had lived in first-class style, and lavishly spent money, giving the unsuspecting inmates of the house to helieve.he was a gentleman of means,.and heir to a large fortune. He had effected such a complete dis- , guise, having shaved off a heavy black beard, and alteredi ; his style of dress, that Sergeant Smith failed to recognise him. The apartments were searched, when about £ll of !thestolen money was found and taken possession of by the ;Police. He afterwards stated that he took the key of the , doctor's trunk from the surgery and unlocked it. The nri- , sonar made imputations against Dr. Murdoch, which the ; l'plyet.rate said were most abommable imputations, and the spirit in which it was given carried tixt lie with it, The pusoner was committed for tri4i.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

The Rev. Dr. Reeves, Dean of Armagh, bad been elected Protestant Bishop of Armagh and Clegter. Major Clayton, the Chief Constable of Carnarvon- shire, died on Friday morning, after an illness of a short duration.

Lord Richard Grosvenor's and Lord Kensington's peer- ages are gantted. The former takes the title Baron Stal- bridge,'and the latter B4rOn Kensington. Mr. Trevelyan, Lord Advocate, and the Scotch Solicitor- General, bad a long conference with the Scotch members, on Friday, respecting the Crofters Bill. The banquet to be given by the American residents in Paris to M. Pasteur, will take place on the 14th April, under the presidency of the United States Minister. The Settle and Carlisle Railway, which was blocked on Thursday through an immense snowslip, has been got clear. The Scotch express trains between Carlisle and Manchester were very little delayed on Friday. FALSB PLAYItid CARDS.—Acting upon the information furnished by the French Government, the Swi4s police have discovered at Berthond a large manufactory of false cards, which are made expressly for the purpose of cheating at play.

THE ST. BELENS RAILWAY.—Mr. Seton-Karr,. M.P., has consented to become cbairman of the new St. Helens Rail- way, by which St. Helens will be connected with the Che- shire Lines and a new route opened to .Manchestsr and the eastern, midland, and southern counties.

FALL OF HOVIES IN BIRMINGITAM.—On Friday morning great excitement was caused in Dale-end, one of the busiest thoroughfares in Birmingham, by the fall of two heu-aes, one a boot shop and the other a fried fish shop. Without the slightest warning the two houses fell in, a great quan- tity of the delfrrig falling into the street. 'lns premises were occupied, but the occupants had a marvellous escape.

THE PIMLICO MYSTZRY.—On Friday Mrs. Bartlett and the hey. George Dyson were again charged, at the West,- minster Police Court, with the murder of the husband of the first-named prisoner, by administering a dose of chloro- form under circumstances already recorded. Mrs. Matthews, who was a friend of Bartlett's, was the chief witness called. She was called to the Bartletts' residence by the receipt of a telegram from Mrs. Bartka, and when she got there MTS. Bartlett told her that she fell asleep about 12 oclock, with her arm around her husband's foot. She was awakened afterwards by feeling pain in her arm, and she than found her husband dead. She asked Mrs. Bartlet4a what he died of, and she replied she did not know ; there must be a post-mortem. Witness described the visit she paid to the house on the 6th January, when Mr. Dvson as d Mrs. Bartlett told him her husband would die soon. Mrs. Bartlett denied she had said so, and Mr. Dyson said "'Oh my God ;" and when he left he said "I am a ruined man."—Other formal wit- nesses were called, and the case was adjourned until Satur- day.

DOUBLE MUBDER IN FRANCE. The Exchange Company's Paris .eorrespondent says : A telegram from Beauvais, published here this morning, adds another to the many terrible crimes committed in France lately. A farmer named Breton, and his wife, both old people, were found murdered in their house, their heads being nearly severed from their b0,.-lies. The house was ransacked, and all the money and valuables stolen. EXTRAORDINARY BOILER EXPLOSION. Shortly before eleven o'clock on 'Friday forenoon a boiler explosion occurred at Accrington, doing n4nsi3erable damage and injuring one person. The boiler belongs to Mr. Thomas Myers. cab proprietor, and was used for driving a chopping machine. Shortly after half-past ten James Myers, son of the proprietor, went into the boiler-house to fire up, and while he was there the boiler exploded. It was blown through the roof, and shot up into the air like a rocket, passing over the Star Music Hall, crossing the river Bynd- burn; and slighting on the roof of a small building, which forms part of 'Messrs. Cueliffe's cotton works. The build- ing was completely demolisted, and the boiler was found standing on its end apparently little damaged. Had the boiler gone a yard further or a little to the right, where a large number of people were at work, the result must have been terrible. Young Myers, who was in the building when the explosion happened, was badly scalded, and is now being attended by medical men. Several persons had a miracu- lous escape.

div.head: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.
div.p: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.

- The House met at four o'clock. TEN. SUNDAY OPENING OF MUSEUIIe —Lord THUBLOW Moved that in the interests of religion and education, the British Museum, National Gallery, and other art and liter- ary collections in the metropolis should be opened on Sun- day. He put the question on the footing of its being the poor man's question, and that it had the support of the clergy and •Itoman Catholic priesthood. The opening of museums would, he argued, decrease Sunday drinking.— Lard MIDDLETON moved the rejection of the motion. He believed that the opening of galleries and museums would tend to secularise Sunday.—Lord BtaavvELL supported Lord Thurlow's motion. At present the English Sunday was mis-spent. He opposed the secularisation of Sunday on the model of the Continental Sunday, but favoured Ilstional enjoyment on Sunday.—Earl'Hanttowny strongly opposed the motion.—Earl GRANVILLB, whilst supporting the motion, trusted that thc..ir lordships would vote on non- party lines.—The House divided:: For the metion 76, against 62, majority 14. The House shortly afterwards adjourned. HOUSE OF COII.V.n.NS. The House met at four o'clock.

RAILWAY BOOKSTALLS. - Mr. T. P. O'CONNOR gave notice that on an early day he should call attention to the present ol*ctionable system of letting bookstalls at railway stations. MR. GLADSTONE AND THE TRIM QUESTION.

Mr. GIADSTONE, replying to Sir M. Beach, aaid he •had no change to announce as to the measures for Ireland. He heped to be able next week to name the day when he would make a statement. In the meantime;he advised the House, with regard to the rumours, to exercise a prudent reserve and wholesome scepticism as to the proposals to be made for Ireland. The House would agree with birn that it would not be wise to make a statement without at the same time being able to state that bills bad beau drawn for carrying those proposals into effect. He amared the House that not one day had been or would be lost in this matter. TUE LIABILITY or TRUsTEES.—On the motion for gbing Into Committee of Supply, Mr. GREGORY called attention to the position of trustees and executors liable to payment of duties to the Crown. He meved that a limitation in point of time should be applicable to liabilities for duties to the Crown.—Mr. DODDS seconded the proposal, and pointed out the hardship of trustees and others being called upon to pay at the time when it was impossible to recoup them- selves.—Mr. A. CONI,OR supported the resolution.—Mr. H. FOWLER thought it would be unwise anA impracticable to put such limit as was proposed upon liability for death duties. He therefore was compelled to oppose the proposal of Mr. Gregory.—Sir R. WEESTER thought a bona fide grievance had been proved that required redress.,—Mr. GLADSTOWR opposed the proposal, and said if hon. members would formulate a substantial proposal on this subject be would promise that it should receive the conoideration of the Government entirely in a practical sphit.--After a few observations from Sir M. Beach, the Proposal was with- drawn.

WAR -MAKING POWERS —Mr. H. ...14tcRARD then moved that in the opinion of the House it was not just now ex- pedient to embark in war contract engagements, involving grave responsibilities for the nation, and add territories to the empire without the knowledge of Parliament. He argued that the supposed check upon war-making in the fact that the Parliament held the power of the purse was purely illusory, for the reason that in most cases war had been made before Parliament had asked for the money.—Mr. PETER, RYLANDS Seconded the resolu- tion, and Mr. LTLeusroNE expressed gratification that on the present occasion the subject had been brought forward with the absence of charges of abuse of treaty-snaking power enjoyed by the Crown. He went with all the mover of the resolution said. about militaryism, but he thought that asking the House•to adopt the proposal was asking it to do an impossibility, and the resolution, if car- ried, might produce results the very reverse of those desired. —Lord R. CuracmiLL also opposed the, motion.—After some discussion, the motion to go into Committee of Supply was negatived by 112 to 108 amid loud cheers and some laughter.—A second division was taken on Mr. Richards' resolution as a substantive motion, when it was rejected by 115 to 109.

SERIOUS CITARS-E AGAINST A, RUNCORN POLICE' SERGEANT. Before Mr. Charles avnelds and Mr. James Handley, sC Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Abner Egerton, geant of police, stationed at Runcorn, was charged with unlawfully assaulting Daniel Gregory, a labourer.. The le'' fendant pleaded guilty—Mr. W. H. Churton, solicitor, Chester, who appeared for the complainant, remarked uporx , the painfulness of his duty, and said cases of that hind were extremely rare. Policemen carried out their duties with great deal of excellent temper, and he must say thavbe, i never met in his experience with .a case of a similar ehtt!se ; ter to the one the Beneh bad to decide that morning; . G-egory was a working-man, and on Saturday, the 3th 0 ' March, he went to a football match. On his way home be I° called at one or two public-houses, and had a pint of beer !. and one or two glasses of whiskey. He was nordrunit and was pursuing his way along Greenway-road wit-Wu' : creating a row when the sergeant, who was in plain clothe, E made some observation to the effect that Gregory vole ' studying economy. Gregory, in reply, said he did stnd9 economy. The sergeant, he would call witnesses to prove, i was drunk; and he said t 3 Gregory" You will lie.va come along with me; you are drunk." Gregory Pr,e- ' tested that he had done nothing, but Egerton tried to sea° hold of him. Gregory dodged *o one side, and Egerton, . simply from his condition, tumbled to the groundl picked himself up, and a struggle ensued between the men, during which they fell', Gregory being uppermost,..bt.lt the sergeant, who is a strong powerful man, succeeded T ; getting Gregory on his back, and placed the "snaps" on.br : wrists. The sergeant then draeged Gregory into the midd! of the road, and for forty minutes continued to twist 1.30 P wrist with tba "mine"' Gregory frequently screamedtvntb pain, and the bystanders asked a constable whe came. upon the scene to take the sergant ay/0'; Th. constable said he dare not interfere. _.,,n''' Inspector Millington : alertly afterwards arrived a nu.' the sergeant, with an oath, refused to let.. hiln take charge of the prisoner. On the way to the polino station the sergeant continued to twist the man's wrist; awl as he was walking up the steps, Egerton gave him a violent blow with the back of Es hand, which was "enough daze a man." Gregory was bleeding profusely from the wrist and head, and when Superintendent Leah saw his cor itition he discharged him, and had him taken to DrialaDone' gall's surgery, and be had been under the doctor's care Sitloo —Gregory showed his wrist to the Bench. It appeared tiP be in a very bad candition.—The Bench coesidered it n°. necessary to call witnesses, and Mr. Cburton agreede—The' . 4 defendant said that on the-occasion in question he bad been on duty from Friday afternoon until Saturday night, hal' ing been closely engaged in invesigating the supposedantir; der at Weston Point. On Saturday he had had no fecu' since half-past five in the morning, but during the day be, did take some stimulants, and was under the initence n' I drink. When he met Gregory in Greenway-road. the reati knocked him into the road, and he fell. Without any provc7 cation Gregory then commenced .to kick himeand he tog- him into custody.—Mr. Churton said be had Nenty of wit' neeses to contradict that statement.—The Chief Constable (Colonel Hamerslev). who was present in court, said before their worships passed judgment, he would like to remind them that besides the punishment the Bench might ioflino upon Egerton, the officer would have t 3 undergo anl punishment he (the Chief Constable) might.thank,it neces- sary to impose.—Tte Bench imposed a fine a..geand costar 9s 6d, or in default a month.

PRUDENTIAL ASSURANCE COMPANY, LIMITED, HOLBORN BARS, LONDON. Thirty-seventh Annual Report for the year ending 31st December, 1885. The Directors have much pleasure in presenting their report and accounts for the year 1885. The Assurance Fuhds have been increased doting the year by the sum of £990,345: namely, the Ordinary branch £232,425, and the Industrial Branch £757,920. The total assets of the company amount to £5.702 862. ortnINARY BRANCH. The number of policies issued during the yeir was 17,353, assuring the sum of £1,887,890, and producing a New Annual Premiam Income of £85,374. The Premiums of the year were £303,275. being an increase of £64,407 over the year 1884. The total itclease for the first four years of the quinquennium is 1162.018. The claims of the year amounted to £108,777. The number of deaths was 712, and 35 endowment assurances matured. The rate of expenditure of the bran= was little more than 10 per cent, on the premium income. The number of policies in force was 55,483. INDUSTRIAL BR.ANCH. The Premiums received during the year wfae £2,794,522. be- ing an increase of £150,0.06. The claims of the year amounted to £1,069,878. The number of deaths was 119,846. The nmnber of policies in force, including 36,671 tree policies, was 6,695,890. The Directors are happy to report that the duration a policies in this Branch is still ste•teilly increasing. The average duration of all policies now in existence exceeds five years. The rate of expenditure of the Branch upon the Premium Income shows a further reduction of more than one-half per cent. The Author of the above-mentioned work wishes to make a few remarks to persons who may apprehend that they are in the early stages or in an advanced state of disease. He would press upon them the necessity of not postponing a step on which their whole future health and happiness may be at stake, but to at once apply for competent and trustworthy advice, on which they can fully rely. These observations are not made with any intention of extolling his own abilities, as bets satisfied to let his reputation rest where it is, as be can fairly lay claim to having succeeded in reator- ing the blessings of health with all its glori- ous attributes to many who had been pro- nounced INCURABLE when they were in- duced to apply to him as a last chance, for them the most happy of chances. He therefore cannot close his eyes to these facts, that the remedies he uses have cured when many other's haci failed, nor do we mention it in disparage- ment of any of our Professional contempora- ries, but as plain unvarnished truths. It is a well known fact that many a e ruined through innorance and wrong treatment. From the daily observatisns ot the author, he can fully corroborate this. Myriads of broken-down, wretched invalids are constantly crowding upon his attention, whose misery and wretchednep are owing wholly or in part to the ignorance of previous medical advisers, and lie feels constrained to admonish invalids of this class to confide the treatment of their cases to none except those who devote their whole energy and abilities to the treatment of nervous and special maladies, and who give undoubted evidence of their superior qualifica- tions and fitness for the same.
